        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Rulers",
        title = "Six rulers who died in office in the 810s, counted by the year of their deaths",
        originalTitle = "Six rulers who died in office in the 810s, counted by the year of their deaths",
        author = "Modern compiler from standard dates",
        year = 810,
        summary = "A short program lists six rulers who died in office in the 810s and prints how many died in each year, and 814 and 820 each saw two deaths.",
        details = "The rulers are Pepin of Italy, Nikephoros I of Byzantium, Krum of Bulgaria, Charlemagne, the Tang emperor Xianzong and Leo V of Byzantium, and the program groups their death years. The years used are the usual dates of death, and 810, the year of Pepin's death, is the earliest of them.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as deaths_1810s.py.
            2. Run it: python3 deaths_1810s.py
        """,
        example = """
            deaths = [
                ("Pepin of Italy", 810),
                ("Nikephoros I", 811),
                ("Krum", 814),
                ("Charlemagne", 814),
                ("Xianzong of Tang", 820),
                ("Leo V", 820),
            ]
            by_year = {}
            for name, year in deaths:
                by_year.setdefault(year, []).append(name)
            for year in sorted(by_year):
                print(year, ":", len(by_year[year]), "death(s)")
            print("rulers in all:", len(deaths))
            print("years with two deaths:", [y for y in sorted(by_year) if len(by_year[y]) == 2])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 800 to 810: the years between the stages of Harun al-Rashid's succession plan, computed in Python and in C. */
val db124Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 124,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Abbasid",
        title = "The years between the stages of Harun al-Rashid's succession plan, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Succession years",
        author = "Harun al-Rashid",
        year = 802,
        summary = "The years between the stages of Harun al-Rashid's succession plan are printed by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The dates used are 792 for the first choice of al-Amin, 799 for the addition of al-Ma'mun, 802 for the Mecca arrangement and 809 for Harun's death, and the four spans printed are 10, 3, 7 and 17 years. The first two dates belong to the mainstream reading of the sources, and historians still debate that reading, so the figures show the arithmetic of the dates rather than settle the question.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as mecca.py, mecca.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### mecca.py
            EVENTS = [("first heir named", 792), ("al-Ma'mun added", 799), ("Mecca arrangement", 802), ("death of Harun", 809)]
            first, added, mecca, death = [year for _, year in EVENTS]
            print("years from the first heir to the Mecca arrangement:", mecca - first)
            print("years from al-Ma'mun's addition to the Mecca arrangement:", mecca - added)
            print("years from the Mecca arrangement to the death of Harun:", death - mecca)
            print("years from the first heir to the death of Harun:", death - first)
            ### mecca.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int first = 792, added = 799, mecca = 802, death = 809;
                printf("years from the first heir to the Mecca arrangement: %d\n", mecca - first);
                printf("years from al-Ma'mun's addition to the Mecca arrangement: %d\n", mecca - added);
                printf("years from the Mecca arrangement to the death of Harun: %d\n", death - mecca);
                printf("years from the first heir to the death of Harun: %d\n", death - first);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 mecca.py > python.txt
            cc -o mecca_c mecca.c
            ./mecca_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 800 to 810: the wolf, goat and cabbage crossing from Alcuin's problem book, solved in seven crossings and checked by a program. */
val db124Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 124,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Puzzles",
        title = "How the wolf, goat and cabbage crossing is solved in seven crossings, checked by a program",
        originalTitle = "De lupo et capra et fasciculo cauli",
        author = "Alcuin of York (attributed)",
        year = 800,
        summary = "The wolf, goat and cabbage crossing, Problem 18 of the Propositiones, is solved in seven crossings, and a short program checks that no bank is left unsafe at any step.",
        details = "The puzzle asks a man to carry a wolf, a goat and a bundle of cabbage across a river in a boat that holds him and one item, so that the wolf is never left alone with the goat and the goat never with the cabbage. The plan in the example takes the goat over first and brings it back once, and after every crossing the program checks the bank the man has just left.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as wolf_goat.py.
            2. Run it: python3 wolf_goat.py
        """,
        example = """
            def unsafe(bank):
                return ("wolf" in bank and "goat" in bank) or ("goat" in bank and "cabbage" in bank)

            PLAN = [
                ("goat", "right"),
                (None, "left"),
                ("wolf", "right"),
                ("goat", "left"),
                ("cabbage", "right"),
                (None, "left"),
                ("goat", "right"),
            ]

            banks = {"left": {"wolf", "goat", "cabbage"}, "right": set()}
            man = "left"
            every_step_safe = True
            for cargo, destination in PLAN:
                if cargo is not None:
                    banks[man].remove(cargo)
                    banks[destination].add(cargo)
                man = destination
                left_behind = "left" if man == "right" else "right"
                if unsafe(banks[left_behind]):
                    every_step_safe = False
            print("crossings:", len(PLAN))
            print("every bank safe:", every_step_safe)
            print("all across:", banks["right"] == {"wolf", "goat", "cabbage"})
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 124,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Japanese",
        title = "Japan's capitals from 710 to 810, the years each one served, summed and ranked",
        originalTitle = "Heijo-kyo, Nagaoka-kyo and Heian-kyo",
        author = "The Japanese court",
        year = 810,
        summary = "The Japanese capitals of Heijo-kyo at Nara, Nagaoka-kyo and Heian-kyo, counted from 710 to 810, held the court for 74, 10 and 16 years, which a short program sums and ranks.",
        details = "The court moved to Nagaoka in 784 and to Heian-kyo in 794, and in 810 Emperor Heizei tried to return to Nara, so the count stops there. The brief moves of the court between 740 and 745 are left out, and Heian-kyo is counted only up to 810.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as japan_capitals.py.
            2. Run it: python3 japan_capitals.py
        """,
        example = """
            CAPITALS = [
                ("Heijo-kyo at Nara", 710, 784),
                ("Nagaoka-kyo", 784, 794),
                ("Heian-kyo", 794, 810),
            ]

            years = {name: end - start for name, start, end in CAPITALS}
            for name, span in years.items():
                print(name, span, "years")
            print("total:", sum(years.values()), "years")
            longest = max(years, key=years.get)
            shortest = min(years, key=years.get)
            print("longest:", longest, years[longest], "years")
            print("shortest:", shortest, years[shortest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind

/** Cross-code piece of 790 to 800: three dates before Charlemagne's imperial coronation, the years between them computed in Python and in C. */
val db125Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 125,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Frankish",
        title = "Three dates before Charlemagne's imperial coronation, 796, 799 and 800, with the years between them in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Three dates before the coronation",
        author = "Charlemagne",
        year = 796,
        summary = "The Avar treasure of 796, the flight of Pope Leo III to Paderborn in 799 and the coronation of 800 are subtracted in Python and in C, and a script checks that both print the same spans.",
        details = "The spans printed are 3, 1 and 4 years, from the treasure to the flight, from the flight to the coronation, and from the treasure to the coronation. The dates are the usual ones, and the figures show only the arithmetic of those dates; they do not claim that the events were planned in this order.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as charlemagne.py, charlemagne.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### charlemagne.py
            DATES = [("Avar treasure at Aachen", 796), ("flight of Leo III", 799), ("coronation at Rome", 800)]
            treasure, flight, crown = [year for _, year in DATES]
            print("years from the Avar treasure to the flight of Leo III:", flight - treasure)
            print("years from the flight of Leo III to the coronation:", crown - flight)
            print("years from the Avar treasure to the coronation:", crown - treasure)
            ### charlemagne.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int treasure = 796, flight = 799, crown = 800;
                printf("years from the Avar treasure to the flight of Leo III: %d\n", flight - treasure);
                printf("years from the flight of Leo III to the coronation: %d\n", crown - flight);
                printf("years from the Avar treasure to the coronation: %d\n", crown - treasure);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 charlemagne.py > python.txt
            cc -o charlemagne_c charlemagne.c
            ./charlemagne_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 125,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Rulers",
        title = "Reign lengths of four rulers who held power in 795, summed and ranked",
        originalTitle = "Reign lengths in 795",
        author = "Offa of Mercia, Alfonso II, Dezong and Kanmu",
        year = 795,
        summary = "Four rulers in power in 795 reigned 141 years between them, and a short program prints each reign, the total, and the longest and shortest reign.",
        details = "Offa's reign ran from 757 to his death in 796, Alfonso II's from 791 to 842, Dezong's from 779 to 805, and Kanmu's from 781 to 806. The sums are arithmetic on these usual accession and death years, and they make no claim about how the four reigns were linked.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as reign_lengths.py.
            2. Run it: python3 reign_lengths.py
        """,
        example = """
            REIGNS = [
                ("Offa of Mercia", 757, 796),
                ("Alfonso II of Asturias", 791, 842),
                ("Dezong of Tang China", 779, 805),
                ("Kanmu of Japan", 781, 806),
            ]
            lengths = []
            for name, start, end in REIGNS:
                lengths.append((end - start, name))
                print(name + ":", end - start, "years")
            print("total:", sum(length for length, _ in lengths), "years")
            ranked = sorted(lengths, reverse=True)
            print("longest:", ranked[0][1] + ",", ranked[0][0], "years")
            print("shortest:", ranked[-1][1] + ",", ranked[-1][0], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db126Cross.kt

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 780 to 790: Greek-era years turned into AD years, as the Syriac date of the Xi'an stele requires, computed in Python and in C. */
val db126Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 126,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Syriac",
        title = "Greek-era years turned into AD years, as the Syriac date of the Xi'an stele requires, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Years of the Greeks",
        author = "Syriac church chronographers",
        year = 781,
        summary = "A Greek-era year changes to an AD year in the middle of the Syriac year, and a Python program and a C program print the same four conversions.",
        details = "The Syriac year begins in October, so dates from January to September take 311 off the Greek-era year and dates from October to December take 312 off. The Xi'an stele is dated in this era as 1092, which gives 781 for January to September, and the program checks four cases.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as seleucid.py, seleucid.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### seleucid.py
            def ad_year(greek_year, month):
                # the Syriac year starts in October, so October to December take the larger offset
                offset = 312 if month >= 10 else 311
                return greek_year - offset

            CASES = [(1092, 1), (1092, 11), (1098, 3), (1099, 10)]
            for greek_year, month in CASES:
                print("Syriac year", greek_year, "month", month, "is AD", ad_year(greek_year, month))
            ### seleucid.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int ad_year(int greek_year, int month) {
                int offset = month >= 10 ? 312 : 311;
                return greek_year - offset;
            }

            int main(void) {
                int cases[4][2] = {{1092, 1}, {1092, 11}, {1098, 3}, {1099, 10}};
                for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
                    printf("Syriac year %d month %d is AD %d\n", cases[i][0], cases[i][1], ad_year(cases[i][0], cases[i][1]));
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 seleucid.py > python.txt
            cc -o seleucid_c seleucid.c
            ./seleucid_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 325 to 787: the seven first ecumenical councils, from Nicaea I to Nicaea II, counted by city and by century in a short program. */
val db126Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 126,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Councils",
        title = "The seven first ecumenical councils, from Nicaea I in 325 to Nicaea II in 787, counted by city and by century",
        originalTitle = "Seven ecumenical councils",
        author = "The bishops of the Christian church",
        year = 787,
        summary = "The seven first ecumenical councils, from Nicaea I in 325 to Nicaea II in 787, are counted by city and by century in a short program that prints the 462 years between the first and the last.",
        details = "Constantinople hosted three of the councils, Nicaea two, and Ephesus and Chalcedon one each, and the program groups the seven by the century in which they met. Only Nicaea II falls in the 780s, and the year 680 given for Constantinople III is the year it opened, though it ended in 681.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as councils.py.
            2. Run it: python3 councils.py
        """,
        example = """
            COUNCILS = [
                ("Nicaea I", 325, "Nicaea"),
                ("Constantinople I", 381, "Constantinople"),
                ("Ephesus", 431, "Ephesus"),
                ("Chalcedon", 451, "Chalcedon"),
                ("Constantinople II", 553, "Constantinople"),
                ("Constantinople III", 680, "Constantinople"),
                ("Nicaea II", 787, "Nicaea"),
            ]
            print("councils:", len(COUNCILS))
            print("years from Nicaea I to Nicaea II:", COUNCILS[-1][1] - COUNCILS[0][1])
            cities = {}
            centuries = {}
            for name, year, city in COUNCILS:
                cities[city] = cities.get(city, 0) + 1
                century = (year - 1) // 100 + 1
                centuries[century] = centuries.get(century, 0) + 1
            for city in sorted(cities):
                print("held at", city + ":", cities[city])
            for century in sorted(centuries):
                print("century", century, "councils:", centuries[century])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 770 to 780: the years between the Lombard end of 774, the Herstal assembly of 779 and the Tang two-tax of 780, computed in Python and in C. */
val db127Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 127,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Reforms",
        title = "The years between the Lombard end, the Herstal assembly and the Tang two-tax, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Intervals between three dated events",
        author = "Charlemagne and Yang Yan",
        year = 774,
        summary = "The years between the Lombard end, the Herstal assembly and the two-tax are printed by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The dates used are 774 for Pavia, 779 for Herstal and 780 for the two-tax, and the three spans printed are 5, 1 and 6 years. The figures show the arithmetic of the dates only, and they do not settle any link between the events.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as gaps.py, gaps.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### gaps.py
            EVENTS = [("Lombard kingdom ends", 774), ("Herstal assembly", 779), ("two-tax reform", 780)]
            lombard, herstal, two_tax = [year for _, year in EVENTS]
            print("years from the Lombard end to Herstal:", herstal - lombard)
            print("years from Herstal to the two-tax:", two_tax - herstal)
            print("years from the Lombard end to the two-tax:", two_tax - lombard)
            ### gaps.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int lombard = 774, herstal = 779, two_tax = 780;
                printf("years from the Lombard end to Herstal: %d\n", herstal - lombard);
                printf("years from Herstal to the two-tax: %d\n", two_tax - herstal);
                printf("years from the Lombard end to the two-tax: %d\n", two_tax - lombard);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 gaps.py > python.txt
            cc -o gaps_c gaps.c
            ./gaps_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

            print("years to 600:", shares[0])
            print("years from 600 to 700:", shares[1])
            print("years from 700 to 774:", shares[2])
            print("total years in Italy:", sum(shares))
        """,
    ),

        details = "Constantine V is usually counted from his accession in 741 to his death in 775, although the usurper Artabasdos held Constantinople in 742 and 743; al-Mansur reigned from 754 to 775, al-Mahdi from 775 to 785 and Leo IV from 775 to 780.             lengths = [(end - start, name) for name, start, end in RULERS]

                print(name + ":", years, "years")
            print("total:", sum(years for years, _ in lengths), "years")
            print("longest:", max(lengths)[1])
            print("shortest:", min(lengths)[1])
        """,

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 760 to 770: the four gates of the Round City placed on a circle, computed in Python and in C. */
val db128Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 128,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Abbasid",
        title = "The four gates of the Round City placed on a circle, computed in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Gates on a circle",
        author = "Planners of the Round City, unnamed",
        year = 762,
        summary = "A Python program and a C program place the four gates of the Round City on a circle, and a script checks that both print the same coordinates.",
        details = "The gates are set at the four diagonal points of a circle of radius 1000 units: northeast for Khorasan, northwest for Sham, southwest for Kufa and southeast for Basra. The radius is an illustration and not the city's measured size, since the gate directions are known but not an exact layout.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as gates.py, gates.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### gates.py
            import math

            R = 1000  # an illustrative radius in units, not the measured size of the city
            GATES = [
                ("Bab al-Khorasan, northeast", 1),
                ("Bab al-Sham, northwest", 3),
                ("Bab al-Kufa, southwest", 5),
                ("Bab al-Basra, southeast", 7),
            ]
            for name, step in GATES:
                angle = step * math.pi / 4
                print(name, round(R * math.cos(angle)), round(R * math.sin(angle)))
            print("chord between Bab al-Khorasan and Bab al-Sham:", round(2 * R * math.sin(math.pi / 4)))
            ### gates.c
            #include <math.h>
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const double pi = 3.141592653589793;
                const double radius = 1000.0; /* an illustrative radius in units */
                const char *names[] = {"Bab al-Khorasan, northeast", "Bab al-Sham, northwest",
                                       "Bab al-Kufa, southwest", "Bab al-Basra, southeast"};
                const int steps[] = {1, 3, 5, 7};
                for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
                    double angle = steps[i] * pi / 4;
                    printf("%s %ld %ld\n", names[i], lround(radius * cos(angle)), lround(radius * sin(angle)));
                }
                printf("chord between Bab al-Khorasan and Bab al-Sham: %ld\n", lround(2 * radius * sin(pi / 4)));
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 gates.py > python.txt
            cc -o gates_c gates.c -lm
            ./gates_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 760 to 770: how a Latin word list is put in alphabetical order by hand, as the Abrogans is arranged. */
val db128Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 128,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Glossaries",
        title = "How a Latin word list is put in alphabetical order by hand, as the Abrogans glossary is arranged",
        originalTitle = "Alphabetical order of a Latin word list",
        author = "Unknown glossary makers",
        year = 765,
        summary = "A glossary such as the Abrogans is put in alphabetical order one word at a time, and a short program repeats that method with hand-written comparisons.",
        details = "The Abrogans is arranged by its Latin headwords in alphabetical order, and the method here compares two words letter by letter, placing each new word ahead of the first word that follows it. The example sorts a small set of Latin words by that method, and the words are a sample chosen for the example, not a copy of the glossary.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as alphabetize.py.
            2. Run it: python3 alphabetize.py
        """,
        example = """
            # compare two words letter by letter: True when a comes before b
            def before(a, b):
                for x, y in zip(a, b):
                    if x != y:
                        return x < y
                return len(a) < len(b)


            WORDS = ["balneum", "abbas", "acer", "aqua", "bos", "abies", "ara"]
            ordered = []
            for word in WORDS:
                place = len(ordered)
                for i, other in enumerate(ordered):
                    if before(word, other):
                        place = i
                        break
                ordered.insert(place, word)
            for word in ordered:
                print(word)
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 128,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Events",
        title = "Four events of 763 to 769 from Tibet, Japan and the Franks, sorted and spaced by the years between them",
        originalTitle = "Event list, 763 to 769",
        author = "The courts named in the list",
        year = 769,
        summary = "A short program puts four events of 763 to 769 in year order, prints the gap from each one to the next and names the longest gap.",
        details = "The events are the Tibetan seizure of Chang'an in 763, the defeat of the Emi rebellion in 764, the end of Pippin's Aquitaine war in 768 and the Usa Hachiman oracle of 769. The first and last events are six years apart, and the longest gap is the four years from 764 to 768.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as event_gaps.py.
            2. Run it: python3 event_gaps.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                ("Tibetan seizure of Chang'an", 763),
                ("defeat of the Emi rebellion", 764),
                ("end of Pippin's Aquitaine war", 768),
                ("Usa Hachiman oracle", 769),
            ]
            events = sorted(EVENTS, key=lambda event: event[1])
            gaps = []
            for (name, year), (_, next_year) in zip(events, events[1:]):
                gaps.append(next_year - year)
                print(year, name, "gap to the next event:", next_year - year)
            print("span from first to last:", events[-1][1] - events[0][1])
            print("longest gap:", max(gaps))
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 750 to 760: the bits needed to number the Man'yoshu poems up to 4516, computed in Python and in C. */
val db129Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 129,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Japanese",
        title = "The bits needed to number the Man'yoshu poems up to 4516, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Poem numbers in binary",
        author = "Compilers of the Man'yoshu",
        year = 759,
        summary = "The bits needed to write the Man'yoshu poem numbers up to 4516 are counted by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The last dated poem, of 759, carries the number 4516 in the usual numbering, and 4516 needs 13 binary digits, since 12 digits stop at 4095. Both programs print the 13 bits, the 421 poems numbered from 4096 to 4516 that need the thirteenth digit, and the largest numbers that 12 and 13 digits can hold, so the figures show the arithmetic of the numbering only.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as poems.py, poems.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### poems.py
            LAST = 4516
            print("bits needed for poem number 4516:", LAST.bit_length())
            print("largest number in 12 bits:", 2 ** 12 - 1)
            print("poems that need the thirteenth bit:", LAST - 4096 + 1)
            print("largest number in 13 bits:", 2 ** 13 - 1)
            ### poems.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int last = 4516;
                int bits = 0;
                int n = last;
                while (n) {
                    bits++;
                    n >>= 1;
                }
                printf("bits needed for poem number 4516: %d\n", bits);
                printf("largest number in 12 bits: %d\n", (1 << 12) - 1);
                printf("poems that need the thirteenth bit: %d\n", last - 4096 + 1);
                printf("largest number in 13 bits: %d\n", (1 << 13) - 1);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 poems.py > python.txt
            cc -o poems_c poems.c
            ./poems_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db12Cross.kt
################################################################################
package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1920 to 1930: the same tables and the same spanning tree, computed in Python and in C and compared by a run script. */
val db12Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Python and C",
        title = "Lukasiewicz three-valued tables in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Three-valued logic (Lukasiewicz, 1920)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1920,
        summary = "The same three-valued truth tables are computed in Python and in C, and the two outputs are compared, as a conformance test does.",
        details = "Lukasiewicz's three-valued logic gives a sentence the value false, possible or true, and the implication is the smaller of 1 and 1 minus a plus b. The two programs share no code. They print the negation, conjunction, disjunction and implication tables with the values 0, 1 and 2, meaning false, possible and true, and the run script checks that the two outputs are identical.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### lukasiewicz.py
            # Lukasiewicz three-valued logic: 0 is false, 1 is possible (one half) and 2 is true, written as integers.
            def neg(a):
                return 2 - a

            def conj(a, b):
                return min(a, b)

            def disj(a, b):
                return max(a, b)

            def impl(a, b):
                return min(2, 2 - a + b)

            print("not:", " ".join(str(neg(a)) for a in range(3)))
            for name, f in [("and", conj), ("or", disj), ("implies", impl)]:
                print(name + ":")
                for a in range(3):
                    print(" ".join(str(f(a, b)) for b in range(3)))
            ### lukasiewicz.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* Lukasiewicz three-valued logic: 0 is false, 1 is possible and 2 is true, written as integers. */
            static int neg(int a) { return 2 - a; }
            static int conj(int a, int b) { return a < b ? a : b; }
            static int disj(int a, int b) { return a > b ? a : b; }
            static int impl(int a, int b) { int v = 2 - a + b; return v < 2 ? v : 2; }

            static void table(const char *name, int (*f)(int, int)) {
                printf("%s:\n", name);
                for (int a = 0; a < 3; a++) {
                    for (int b = 0; b < 3; b++) {
                        printf(b ? " %d" : "%d", f(a, b));
                    }
                    printf("\n");
                }
            }

            int main(void) {
                printf("not: %d %d %d\n", neg(0), neg(1), neg(2));
                table("and", conj);
                table("or", disj);
                table("implies", impl);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 lukasiewicz.py > python.txt
            cc -o lukasiewicz lukasiewicz.c
            ./lukasiewicz > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Python and C",
        title = "Boruvka's spanning tree in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Minimum spanning trees by cheapest edges (Boruvka, 1926)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1926,
        summary = "Boruvka's method grows a minimum spanning tree in rounds, each component taking its cheapest edge out, and the Python and C programs must print the same rounds.",
        details = "In each round every component picks the cheapest edge that leaves it, and the picked edges join the components until one component remains. The graph has five vertices and seven edges with distinct weights, so its spanning tree is unique. Both programs print each round and the total weight, 11, and the run script checks that the two outputs are identical.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### boruvka.py
            # Edges as (u, v, weight) on vertices 0 to 4. All weights differ, so the minimum spanning tree is unique.
            EDGES = [(0, 1, 4), (0, 2, 1), (1, 2, 2), (1, 3, 5), (2, 3, 8), (2, 4, 6), (3, 4, 3)]
            N = 5

            def run():
                parent = list(range(N))

                def find(x):
                    while parent[x] != x:
                        x = parent[x]
                    return x

                total = 0
                count = 0
                rnd = 0
                while True:
                    # Every component picks its cheapest edge that leaves it.
                    cheapest = {}
                    for idx, (u, v, w) in enumerate(EDGES):
                        cu, cv = find(u), find(v)
                        if cu == cv:
                            continue
                        for c in (cu, cv):
                            if c not in cheapest or w < EDGES[cheapest[c]][2]:
                                cheapest[c] = idx
                    if not cheapest:
                        break
                    rnd += 1
                    picked = []
                    for idx in sorted(set(cheapest.values())):
                        u, v, w = EDGES[idx]
                        if find(u) != find(v):
                            parent[find(u)] = find(v)
                            picked.append(f"{u}-{v} {w}")
                            total += w
                            count += 1
                    print(f"round {rnd}: " + ", ".join(picked))
                print(f"tree edges: {count}, total weight {total}")

            run()
            ### boruvka.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* Edges as (u, v, weight) on vertices 0 to 4. All weights differ, so the minimum spanning tree is unique. */
            static const int EU[7] = {0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3};
            static const int EV[7] = {1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4};
            static const int EW[7] = {4, 1, 2, 5, 8, 6, 3};
            #define NE 7
            #define N 5

            static int parent[N];

            static int find(int x) {
                while (parent[x] != x) {
                    x = parent[x];
                }
                return x;
            }

            int main(void) {
                int total = 0, count = 0, rnd = 0;
                for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) parent[i] = i;
                for (;;) {
                    int cheapest[N];
                    int picked_flag[NE] = {0};
                    int any = 0;
                    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) cheapest[i] = -1;
                    for (int idx = 0; idx < NE; idx++) {
                        int cu = find(EU[idx]), cv = find(EV[idx]);
                        if (cu == cv) continue;
                        int cs[2] = {cu, cv};
                        for (int k = 0; k < 2; k++) {
                            int c = cs[k];
                            if (cheapest[c] < 0 || EW[idx] < EW[cheapest[c]]) cheapest[c] = idx;
                        }
                    }
                    for (int c = 0; c < N; c++) {
                        if (cheapest[c] >= 0) {
                            picked_flag[cheapest[c]] = 1;
                            any = 1;
                        }
                    }
                    if (!any) break;
                    rnd++;
                    printf("round %d: ", rnd);
                    int first = 1;
                    for (int idx = 0; idx < NE; idx++) {
                        if (!picked_flag[idx]) continue;
                        int ru = find(EU[idx]), rv = find(EV[idx]);
                        if (ru != rv) {
                            parent[ru] = rv;
                            printf(first ? "%d-%d %d" : ", %d-%d %d", EU[idx], EV[idx], EW[idx]);
                            first = 0;
                            total += EW[idx];
                            count++;
                        }
                    }
                    printf("\n");
                }
                printf("tree edges: %d, total weight %d\n", count, total);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 boruvka.py > python.txt
            cc -o boruvka boruvka.c
            ./boruvka > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),
)

        instructions = """

        """,
        example = """
            # Primitive recursion: each function has a base case and one recursive step.
            def add(x, y):
                # add(x, 0) = x and add(x, succ(y)) = succ(add(x, y))
                if y == 0:
                    return x
                return add(x, y - 1) + 1

            def mul(x, y):
                # mul(x, 0) = 0 and mul(x, succ(y)) = add(mul(x, y), x)
                if y == 0:
                    return 0
                return add(mul(x, y - 1), x)

            def power(x, y):
                # power(x, 0) = 1 and power(x, succ(y)) = mul(power(x, y), x)
                if y == 0:
                    return 1
                return mul(power(x, y - 1), x)

            print("add(3, 4) =", add(3, 4))
            print("mul(3, 4) =", mul(3, 4))
            print("power(2, 5) =", power(2, 5))
            print("mul(6, 7) =", mul(6, 7))
        """,

        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as hebern.py.
            2. Run it: python3 hebern.py
        """,
        example = """
            # A made-up rotor on the letters A to E. The rotor turns one step after each letter.
            WIRING = [2, 4, 0, 1, 3]   # A to C, B to E, C to A, D to B, E to D
            N = 5

            def encrypt_letter(i, k):
                # Input letter i at rotor position k: pass through the wiring, then shift back by k.
                return (WIRING[(i + k) % N] - k) % N

            def decrypt_letter(c, k):
                # Find the input letter that encrypts to c at position k.
                for i in range(N):
                    if encrypt_letter(i, k) == c:
                        return i
                raise ValueError("no letter")

            def run(text, decrypt=False):
                out = []
                for k, ch in enumerate(text):
                    if decrypt:
                        out.append(decrypt_letter(ord(ch) - ord("A"), k))
                    else:
                        out.append(encrypt_letter(ord(ch) - ord("A"), k))
                return "".join(chr(v + ord("A")) for v in out)

            cipher = run("AAAA")
            print("encrypt AAAA:", cipher)
            plain = run(cipher, decrypt=True)
            print("decrypt", cipher + ":", plain)
            print("round trip ok:", plain == "AAAA")
        """,
    ),
)

            import math

            # Cholesky factor of a symmetric positive definite matrix: A = L times the transpose of L, with L lower triangular.
            A = [[4.0, 12.0, -16.0], [12.0, 37.0, -43.0], [-16.0, -43.0, 98.0]]
            n = len(A)
            L = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
            for i in range(n):
                for j in range(i + 1):
                    s = sum(L[i][k] * L[j][k] for k in range(j))
                    if i == j:
                        L[i][j] = math.sqrt(A[i][i] - s)

/** Guides of 1920 to 1930: the techniques of the decade, each with a small program that runs today. */
val db12Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Notation",
        title = "How Polish notation evaluates an expression",
        originalTitle = "Polish notation (Jan Lukasiewicz, 1924)",
        author = "Jan Lukasiewicz",
        year = 1924,
        summary = "Prefix notation puts each operator before its operands, so no brackets are needed and one pass with a stack evaluates the expression.",
        details = "Lukasiewicz introduced the notation in 1924, and his own 1931 account dates the idea to 1924 and says it first appeared in an earlier footnote. The example reads the tokens from right to left, so each operator finds its two operands on the stack. It prints four expressions with their values, and each value can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as polish.py.
            2. Run it: python3 polish.py
        """,
        example = """
            def evaluate(tokens):
                # Read the tokens from right to left: each operator takes the two values that come after it.
                stack = []
                for tok in reversed(tokens):
                    if tok in ("+", "-", "*"):
                        left = stack.pop()
                        right = stack.pop()
                        if tok == "+":
                            stack.append(left + right)
                        elif tok == "-":
                            stack.append(left - right)
                        else:
                            stack.append(left * right)
                    else:
                        stack.append(int(tok))
                return stack.pop()

            for text in ["+ 2 3", "* + 2 3 4", "- 10 * 2 3", "+ * 2 3 * 4 5"]:
                print(text, "=", evaluate(text.split()))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Rewriting",
        title = "How a tag system runs step by step",
        originalTitle = "Tag systems (Post, 1921; printed 1943)",
        author = "Emil Post",
        year = 1921,
        summary = "A word is rewritten by deleting a fixed number of symbols from its front and appending a production for the first symbol, until a halt symbol appears.",
        details = "Post worked out the idea in 1920 and 1921, but the systems were first printed in 1943, so the year is a choice. The example runs a 2-tag system: each step deletes two symbols, appends the production of the first symbol, and stops when the first symbol is the halt symbol h. It prints the word at every step.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as tag.py.
            2. Run it: python3 tag.py
        """,
        example = """
            # A 2-tag system: each step deletes the first two symbols, then appends the production of the first symbol.
            PRODUCTIONS = {"a": "bb", "b": "h"}
            HALT = "h"

            def run(word, max_steps=10):
                print(word)
                for _ in range(max_steps):
                    if word[0] == HALT:
                        print("halt: the first symbol is h")
                        return
                    word = word[2:] + PRODUCTIONS[word[0]]
                    print(word)
                print("stopped after", max_steps, "steps")

            run("ab")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Eigenvalues",
        title = "How the power method finds the largest eigenvalue",
        originalTitle = "The power method for a dominant eigenvalue (von Mises, 1929)",
        author = "Richard von Mises and Hilda Pollaczek-Geiringer",
        year = 1929,
        summary = "Repeated multiplication by a matrix turns a starting vector toward the eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue, and a quotient of two dot products reads that eigenvalue off.",
        details = "Each step multiplies the vector by the matrix, and the Rayleigh quotient of the vector estimates the dominant eigenvalue. The example uses the symmetric matrix with rows [2, 1] and [1, 2], whose eigenvalues are 3 and 1, starts from the vector [1, 0], and prints four estimates. The error of the quotient shrinks as the square of the eigenvalue ratio, one third here, so it falls by about a factor of 9 per step.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as power_method.py.
            2. Run it: python3 power_method.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            # Power method for the symmetric matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], whose eigenvalues are 3 and 1.
            A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]

            def apply(M, v):
                return [M[0][0] * v[0] + M[0][1] * v[1], M[1][0] * v[0] + M[1][1] * v[1]]

            def dot(a, b):
                return a[0] * b[0] + a[1] * b[1]

            v = [1, 0]
            for step in range(1, 5):
                v = apply(A, v)
                # Rayleigh quotient of the current vector: an estimate of the dominant eigenvalue.
                estimate = Fraction(dot(v, apply(A, v)), dot(v, v))
                print(f"step {step}: estimate {float(estimate):.4f}")
            print("exact dominant eigenvalue: 3")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Classical ciphers",
        title = "How a Hill cipher encrypts a pair of letters",
        originalTitle = "Cryptography in an Algebraic Alphabet (Hill, 1929)",
        author = "Lester S. Hill",
        year = 1929,
        summary = "Hill's cipher turns each pair of letters into a pair of letters by multiplying a vector of numbers by a key matrix, modulo 26.",
        details = "Hill published the idea in the American Mathematical Monthly in 1929. The key matrix has an inverse modulo 26 when its determinant shares no factor with 26, and then the inverse matrix decrypts. The example encrypts HELP with the matrix [[3, 3], [2, 5]], decrypts the result with its inverse [[15, 17], [20, 9]], and checks the round trip.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as hill.py.
            2. Run it: python3 hill.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Hill cipher with the key matrix [[3, 3], [2, 5]] over the letters A = 0 to Z = 25.
            KEY = [[3, 3], [2, 5]]
            # Inverse of KEY modulo 26: the determinant is 9, and 9 * 3 = 27 = 1 modulo 26.
            INVERSE = [[15, 17], [20, 9]]

            def to_numbers(text):
                return [ord(c) - ord("A") for c in text]

            def to_text(numbers):
                return "".join(chr(n % 26 + ord("A")) for n in numbers)

            def apply(matrix, text):
                # Each pair of letters is multiplied by the matrix, modulo 26.
                nums = to_numbers(text)
                out = []
                for i in range(0, len(nums), 2):
                    a, b = nums[i], nums[i + 1]
                    out.append((matrix[0][0] * a + matrix[0][1] * b) % 26)
                    out.append((matrix[1][0] * a + matrix[1][1] * b) % 26)
                return to_text(out)

            cipher = apply(KEY, "HELP")
            print("cipher:", cipher)
            plain = apply(INVERSE, cipher)
            print("decrypted:", plain)
            print("round trip ok:", plain == "HELP")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Urns",
        title = "How a Polya urn fills",
        originalTitle = "Ueber die Statistik verketteter Vorgaenge (Eggenberger and Polya, 1923)",
        author = "F. Eggenberger and G. Polya",
        year = 1923,
        summary = "A ball is drawn, returned and joined by one more of its colour, and every count of red balls is equally likely when the urn starts with one of each.",
        details = "The model appeared in the Zeitschrift fur Angewandte Mathematik und Mechanik in 1923, volume 3, on pages 279 to 289 by most references. The example computes exact probabilities with fractions and no random numbers: the chance of a sequence is a product of ratios, and the chance of k reds after three draws is one quarter for every k.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as polya_urn.py.
            2. Run it: python3 polya_urn.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction
            from itertools import product

            # One red and one black ball; each draw returns the ball and adds one more of its colour.
            def probability(sequence):
                red, black = 1, 1
                p = Fraction(1)
                for colour in sequence:
                    total = red + black
                    if colour == "R":
                        p *= Fraction(red, total)
                        red += 1
                    else:
                        p *= Fraction(black, total)
                        black += 1
                return p

            print("P(RRB) =", probability("RRB"))

            n = 3
            dist = {}
            for seq in product("RB", repeat=n):
                k = seq.count("R")
                dist[k] = dist.get(k, Fraction(0)) + probability(seq)
            print("P(k reds), k = 0..3:", " ".join(str(dist[k]) for k in range(n + 1)))
            print("uniform:", all(dist[k] == Fraction(1, n + 1) for k in range(n + 1)))
        """,
    ),
)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 1920 to 1930: a truth-table checker, a combinator reducer, a process chart and a sampling plan. */
val db12Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Logic",
        title = "Truth-table checker for propositional formulas",
        originalTitle = "Truth tables (Wittgenstein and Post, 1921)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1921,
        summary = "Prints the truth table of two formulas and reports whether each one is a tautology.",
        details = "Wittgenstein's Tractatus and Post's thesis both reached truth tables in 1921, and the priority between them is disputed. The example writes each formula as a Python expression over two variables, enumerates the four assignments, prints the table with 1 for true and 0 for false, and counts the true rows to decide whether the formula is a tautology.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as truth_table.py.
            2. Run it: python3 truth_table.py
        """,
        example = """
            from itertools import product

            # Two formulas written as Python expressions over the variables p and q.
            FORMULAS = [
                ("(not p) or q", lambda p, q: (not p) or q),
                ("p or (not p)", lambda p, q: p or (not p)),
            ]

            print("p q  " + "  ".join(name for name, _ in FORMULAS))
            for p, q in product([True, False], repeat=2):
                row = " ".join(str(int(f(p, q))) for _, f in FORMULAS)
                print(f"{int(p)} {int(q)}  {row}")

            for name, f in FORMULAS:
                rows = sum(1 for p, q in product([True, False], repeat=2) if f(p, q))
                print(f"{name}: true in {rows} of 4 rows, tautology: {rows == 4}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Combinators",
        title = "Combinator reducer with a step limit",
        originalTitle = "Combinatory logic (Schonfinkel, 1924)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1924,
        summary = "Reduces a term built from the combinators S, K and I by their three rewriting rules, and prints each step until no rule applies.",
        details = "Schonfinkel gave the lecture behind the theory in December 1920 and published it in Mathematische Annalen in 1924, so the year is 1924. Curry developed the theory later. The example reduces S K K a, which equals a, in two steps. It prints each term, the way a reduction is written on paper, and it stops when no rule applies.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as combinators.py.
            2. Run it: python3 combinators.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Terms are atoms (S, K, I or a variable name) or pairs (function, argument).
            def app(f, x):
                return (f, x)

            def show(term):
                if isinstance(term, str):
                    return term
                f, x = term
                left = show(f)
                right = show(x)
                if isinstance(x, tuple):
                    right = "(" + right + ")"
                return left + " " + right

            def step(term):
                # Leftmost-outermost rewriting: returns the reduced term, or None if no rule applies.
                if not isinstance(term, tuple):
                    return None
                f, x = term
                if f == "I":
                    return x
                if isinstance(f, tuple) and f[0] == "K":
                    return f[1]
                if isinstance(f, tuple) and isinstance(f[0], tuple) and f[0][0] == "S":
                    a, b = f[0][1], f[1]
                    return app(app(a, x), app(b, x))
                reduced = step(f)
                if reduced is not None:
                    return app(reduced, x)
                reduced = step(x)
                if reduced is not None:
                    return app(f, reduced)
                return None

            def run(term, limit=10):
                print(show(term))
                for _ in range(limit):
                    term = step(term)
                    if term is None:
                        print("normal form reached")
                        return
                    print(show(term))
                print("stopped after", limit, "steps")

            run(app(app(app("S", "K"), "K"), "a"))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Process charts",
        title = "Flow process chart in text",
        originalTitle = "Process charts, presented to ASME (Gilbreth, 1921)",
        author = "Frank and Lillian Gilbreth",
        year = 1921,
        summary = "Lists each step of a job with a letter for its kind, then totals the minutes by kind, as a flow process chart does.",
        details = "Frank and Lillian Gilbreth presented the process chart to the American Society of Mechanical Engineers in 1921, and the 1947 ASME standard formalised its symbols. Accounts differ on whether Frank alone or both spouses are credited. The example uses letters for the five kinds of step: operation, transport, inspection, delay and storage. It prints the steps, the minutes for each kind and the total.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as flow_chart.py.
            2. Run it: python3 flow_chart.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Each step: a letter for its kind (O operation, T transport, I inspection, D delay, S storage), a description and minutes.
            STEPS = [
                ("O", "Pick up part", 0.5),
                ("T", "Carry to press", 1.0),
                ("I", "Check size", 0.25),
                ("D", "Wait for press", 2.0),
                ("S", "Put in bin", 0.5),
            ]
            NAMES = {"O": "operation", "T": "transport", "I": "inspection", "D": "delay", "S": "storage"}

            print("step sym description minutes")
            for number, (sym, text, minutes) in enumerate(STEPS, start=1):
                print(f"{number} {sym} {text} {minutes:.2f}")

            totals = {}
            for sym, _, minutes in STEPS:
                totals[sym] = totals.get(sym, 0.0) + minutes
            for sym in "OTIDS":
                print(f"{NAMES[sym]}: {totals.get(sym, 0.0):.2f} minutes")
            print(f"total: {sum(m for _, _, m in STEPS):.2f} minutes")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 12,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Sampling inspection",
        title = "Single sampling plan acceptance probability",
        originalTitle = "A Method of Sampling Inspection (Dodge and Romig, 1929)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1929,
        summary = "Computes the chance that a lot is accepted under a single sampling plan, which samples five items and accepts the lot if at most one is defective.",
        details = "Dodge and Romig's method appeared in the October 1929 Bell System Technical Journal. It judged lots by probabilities and kept the exposure to defective goods low at minimal inspection cost. The example uses a simple single plan rather than their tables: it draws five items and accepts the lot if at most one is defective, and it computes the acceptance probability with exact fractions at two fractions defective.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as sampling.py.
            2. Run it: python3 sampling.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction
            from math import comb

            # Single sampling plan: draw n items from a large lot and accept the lot if at most c are defective.
            def accept_probability(n, c, p):
                return sum(comb(n, k) * p ** k * (1 - p) ** (n - k) for k in range(c + 1))

            n, c = 5, 1
            for p in (Fraction(1, 10), Fraction(3, 10)):
                prob = accept_probability(n, c, p)
                print(f"fraction defective {float(p):.2f}: accept with probability {float(prob):.5f}")
        """,
    ),
)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 740 to 750: the years between the death of Leo III and two decrees of 743, computed in Python and in C. */
val db130Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 130,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Decrees",
        title = "The years between the death of Leo III and two decrees of 743, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Leo III to the decrees of 743",
        author = "Leo III and Shomu",
        year = 741,
        summary = "The years between the death of Leo III and two decrees of 743 are printed by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "Leo III died in June 741, and the two decrees counted here, the Konden Einen Shizaiho and Shomu's decree for the Great Buddha, were both issued in 743. The spans from the death are 2 years to each decree, the two decrees fall in the same year, and the arithmetic uses only the usual dates.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as decrees.py, decrees.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### decrees.py
            DEATH_LEO = 741
            KONDEN = 743
            BUDDHA = 743
            print("years from the death of Leo III to the Konden law:", KONDEN - DEATH_LEO)
            print("years from the death of Leo III to the Great Buddha decree:", BUDDHA - DEATH_LEO)
            print("years from the Konden law to the Great Buddha decree:", BUDDHA - KONDEN)
            ### decrees.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int death = 741, konden = 743, buddha = 743;
                printf("years from the death of Leo III to the Konden law: %d\n", konden - death);
                printf("years from the death of Leo III to the Great Buddha decree: %d\n", buddha - death);
                printf("years from the Konden law to the Great Buddha decree: %d\n", buddha - konden);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 decrees.py > python.txt
            cc -o decrees_c decrees.c
            ./decrees_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 130,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Umayyad",
        title = "The Umayyad caliphs of 724 to 750, each reign counted from one accession to the next",
        originalTitle = "Hisham, al-Walid II, Yazid III, Ibrahim and Marwan II",
        author = "The Umayyad caliphs",
        year = 743,
        summary = "Five Umayyad caliphs ruled between 724 and 750, and a short program counts each reign from accession to the next and ranks the reigns.",
        details = "Hisham died in 743 and was followed by al-Walid II, Yazid III, Ibrahim and Marwan II, the last Umayyad caliph, who fell in 750. A reign that begins and ends in one year counts as one year, so the figures show the order of the accessions and not the exact months of rule.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as umayyad_caliphs.py.
            2. Run it: python3 umayyad_caliphs.py
        """,
        example = """
            CALIPHS = [
                ("Hisham", 724, 743),
                ("al-Walid II", 743, 744),
                ("Yazid III", 744, 744),
                ("Ibrahim", 744, 744),
                ("Marwan II", 744, 750),
            ]
            spans = {name: max(1, end - start) for name, start, end in CALIPHS}
            for name, span in spans.items():
                print(name, span, "years")
            print("total:", sum(spans.values()), "years")
            longest = max(spans, key=spans.get)
            shortest = min(spans, key=spans.get)
            print("longest:", longest, spans[longest], "years")
            print("shortest:", shortest, spans[shortest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 730 to 740: the years between three Kaiyuan books of 730, 737 and 738, computed in Python and in C. */
val db131Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 131,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Tang",
        title = "The years between three Kaiyuan books, the catalogue of 730, the code of 737 and the handbook of 738, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Kaiyuan year spans",
        author = "Tang government",
        year = 730,
        summary = "The years between Zhisheng's catalogue of 730, the Kaiyuan Code of 737 and the Tang handbook of 738 are printed by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The spans printed are 7 years from the catalogue to the code, 1 year from the code to the handbook and 8 years from the catalogue to the handbook. The dates used are the usual ones for the three works, and the figures show only the arithmetic of those dates.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as kaiyuan.py, kaiyuan.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### kaiyuan.py
            CATALOGUE = 730   # Zhisheng's Kaiyuan catalogue of Buddhist scriptures
            CODE = 737        # the Kaiyuan Code
            HANDBOOK = 738    # the Tang handbook of offices
            print("years from the catalogue to the code:", CODE - CATALOGUE)
            print("years from the code to the handbook:", HANDBOOK - CODE)
            print("years from the catalogue to the handbook:", HANDBOOK - CATALOGUE)
            ### kaiyuan.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int catalogue = 730, code = 737, handbook = 738;
                printf("years from the catalogue to the code: %d\n", code - catalogue);
                printf("years from the code to the handbook: %d\n", handbook - code);
                printf("years from the catalogue to the handbook: %d\n", handbook - catalogue);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 kaiyuan.py > python.txt
            cc -o kaiyuan_c kaiyuan.c
            ./kaiyuan_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

/** One guide of 730 to 740: the Tang land statute of 737 that gives an adult man 100 mu, worked out in code as 80 allotted and 20 hereditary mu. */
val db131Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 131,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Land",
        title = "How the Tang land statute of 737 splits an adult man's 100 mu into 80 allotted and 20 hereditary mu, in code",
        originalTitle = "Kaiyuan ershiwu nian ling, juntian",
        author = "Tang government",
        year = 737,
        summary = "The Tang statute of the twenty-fifth year of Kaiyuan, 737, gave an adult man 100 mu of equal-field land, 80 mu to be allotted and 20 mu hereditary, and a short program works out the grant for a household.",
        details = "The allotted part went back to the state when its holder died, while the hereditary part could pass to his heirs. The total of 100 mu for an adult man was already the grant in the Wude statute of 624, and the program prints the grant for a household of three adult men.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as equal_field.py.
            2. Run it: python3 equal_field.py
        """,
        example = """
            ADULT_MAN_MU = 100                          # the equal-field grant for an adult man, in mu
            HEREDITARY_MU = 20                          # the part kept as hereditary land
            ALLOTTED_MU = ADULT_MAN_MU - HEREDITARY_MU  # the part returned to the state at death

            def household_grant(adult_men):
                return {
                    "allotted": ALLOTTED_MU * adult_men,
                    "hereditary": HEREDITARY_MU * adult_men,
                    "total": ADULT_MAN_MU * adult_men,
                }

            grant = household_grant(3)
            print("allotted mu for three adult men:", grant["allotted"])
            print("hereditary mu for three adult men:", grant["hereditary"])
            print("total mu for three adult men:", grant["total"])
            print("hereditary share of the grant:", HEREDITARY_MU / ADULT_MAN_MU)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 720 to 730: the years between the Nihon Shoki, the Sanze Isshin no Ho and the Konden Einen Shizai Ho, computed in Python and in C. */
val db132Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 132,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Japanese",
        title = "The years between the Nihon Shoki, the Sanze law and the Konden law, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Japanese year spans",
        author = "The Japanese court",
        year = 720,
        summary = "The years between the Nihon Shoki, the Sanze law and the Konden law are printed by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The dates used are 720 for the Nihon Shoki, 723 for the Sanze Isshin no Ho and 743 for the Konden Einen Shizai Ho, and the programs print the spans of 3 and 20 years and the total of 23. The dates are the usual ones, and the Sanze law's own date is the one in the Sanze record, so the figures show arithmetic rather than a claim about how the laws were linked.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as japan_years.py, japan_years.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### japan_years.py
            EVENTS = [("Nihon Shoki", 720), ("Sanze Isshin no Ho", 723), ("Konden Einen Shizai Ho", 743)]
            spans = [later[1] - earlier[1] for earlier, later in zip(EVENTS, EVENTS[1:])]
            print("spans:", " ".join(str(s) for s in spans))
            print("first to last:", EVENTS[-1][1] - EVENTS[0][1], "years")
            ### japan_years.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int shoki = 720, sanze = 723, konden = 743;
                printf("spans: %d %d\n", sanze - shoki, konden - sanze);
                printf("first to last: %d years\n", konden - shoki);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 japan_years.py > python.txt
            cc -o japan_years_c japan_years.c
            ./japan_years_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 720 to 730: three Chinese reference compilations from 727 to 983, the years between them summed and ranked by a short program. */
val db132Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 132,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "Three Chinese reference compilations from 727 to 983, the years between them counted and ranked",
        originalTitle = "Chuxueji, Kaiyuan Zhanjing and Taiping Yulan",
        author = "Tang and Song compilers",
        year = 727,
        summary = "The Chuxueji of 727, the Kaiyuan Zhanjing of 729 and the Taiping Yulan of 983 are three Chinese reference compilations, and a short program counts and ranks the years between them.",
        details = "The Chuxueji and the Kaiyuan Zhanjing are Tang works of the Kaiyuan period, dated here to 727 and 729, and the Taiping Yulan is a Song encyclopedia of 983. The spans are 2 years and 254 years, the total from 727 to 983 is 256 years, and the longest span runs from the Kaiyuan Zhanjing to the Taiping Yulan.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as compilations.py.
            2. Run it: python3 compilations.py
        """,
        example = """
            COMPILATIONS = [
                ("Chuxueji", 727),
                ("Kaiyuan Zhanjing", 729),
                ("Taiping Yulan", 983),
            ]

            gaps = {}
            for (name_a, year_a), (name_b, year_b) in zip(COMPILATIONS, COMPILATIONS[1:]):
                gaps[name_a + " to " + name_b] = year_b - year_a
            for label, years in gaps.items():
                print(label, years, "years")
            print("total from 727 to 983:", COMPILATIONS[-1][1] - COMPILATIONS[0][1], "years")
            longest = max(gaps, key=gaps.get)
            print("longest gap:", longest, gaps[longest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code piece of 710 to 720: the years between Liutprand's accession, the Fudoki decree and the Codex Amiatinus, computed in Python and in C. */
val db133Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 133,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Years",
        title = "The years between Liutprand's accession in 712, the Fudoki decree of 713 and the Codex Amiatinus of 716, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Years between three events",
        author = "Liutprand, king of the Lombards",
        year = 712,
        summary = "The years between Liutprand's accession, the Fudoki decree and the Codex Amiatinus are printed by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The dates used are 712 for Liutprand's accession, 713 for the Fudoki decree and 716 for the Codex Amiatinus, and the three spans printed are 1, 3 and 4 years. The dates are the usual ones for these events, and the figures show only the arithmetic of the dates, not any link between a Lombard king, a Japanese court and a Northumbrian monastery.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as spans.py, spans.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### spans.py
            ACCESSION = 712
            FUDOKI = 713
            CODEX = 716
            print("years from Liutprand's accession to the Fudoki decree:", FUDOKI - ACCESSION)
            print("years from the Fudoki decree to the Codex Amiatinus:", CODEX - FUDOKI)
            print("years from Liutprand's accession to the Codex Amiatinus:", CODEX - ACCESSION)
            ### spans.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int accession = 712, fudoki = 713, codex = 716;
                printf("years from Liutprand's accession to the Fudoki decree: %d\n", fudoki - accession);
                printf("years from the Fudoki decree to the Codex Amiatinus: %d\n", codex - fudoki);
                printf("years from Liutprand's accession to the Codex Amiatinus: %d\n", codex - accession);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 spans.py > python.txt
            cc -o spans_c spans.c
            ./spans_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 710 to 720: the rules of the regulated eight-line Tang poem, checked by a short program for line length and for rhyme on the even lines. */
val db133Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 133,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "How a regulated eight-line Tang poem is tested for line length and for rhyme on its even lines",
        originalTitle = "Lushi, the regulated verse",
        author = "Shen Quanqi and Song Zhiwen (credited)",
        year = 710,
        summary = "A regulated Tang poem has eight lines of five or seven characters that rhyme on the even lines, and a short program checks both rules.",
        details = "Shen Quanqi (656 to 714) and Song Zhiwen (about 660 to 712) are credited with fixing the form, and accounts differ on when its rules were settled, from the late seventh century to the Jinglong era of 707 to 710, so 710 is the year used here. The labels in the example stand for line lengths and rhyme groups, not for real lines of verse, and the program shows that a rhyme broken on line six is caught.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as lushi_check.py.
            2. Run it: python3 lushi_check.py
        """,
        example = """
            LINES = 8

            def regulated(poem):
                lengths = {length for length, rhyme in poem}
                rhymes = {rhyme for number, (length, rhyme) in enumerate(poem, start=1) if number % 2 == 0}
                return len(poem) == LINES and len(lengths) == 1 and lengths <= {5, 7} and len(rhymes) == 1

            FIVE = [(5, "B"), (5, "A"), (5, "C"), (5, "A"), (5, "D"), (5, "A"), (5, "E"), (5, "A")]
            SEVEN = [(7, "B"), (7, "A"), (7, "C"), (7, "A"), (7, "D"), (7, "A"), (7, "E"), (7, "A")]
            BROKEN = [(5, "B"), (5, "A"), (5, "C"), (5, "A"), (5, "D"), (5, "F"), (5, "E"), (5, "A")]
            MIXED = [(5, "B"), (7, "A"), (5, "C"), (5, "A"), (5, "D"), (5, "A"), (5, "E"), (5, "A")]
            SHORT = [(5, "B"), (5, "A"), (5, "C"), (5, "A"), (5, "D"), (5, "A"), (5, "E")]

            print("five-character poem regulated:", regulated(FIVE))
            print("seven-character poem regulated:", regulated(SEVEN))
            print("rhyme broken on line six:", regulated(BROKEN))
            print("mixed line lengths:", regulated(MIXED))
            print("seven lines only:", regulated(SHORT))
        """,
    ),

)
