    entry(
        databaseId = 133,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Umayyad",
        title = "The reigns of Walid I, Sulayman and Umar II from 705 to 720, summed and ranked",
        originalTitle = "Umayyad reigns from 705 to 720",
        author = "The Umayyad caliphs",
        year = 720,
        summary = "Three Umayyad caliphs ruled between 705 and 720, Walid I for 10 years, Sulayman for 2 and Umar II for 3, and a short program sums and ranks those spans.",
        details = "Walid I came to the throne in 705 and died in 715, Sulayman ruled from 715 to 717, and Umar II from 717 until his death in 720, so the count stops there. The spans use the usual dates of accession and death, and Walid's reign, under which Tariq and Musa ibn Nusayr began the conquest of Spain, is the longest of the three.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as umayyad_reigns.py.
            2. Run it: python3 umayyad_reigns.py
        """,
        example = """
            REIGNS = [
                ("Walid I", 705, 715),
                ("Sulayman", 715, 717),
                ("Umar II", 717, 720),
            ]

            spans = {name: end - start for name, start, end in REIGNS}
            for name, span in spans.items():
                print(name, span, "years")
            print("total:", sum(spans.values()), "years")
            longest = max(spans, key=spans.get)
            shortest = min(spans, key=spans.get)
            print("longest:", longest, spans[longest], "years")
            print("shortest:", shortest, spans[shortest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 700 to 710: Liu Zhiji's age when the Shitong was completed and at his death, counted in Python and in C. */
val db134Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 134,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "Liu Zhiji's age when the Shitong was completed in 710 and at his death in 721, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Shitong",
        author = "Liu Zhiji",
        year = 710,
        summary = "Liu Zhiji's age at the completion of the Shitong and at his death is counted by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "Liu Zhiji's lifespan is usually given as 661 to 721, so he was 49 when the Shitong was completed in 710 and 60 at his death. The two programs print the same three figures, so the check confirms the arithmetic, while the dates come from the sources on his life.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as liu_ages.py, liu_ages.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### liu_ages.py
            BIRTH = 661    # the start of Liu Zhiji's lifespan, as usually given
            SHITONG = 710  # the Shitong completed in 710
            DEATH = 721    # the end of his lifespan, as usually given
            print("age at the completion of the Shitong:", SHITONG - BIRTH)
            print("age at his death:", DEATH - BIRTH)
            print("years between the Shitong and his death:", DEATH - SHITONG)
            ### liu_ages.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int birth = 661, shitong = 710, death = 721;
                printf("age at the completion of the Shitong: %d\n", shitong - birth);
                printf("age at his death: %d\n", death - birth);
                printf("years between the Shitong and his death: %d\n", death - shitong);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 liu_ages.py > python.txt
            cc -o liu_ages_c liu_ages.c
            ./liu_ages_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        year = 705,
        summary = "A Roman pound of gold was cut into 72 solidi, the Byzantine gold coin kept at that standard, and a short program works out how many coins a weight of gold makes.",
        details = "The standard of 72 solidi to the pound dates from the 4th century, so 705, the year Justinian II returned to the throne, is only the anchor used here for coins of that reign, not the year the standard was set.         originalTitle = "Wu Zetian, Zhongzong and Ruizong",
        author = "Empress Wu and her successors",
        year = 705,
        summary = "Empress Wu's reign from 690 to 705, Zhongzong's second reign from 705 to 710 and Ruizong's second reign from 710 to 712 are summed and ranked by a short program.",
        details = "Empress Wu proclaimed her Zhou dynasty in 690 and gave up the throne in 705, when Zhongzong was restored. Zhongzong died in 710, and Ruizong came to the throne again, so the lengths are counted from years of accession and not from exact days.",

            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### adomnan.py
            START = 679  # the start of Adomnan's abbacy of Iona, as recorded
            CAIN = 697   # the Cain issued at the Synod of Birr
            END = 704    # the end of his abbacy, as recorded
            print("years in office at the Cain:", CAIN - START)
            print("years in office at the end of his abbacy:", END - START)
            print("years between the Cain and the end of his abbacy:", END - CAIN)
            ### adomnan.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int start = 679, cain = 697, end = 704;
                printf("years in office at the Cain: %d\n", cain - start);
                printf("years in office at the end of his abbacy: %d\n", end - start);
                printf("years between the Cain and the end of his abbacy: %d\n", end - cain);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 adomnan.py > python.txt
            cc -o adomnan_c adomnan.c
            ./adomnan_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

val db135Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 135,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "How the degree of kinship is counted by the Roman civil method, one step up and one step down, worked out by a program",
        originalTitle = "gradus cognationis",
        author = "Roman jurists and the Byzantine courts",
        year = 692,
        summary = "The Roman civil count of kinship adds the generations from each of two people up to their common ancestor, so siblings are in the second degree and first cousins in the fourth.",
        details = "The Roman civil count, used in the law that the Byzantine courts followed in the 690s, adds one degree for each generation up to the common ancestor and one for each generation down. The year 692, that of the Quinisext Council, is only the anchor of this placed record and not the date of the method.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as kinship_degrees.py.
            2. Run it: python3 kinship_degrees.py
        """,
        example = """
            def roman_degree(up_a, up_b):
                # one degree for each generation up from each person to the common ancestor
                return up_a + up_b

            pairs = [
                ("siblings", 1, 1),
                ("uncle and nephew", 1, 2),
                ("first cousins", 2, 2),
                ("second cousins", 3, 3),
            ]
            for name, up_a, up_b in pairs:
                print(name, "degree", roman_degree(up_a, up_b))
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 690 to 700: the first reign of Justinian II, the reign of Leontius and the reign of Tiberius III, from 685 to 705, summed and ranked by a short program. */
val db135Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 135,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "Justinian II's first reign, from 685 to 695, and the reigns of Leontius and Tiberius III to 705, summed and ranked by a short program",
        originalTitle = "Iustinianus II, Leontius, Tiberius III",
        author = "Byzantine emperors",
        year = 695,
        summary = "Justinian II's first reign from 685 to 695, the reign of Leontius from 695 to 698 and the reign of Tiberius III from 698 to 705 are summed and ranked by a short program.",
        details = "Justinian II lost the throne in 695 to Leontius, who was overthrown by Tiberius III in 698, and Justinian returned only in 705, so the lengths are counted from years of accession and not from exact days. The program prints each length, the total and the longest and shortest reign, which come to 20 years in all.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as byzantine_reigns.py.
            2. Run it: python3 byzantine_reigns.py
        """,
        example = """
            REIGNS = [
                ("Justinian II, first reign", 685, 695),
                ("Leontius", 695, 698),
                ("Tiberius III", 698, 705),
            ]

            lengths = {name: end - start for name, start, end in REIGNS}
            for name, span in lengths.items():
                print(name, span, "years")
            print("total:", sum(lengths.values()), "years")
            longest = max(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            shortest = min(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            print("longest:", longest, lengths[longest], "years")
            print("shortest:", shortest, lengths[shortest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 136,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Arabic and Old Malay",
        title = "Years from the siege of Mecca in 683 to the Kota Kapur stone of 686, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Mecca and Kota Kapur",
        author = "Husayn ibn Numayr and the court of Srivijaya",
        year = 683,
        summary = "The siege of Mecca in 683 and the Kota Kapur stone of 686 are three years apart, and a Python program and a C program print the same gap.",
        details = "The two dates are the usual years given for the siege and the stone, so the programs check the arithmetic, while the dates come from the sources on the two events. Accounts of the siege differ in their length, but the programs use the year 683 for it.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """

            ### mecca_kota.c

                int mecca = 683, kota_kapur = 686;

                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 mecca_kota.py > python.txt
            cc -o mecca_kota_c mecca_kota.c
            ./mecca_kota_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,

val db136Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 136,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Insular",
        title = "Seven monasteries founded by Irish and Anglo-Saxon monks, from Iona in 563 to Jarrow in 681, with the gaps between them counted by a program",
        originalTitle = "Monastic foundations",
        author = "Columba, Columbanus, Aidan, Hild and Benedict Biscop",
        year = 681,
        summary = "A short program lists seven monastic foundations from Iona to Jarrow and prints the gap between each pair of founding years.",
        details = "The founding years used are the usual dates: Iona 563, Luxeuil 590, Bobbio 614, Lindisfarne 635, Whitby 657, Monkwearmouth 674 and Jarrow 681. The program prints the six gaps, the total span of 118 years, and the longest and shortest gaps, so its results depend only on these dates.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as monastery_gaps.py.
            2. Run it: python3 monastery_gaps.py
        """,
        example = """
            FOUNDATIONS = [
                ("Iona", 563),
                ("Luxeuil", 590),
                ("Bobbio", 614),
                ("Lindisfarne", 635),
                ("Whitby", 657),
                ("Monkwearmouth", 674),
                ("Jarrow", 681),
            ]
            gaps = []
            for (name, first), (other, second) in zip(FOUNDATIONS, FOUNDATIONS[1:]):
                gap = second - first
                gaps.append((gap, name + " to " + other))
                print(name, "to", other, ":", gap, "years")
            print("total span:", FOUNDATIONS[-1][1] - FOUNDATIONS[0][1], "years")
            longest = max(gaps)
            shortest = min(gaps)
            print("longest gap:", longest[1], longest[0], "years")
            print("shortest gap:", shortest[1], shortest[0], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 670 to 680: the years of the Arab siege of Constantinople, 674 to 678, counted in Python and in C. */
val db137Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 137,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Umayyad",
        title = "The years of the Arab siege of Constantinople, 674 to 678, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "The siege of Constantinople",
        author = "The Umayyad caliphate",
        year = 674,
        summary = "A Python program and a C program count the years of the Arab siege of Constantinople, 674 to 678, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The siege is dated 674 to 678, so it covers five years counted inclusively and four years between its first and last year. The two programs print the same figures, so the check confirms the arithmetic, while the dates come from the commonly given span of the siege.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as siege_years.py, siege_years.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### siege_years.py
            FIRST = 674  # the siege begins, as commonly dated
            LAST = 678   # the siege ends, as commonly dated
            print("first year:", FIRST)
            print("last year:", LAST)
            print("years counted inclusively:", LAST - FIRST + 1)
            print("years between the first and last:", LAST - FIRST)
            ### siege_years.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int first = 674, last = 678;
                printf("first year: %d\n", first);
                printf("last year: %d\n", last);
                printf("years counted inclusively: %d\n", last - first + 1);
                printf("years between the first and last: %d\n", last - first);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 siege_years.py > python.txt
            cc -o siege_years_c siege_years.c
            ./siege_years_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 137,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Rulers",
        title = "The reigns of Ecgfrith, Tenmu and Wamba, from 670 to 686, summed and ranked by a short program",
        originalTitle = "Reign lengths",
        author = "Ecgfrith, Tenmu and Wamba",
        year = 670,
        summary = "The reigns of Ecgfrith of Northumbria, Tenmu of Japan and Wamba of the Visigoths are summed and ranked by a short program.",
        details = "Ecgfrith's reign is counted from 670 to 685, Tenmu's from 673 to 686 and Wamba's from 672 to 680, so the lengths are 15, 13 and 8 years. The counts use the years of accession and of death as commonly given, not exact days, and the program prints the total and the longest and shortest reign.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as reign_ranks.py.
            2. Run it: python3 reign_ranks.py
        """,
        example = """
            REIGNS = [
                ("Ecgfrith of Northumbria", 670, 685),
                ("Tenmu of Japan", 673, 686),
                ("Wamba of the Visigoths", 672, 680),
            ]

            lengths = {name: end - start for name, start, end in REIGNS}
            for name, span in lengths.items():
                print(name, span, "years")
            print("total:", sum(lengths.values()), "years")
            longest = max(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            shortest = min(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            print("longest:", longest, lengths[longest], "years")
            print("shortest:", shortest, lengths[shortest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 660 to 670: the years of use of the Linde calendar from 665 to 728, counted in Python and C. */
val db138Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 138,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The years of use of the Linde calendar, from 665 to 728, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Linde li",
        author = "Li Chunfeng",
        year = 665,
        summary = "The Linde calendar, issued in 665 and last used in 728, is counted by a Python program and a C program that print the same two figures.",
        details = "The difference between the two years is 63, but counting both the year of issue and the last year gives 64 years of use, and the two programs print both figures. The sources give 728 as the calendar's end, and the Dayan calendar of 729 replaced it.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as linde_span.py, linde_span.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### linde_span.py
            ISSUED = 665     # the Linde calendar issued in 665, as usually given
            LAST_USED = 728  # its last year in use, as usually given
            print("difference between 665 and 728:", LAST_USED - ISSUED)
            print("years of use counting both ends:", LAST_USED - ISSUED + 1)
            ### linde_span.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int issued = 665, last_used = 728;
                printf("difference between 665 and 728: %d\n", last_used - issued);
                printf("years of use counting both ends: %d\n", last_used - issued + 1);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 linde_span.py > python.txt
            cc -o linde_span_c linde_span.c
            ./linde_span_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 660 to 670: how one Tang catty nests into taels, mace and fen, a placed record with 660 as its anchor year. */
val db138Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 138,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Tang",
        title = "How one Tang catty nests into taels, mace and fen, written out as code, placed at 660",
        originalTitle = "jin liang qian fen",
        author = "The Tang weights and measures",
        year = 660,
        summary = "One Tang catty is nested into sixteen taels, 160 qian and 1600 fen by a short program that prints the nesting for three weights.",
        details = "The nesting is a Tang weight rule: one jin is sixteen liang, a liang is ten qian, and a qian is ten fen. The record's year is an anchor and not the date of the weights: 660 is the year Empress Wu began to share the government while Gaozong was ill.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as tang_catty.py.
            2. Run it: python3 tang_catty.py
        """,
        example = """
            FEN_PER_QIAN = 10
            QIAN_PER_LIANG = 10
            LIANG_PER_JIN = 16

            def nest(jin):
                liang = jin * LIANG_PER_JIN
                qian = liang * QIAN_PER_LIANG
                fen = qian * FEN_PER_QIAN
                return liang, qian, fen

            for jin in (1, 3, 10):
                liang, qian, fen = nest(jin)
                print(jin, "jin =", liang, "liang =", qian, "qian =", fen, "fen")
        """,
    ),

)

val db138Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 138,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "The reigns of Heraclius, Constans II and Constantine IV, from 610 to 685, counted and ranked by a short program",
        originalTitle = "Heraclius, Constans II and Constantine IV",
        author = "The Byzantine emperors Heraclius, Constans II and Constantine IV",
        year = 668,
        summary = "The reigns of Heraclius, Constans II and Constantine IV are counted from their years of accession, then summed and ranked by a short program.",
        details = "Heraclius ruled from 610 to 641, Constans II from 641 until his death at Syracuse in 668, and Constantine IV from 668 to 685, so the spans are counted in whole years. The figures are approximate because the sources give years and not exact days.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as byzantine_reigns.py.
            2. Run it: python3 byzantine_reigns.py
        """,
        example = """
            REIGNS = [
                ("Heraclius", 610, 641),
                ("Constans II", 641, 668),
                ("Constantine IV", 668, 685),
            ]

            lengths = {name: end - start for name, start, end in REIGNS}
            for name, span in lengths.items():
                print(name, span, "years")
            print("total:", sum(lengths.values()), "years")
            longest = max(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            shortest = min(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            print("longest:", longest, lengths[longest], "years")
            print("shortest:", shortest, lengths[shortest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 650 to 660: the years between four dated items of the 650s, counted in Python and in C. */
val db139Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 139,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Mixed",
        title = "The years between the Yongwei code of 651, the Naniwa palace of 652, the Liber Iudiciorum of 654 and the Ten Canons of 656, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Yongwei lu, Liber Iudiciorum",
        author = "Several authors",
        year = 651,
        summary = "The years between four dated items of the 650s are counted by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The dates are the commonly given years of the four items, so the gaps of one, two and two years, and five from the first to the last, are arithmetic and not a claim about cause. The two programs print the same lines, and the script confirms the match.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as cross_gaps.py, cross_gaps.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### cross_gaps.py
            DATES = [
                ("Yongwei code", 651),
                ("Naniwa palace", 652),
                ("Liber Iudiciorum", 654),
                ("Ten Canons", 656),
            ]
            for (name_a, year_a), (name_b, year_b) in zip(DATES, DATES[1:]):
                print(f"{name_a} to {name_b}: {year_b - year_a} years")
            print(f"first to last: {DATES[-1][1] - DATES[0][1]} years")
            ### cross_gaps.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int yongwei = 651, naniwa = 652, liber = 654, canons = 656;
                printf("Yongwei code to Naniwa palace: %d years\n", naniwa - yongwei);
                printf("Naniwa palace to Liber Iudiciorum: %d years\n", liber - naniwa);
                printf("Liber Iudiciorum to Ten Canons: %d years\n", canons - liber);
                printf("first to last: %d years\n", canons - yongwei);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 cross_gaps.py > python.txt
            cc -o cross_gaps_c cross_gaps.c
            ./cross_gaps_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 650 to 660: the fangcheng method of the Nine Chapters, which solves three grades of grain by elimination, worked out by a program. */
val db139Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 139,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "How three grades of grain are found by elimination, the fangcheng method of the Nine Chapters, worked out by a program",
        originalTitle = "Jiuzhang suanshu",
        author = "Anonymous, Han period",
        year = 656,
        summary = "The fangcheng method, which finds the values of three grades of grain by elimination, comes from the Nine Chapters and is worked out here by a program.",
        details = "The sources do not date this method, which is far older than 656, so the year here is the anchor of the Tang edition of the Ten Canons that carries it, not the year of the method. Its grain problem gives 9 and a quarter, 4 and a quarter, and 2 and three quarters dou per bundle, and the program prints each figure with a check on the three totals.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as fangcheng_grain.py.
            2. Run it: python3 fangcheng_grain.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            # Three fields of grain, one row each: the coefficients of the superior, medium and inferior bundles, then the total.
            FIELDS = [
                [Fraction(3), Fraction(2), Fraction(1), Fraction(39)],
                [Fraction(2), Fraction(3), Fraction(1), Fraction(34)],
                [Fraction(1), Fraction(2), Fraction(3), Fraction(26)],
            ]
            GRADES = ["superior", "medium", "inferior"]


            def solve(rows):
                size = len(rows)
                table = [list(row) for row in rows]
                for col in range(size):
                    pivot = table[col][col]
                    table[col] = [value / pivot for value in table[col]]
                    for other in range(size):
                        if other != col and table[other][col] != 0:
                            factor = table[other][col]
                            table[other] = [a - factor * b for a, b in zip(table[other], table[col])]
                return [table[i][size] for i in range(size)]


            answer = solve(FIELDS)
            for grade, value in zip(GRADES, answer):
                print(grade, "bundle:", float(value), "dou")
            for number, row in enumerate(FIELDS, start=1):
                total = sum(c * x for c, x in zip(row[:3], answer))
                print("field", number, "check:", total)
        """,
    ),

)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db13Cross.kt
################################################################################
package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1910 to 1920: the same integers from C and Python, checked by a run script. */
val db13Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "C and Python",
        title = "C and Python compute Ramanujan's tau coefficients",
        originalTitle = "On certain arithmetical functions (Ramanujan, 1916)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1916,
        summary = "Expanding q times the product of (1 - q^n) to the 24th power gives Ramanujan's tau function, and a C program and a Python program print the same first five values.",
        details = "Ramanujan's 1916 paper introduced tau(n) as the coefficient of q^n in q times the product of (1 - q^n) to the power 24. The two programs multiply truncated power series and print the coefficients of the first five terms, and the run script checks that the two outputs match, as a conformance test does.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### tau.py
            def mul(a, b, n):
                # Product of two truncated power series, keeping the coefficients of q to the power 0 up to n - 1.
                out = [0] * n
                for i, x in enumerate(a[:n]):
                    for j, y in enumerate(b[:n - i]):
                        out[i + j] += x * y
                return out


            N = 5   # coefficients of q to the power 0 to 4
            P = [1] + [0] * (N - 1)
            for k in range(1, N):
                factor = [0] * N
                factor[0] = 1
                factor[k] = -1   # the factor 1 - q^k
                for _ in range(24):
                    P = mul(P, factor, N)
            print(" ".join(str(c) for c in P))
            ### tau.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            #define N 5

            /* Product of two power series, keeping the coefficients of q to the power 0 up to N - 1. */
            static void mul(const long a[N], const long b[N], long out[N]) {
                long tmp[N] = {0};
                for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
                    for (int j = 0; i + j < N; j++)
                        tmp[i + j] += a[i] * b[j];
                for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
                    out[i] = tmp[i];
            }

            int main(void) {
                long P[N] = {1, 0, 0, 0, 0};
                for (int k = 1; k < N; k++) {
                    long factor[N] = {0};
                    factor[0] = 1;
                    factor[k] = -1;
                    for (int e = 0; e < 24; e++) {
                        long next[N];
                        mul(P, factor, next);
                        for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
                            P[i] = next[i];
                    }
                }
                for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
                    printf("%ld%s", P[i], i + 1 < N ? " " : "\n");
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 tau.py > python.txt
            cc -o tau tau.c
            ./tau > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "C and Python",
        title = "C and Python check Ramanujan's partition congruence",
        originalTitle = "Congruence properties of the partition function (Ramanujan, 1919)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1919,
        summary = "The number of partitions of 5n plus 4 is a multiple of 5, and a Python program and a C program print six such values that agree.",
        details = "Ramanujan announced congruences for the partition function in 1919, among them p(5n+4) divisible by 5. The two programs count partitions with the same table of part sizes, print p(n) for n equal to 4, 9, 14, 19, 24 and 29 with a divisibility check, and the run script compares the two outputs.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### partitions.py
            def partitions(limit):
                # p[n] counts the partitions of n; each allowed part size is added in turn, as in a coin-change table.
                p = [1] + [0] * limit
                for part in range(1, limit + 1):
                    for n in range(part, limit + 1):
                        p[n] += p[n - part]
                return p


            p = partitions(30)
            for n in range(4, 31, 5):
                print(n, p[n], p[n] % 5 == 0)
            ### partitions.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                long p[31] = {0};
                p[0] = 1;
                for (int part = 1; part <= 30; part++)
                    for (int n = part; n <= 30; n++)
                        p[n] += p[n - part];
                for (int n = 4; n <= 30; n += 5)
                    printf("%d %ld %s\n", n, p[n], p[n] % 5 == 0 ? "True" : "False");
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 partitions.py > python.txt
            cc -o partitions partitions.c
            ./partitions > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),
)

        details = "Carmichael's 1910 note identified 561 as a composite number that passes Fermat's test for every base coprime to it. The example checks every odd number below 1000 in two ways, by testing all bases and by Korselt's criterion, and both give 561 alone.         instructions = """

        example = """
            import math


            def is_prime(n):
                return n > 1 and all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))


            def fermat_for_all_bases(n):
                # A composite n that passes Fermat's test for every base coprime to n is a Carmichael number.
                return not is_prime(n) and all(pow(a, n - 1, n) == 1 for a in range(2, n) if math.gcd(a, n) == 1)


            def korselt(n):
                # Korselt's criterion: n is squarefree and p - 1 divides n - 1 for every prime p dividing n.
                primes = [p for p in range(2, n + 1) if n % p == 0 and is_prime(p)]
                squarefree = all(n % (p * p) != 0 for p in primes)
                return len(primes) >= 2 and squarefree and all((n - 1) % (p - 1) == 0 for p in primes)


            odd = range(3, 1000, 2)
            print("Fermat test:", [n for n in odd if fermat_for_all_bases(n)])
            print("Korselt:", [n for n in odd if korselt(n)])
            print("3 * 11 * 17 = 561:", 3 * 11 * 17 == 561)
        """,

        originalTitle = "On an absolute criterion for fitting frequency curves (Fisher, 1912)",
        author = "Ronald Aylmer Fisher",
        year = 1912,
        summary = "Fisher's 1912 criterion picks the parameter that makes the observed data most probable, which for seven heads in ten tosses is p = 0.7.",
        details = "Fisher's first paper on the method appeared in 1912 in the Messenger of Mathematics. The example takes seven heads in ten tosses, writes the likelihood as p to the seventh power times (1 - p) cubed, and searches a grid of probabilities for its largest value. The grid search lands on 0.70, the observed fraction, as setting the derivative to zero predicts.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as mle.py.
            2. Run it: python3 mle.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            heads, tosses = 7, 10


            def log_likelihood(p):
                # Log of p to the power of the heads, times (1 - p) to the power of the tails.
                return heads * math.log(p) + (tosses - heads) * math.log(1 - p)


            grid = [k / 100 for k in range(1, 100)]
            best = max(grid, key=log_likelihood)
            print(f"best p on the grid: {best:.2f}")
            print(f"log-likelihood at best: {log_likelihood(best):.4f}")
            print(f"heads/tosses: {heads / tosses:.2f}")

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Ciphers",
        title = "How the ADFGVX cipher works, step by step",
        originalTitle = "ADFGVX field cipher of the German army (Nebel, 1918)",
        author = "Fritz Nebel",
        year = 1918,
        summary = "A six-by-six square turns each letter into a pair of ADFGVX letters, and a columnar transposition then scrambles the pairs, which made the German field cipher hard to read in 1918.",
        details = "Fritz Nebel's cipher entered German army use in March 1918. The six-letter form, in use from 1 June 1918, was broken by Georges Painvin in early June. The example uses a plain square with no keyword, so each stage is visible: it fractionates ATTACK, transposes the result with the key CAB, then reverses both stages to recover the message.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as adfgvx.py.
            2. Run it: python3 adfgvx.py
        """,
        example = """
            ALPHABET = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789"
            LABELS = "ADFGVX"


            def fractionate(text):
                # Each character becomes two labels: its row, then its column in the 6 by 6 square.
                out = []
                for ch in text:
                    i = ALPHABET.index(ch)
                    out.append(LABELS[i // 6] + LABELS[i % 6])
                return "".join(out)


            def transpose(text, key):
                # Write the text in rows under the key, then read the columns in alphabetical order of the key letters.
                columns = [text[c::len(key)] for c in range(len(key))]
                order = sorted(range(len(key)), key=lambda c: key[c])
                return "".join(columns[c] for c in order)


            def untranspose(text, key):
                n = len(key)
                rows = len(text) // n
                order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda c: key[c])
                columns = {}
                pos = 0
                for c in order:
                    columns[c] = text[pos:pos + rows]
                    pos += rows
                return "".join(columns[c][r] for r in range(rows) for c in range(n))


            def defractionate(text):
                out = []
                for i in range(0, len(text), 2):
                    row = LABELS.index(text[i])
                    col = LABELS.index(text[i + 1])
                    out.append(ALPHABET[row * 6 + col])
                return "".join(out)


            key = "CAB"
            fractions = fractionate("ATTACK")
            cipher = transpose(fractions, key)
            print("fractionated:", fractions)
            print("cipher:", cipher)
            print("recovered:", defractionate(untranspose(cipher, key)))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Signals",
        title = "How the Haar transform splits a signal",
        originalTitle = "Zur Theorie der orthogonalen Funktionensysteme (Haar, 1910)",
        author = "Alfred Haar",
        year = 1910,
        summary = "The Haar transform replaces each pair of values by their average and half difference and repeats on the averages, so a signal splits into one coarse average and finer details.",
        details = "Haar's 1910 paper on orthogonal function systems on the interval [0,1] contains the system now called the Haar system, which is usually cited as the first wavelet basis. The example applies the step three times to an eight-value signal, prints the detail coefficients from coarse to fine, and rebuilds the signal exactly from them.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as haar.py.
            2. Run it: python3 haar.py
        """,
        example = """
            def haar(values):
                # Replace each pair by its average and its half difference, then repeat on the averages.
                details = []
                current = list(values)
                while len(current) > 1:
                    averages = [(current[i] + current[i + 1]) // 2 for i in range(0, len(current), 2)]
                    diffs = [(current[i] - current[i + 1]) // 2 for i in range(0, len(current), 2)]
                    details.append(diffs)
                    current = averages
                return current[0], details


            def inverse(average, details):
                # Undo the steps from the coarsest level down: each average splits into average plus and minus its difference.
                current = [average]
                for diffs in reversed(details):
                    rebuilt = []
                    for a, d in zip(current, diffs):
                        rebuilt.extend([a + d, a - d])
                    current = rebuilt
                return current


            signal = [8, 6, 2, 4, 10, 2, 6, 10]
            average, details = haar(signal)
            print("average:", average)
            for level, diffs in enumerate(reversed(details), start=1):
                print(f"detail level {level}:", diffs)
            print("reconstructed equals input:", inverse(average, details) == signal)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,

        title = "How Pocklington's test proves a number prime",

        author = "Henry Cabourn Pocklington",
        year = 1914,
        summary = "If a factored part of n minus 1 is larger than the square root of n, and a base passes the test for each of its prime factors, then n is prime, without factoring all of n minus 1.",
        details = "Pocklington presented the method in 1914 in a paper on the determination of prime or composite nature by Fermat's theorem. The example certifies 101 from the factors of 100, and shows that 91 is composite because base 2 fails the Fermat congruence. Taking only the factors 2 and 5 of 100, the product 10 is too small for 101, and the program reports that.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as pocklington.py.
            2. Run it: python3 pocklington.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math


            def certify(n, factors):
                # factors maps each prime q dividing n - 1 to its exponent; F is the product of the known prime powers.
                f = 1
                for q, e in factors.items():
                    f *= q ** e
                if f * f <= n:
                    return "not enough factors"
                for a in range(2, 20):
                    if pow(a, n - 1, n) != 1:
                        return f"composite: base {a} gives {a}^{n - 1} mod {n} = {pow(a, n - 1, n)}"
                    if all(math.gcd(pow(a, (n - 1) // q, n) - 1, n) == 1 for q in factors):
                        return f"prime, certified with base {a}"
                return "no certificate found"


            known = {2: 2, 5: 2}
            print(f"101: {certify(101, known)}")
            print("101 with F = 10: " + certify(101, {2: 1, 5: 1}))
            print(f"91: {certify(91, {2: 1, 3: 2, 5: 1})}")
        """,

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind

/** Projects of 1910 to 1920: small programs for a moving line, a text Gantt chart, a loaded bar and a nested radical. */
val db13Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Production",
        title = "A moving assembly line simulator",
        originalTitle = "Highland Park moving assembly line, chassis line of 1913",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1913,
        summary = "A belt moves each car past four stations at a fixed pace set by the slowest task, so a car leaves every five minutes and the line turns out twelve cars an hour.",
        details = "Ford's chassis line of October 1913 used a belt with one task at each station, and the magneto work of April 1913 had been split into 29 operations. The example uses four stations with work times of 3, 5, 4 and 2 minutes and five cars, and prints the belt pace, the idle time at each station and the times at which the first and the fifth cars leave.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as ford_line.py.
            2. Run it: python3 ford_line.py
        """,
        example = """
            TASKS = [3, 5, 4, 2]   # minutes of work at each station along the line
            CARS = 5
            PACE = max(TASKS)      # the belt moves once the slowest station has finished its task
            stations = len(TASKS)
            leave = []
            for car in range(CARS):
                # Car number car is at station s during slot car + s, and it leaves after the last slot.
                last_slot = car + stations - 1
                leave.append((last_slot + 1) * PACE)
            print("belt pace:", PACE, "minutes")
            print("cars per hour:", 60 // PACE)
            print("idle minutes at each station:", [PACE - t for t in TASKS])
            print("idle minutes per car:", sum(PACE - t for t in TASKS))
            print("first car leaves at minute", leave[0])
            print("fifth car leaves at minute", leave[-1])
            print("one worker per car, five cars:", CARS * sum(TASKS), "minutes")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Scheduling",
        title = "A Gantt chart drawn in plain text",
        originalTitle = "Gantt's charts of schedules, from his articles of 1910 and 1915",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1910,
        summary = "A Gantt chart puts each task on a time axis as a bar, so the length of a schedule and the overlap of tasks can be read at a glance.",
        details = "Gantt's charts of the 1910s spread the bar of time in the West, after Karol Adamiecki had used a similar chart, his harmonogram, in the 1890s. The example draws four tasks as text bars over eight weeks, with a header line of week numbers, and prints the length of the project.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as gantt.py.
            2. Run it: python3 gantt.py
        """,
        example = """
            TASKS = [
                ("design", 0, 2),
                ("build", 2, 3),
                ("test", 5, 2),
                ("ship", 7, 1),
            ]
            weeks = max(start + length for _, start, length in TASKS)
            print("week:  " + "".join(str(w % 10) for w in range(weeks)))
            for name, start, length in TASKS:
                bar = "." * start + "#" * length + "." * (weeks - start - length)
                print(f"{name:<6} " + bar)
            print(f"project length: {weeks} weeks")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Elasticity",
        title = "A Galerkin approximation for a loaded bar",
        originalTitle = "Rods and plates, a paper in Vestnik inzhenerov i tekhnikov (Galerkin, 1915)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1915,
        summary = "Galerkin's method makes the error orthogonal to each basis function, and with one basis function the answer is exact at the midpoint of the bar but not at a quarter point.",
        details = "Galerkin's 1915 paper on rods and plates gave the method, which chooses coefficients so that the error is orthogonal to the basis. The example solves minus u'' equals x on the unit interval, with u zero at both ends, using the single basis function x(1 - x). It evaluates the integrals with Simpson's rule, which is exact for cubics.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as galerkin.py.
            2. Run it: python3 galerkin.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction as F


            def simpson(g):
                # Simpson's rule on [0, 1] with two panels, which is exact for polynomials up to degree three.
                return (g(F(0)) + 4 * g(F(1, 2)) + g(F(1))) / 6


            stiffness = simpson(lambda x: (1 - 2 * x) ** 2)   # integral of the square of the derivative of x(1 - x)
            load = simpson(lambda x: x * x * (1 - x))         # integral of f(x) = x times the basis function x(1 - x)
            c = load / stiffness
            print("coefficient:", c)
            for x in (F(1, 4), F(1, 2)):
                print(f"x={x}: galerkin {c * x * (1 - x)}, exact {(x - x ** 3) / 6}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 13,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Algebra",
        title = "Ramanujan's nested radical converging to 3",
        originalTitle = "Question 289, Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society (Ramanujan, 1911)",
        author = "Srinivasa Ramanujan",
        year = 1911,
        summary = "The nested radical with coefficients 2, 3, 4 and so on equals 3, and each level of its inner folding has the exact value k plus 2.",
        details = "Ramanujan posed the nested radical as Question 289 in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society in 1911 and gave the answer himself. The example folds outward from the exact tail value 7 and prints the four levels, which are 6, 5, 4 and 3, then checks the identity that holds at every level.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as nested_radical.py.
            2. Run it: python3 nested_radical.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            # Ramanujan's nested radical: 3 = sqrt(1 + 2 sqrt(1 + 3 sqrt(1 + 4 sqrt(...)))).
            # Level k satisfies g(k) = sqrt(1 + (k + 1) g(k + 1)), and the exact value at every level is k + 2.
            levels = []
            g = 7.0   # exact value at level 5, which is 5 + 2
            for k in range(4, 0, -1):
                g = math.sqrt(1 + (k + 1) * g)
                levels.append(g)
            print("levels from the tail 7:", levels)
            print("identity holds for k = 1 to 6:", all(1 + (k + 1) * (k + 3) == (k + 2) ** 2 for k in range(1, 7)))
        """,
    ),
)

    entry(
        databaseId = 140,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The lifespan of Taizong, 598 to 649, computed in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Taizong",
        author = "Li Shimin, Emperor Taizong of Tang",
        year = 649,
        summary = "Taizong, the second Tang emperor, lived from 598 to 649, and a Python program and a C program both print his age at death as 51.",
        details = "Taizong was born in 598 and died in 649, so by the simple count of years he was 51 at his death. The two programs print the same figure, which checks the subtraction only.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as taizong_age.py, taizong_age.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### taizong_age.py
            BIRTH = 598  # Taizong's birth year, as usually given
            DEATH = 649  # Taizong's death year, as usually given
            print("age at death:", DEATH - BIRTH)
            ### taizong_age.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int birth = 598, death = 649;
                printf("age at death: %d\n", death - birth);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 taizong_age.py > python.txt
            cc -o taizong_age_c taizong_age.c
            ./taizong_age_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 640 to 650: how a split vote among Umar's six electors of 644 is settled, worked out by a short program. */
val db140Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 140,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Arabic",
        title = "How a split vote among Umar's six electors of 644 is settled, worked out by a short program",
        originalTitle = "al-shura",
        author = "Umar ibn al-Khattab",
        year = 644,
        summary = "A split vote among six electors is settled by counting the ballots and, in a tie, by the choice of the arbiter, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf.",
        details = "The tie rule is the one most often reported for Umar's council, and the two ballot sets in the example are illustrations, not the recorded votes. Accounts differ on the exact wording of Umar's instruction, so the rule is given here in its most common form.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as umar_council.py.
            2. Run it: python3 umar_council.py
        """,
        example = """
            ARBITER = "Abd al-Rahman"

            SAMPLE_A = [
                ("Ali", "Ali"),
                ("Uthman", "Uthman"),
                ("Talha", "Ali"),
                ("Zubayr", "Uthman"),
                ("Sa'd", "Ali"),
                ("Abd al-Rahman", "Uthman"),
            ]
            SAMPLE_B = [
                ("Ali", "Uthman"),
                ("Uthman", "Uthman"),
                ("Talha", "Uthman"),
                ("Zubayr", "Ali"),
                ("Sa'd", "Uthman"),
                ("Abd al-Rahman", "Ali"),
            ]

            def settle(ballots):
                counts = {}
                for voter, choice in ballots:
                    counts[choice] = counts.get(choice, 0) + 1
                top = max(counts.values())
                leaders = [name for name, n in counts.items() if n == top]
                if len(leaders) == 1:
                    return leaders[0], "majority of " + str(top)
                return dict(ballots)[ARBITER], "tie settled by the arbiter"

            for label, ballots in (("sample A", SAMPLE_A), ("sample B", SAMPLE_B)):
                winner, how = settle(ballots)
                print(label + ":", winner, "via", how)
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 140,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Visigothic",
        title = "The Councils of Toledo from 633 to 653, the gaps between them counted by a short program",
        originalTitle = "Concilium Toletanum",
        author = "Visigothic bishops and kings",
        year = 646,
        summary = "The Visigothic councils of Toledo, held in 633, 636, 638, 646 and 653, are spaced out by a short program that prints each gap and the total span.",
        details = "The councils were church assemblies held in the Visigothic kingdom of Spain, and the seventh of them met in 646. The gaps the program prints are 3, 2, 8 and 7 years, which add up to a span of 20 years from the first council to the last.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as toledo_gaps.py.
            2. Run it: python3 toledo_gaps.py
        """,
        example = """
            COUNCILS = [("Fourth", 633), ("Fifth", 636), ("Sixth", 638), ("Seventh", 646), ("Eighth", 653)]
            gaps = []
            for (name_a, year_a), (name_b, year_b) in zip(COUNCILS, COUNCILS[1:]):
                gaps.append(year_b - year_a)
                print(name_a, "council", year_a, "to", name_b, "council", year_b, ":", year_b - year_a, "years")
            print("longest gap:", max(gaps), "years")
            print("total span:", COUNCILS[-1][1] - COUNCILS[0][1], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 630 to 640: Isidore's twenty books of the Etymologies, counted in Python and in C. */
val db141Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 141,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Latin",
        title = "Isidore's twenty books of the Etymologies, counted in Python and C, with the books on words and on things counted apart",
        originalTitle = "Etymologiae sive Originum libri XX",
        author = "Isidore of Seville",
        year = 630,
        summary = "A Python program and a C program count the twenty books of Isidore's Etymologies, ten on words and ten on things, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The work is usually described as twenty books, the first ten on words and learning and the last ten on things, so both programs print the same three figures. The check confirms the arithmetic only, while the book count and the grouping come from the usual description of the work.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as etym_books.py, etym_books.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### etym_books.py
            BOOKS = 20   # the twenty books of the Etymologies
            WORDS = 10   # the books on words and learning, I to X
            THINGS = BOOKS - WORDS
            print("books in the Etymologies:", BOOKS)
            print("books on words and learning:", WORDS)
            print("books on things:", THINGS)
            ### etym_books.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int books = 20, words = 10;
                printf("books in the Etymologies: %d\n", books);
                printf("books on words and learning: %d\n", words);
                printf("books on things: %d\n", books - words);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 etym_books.py > python.txt
            cc -o etym_books_c etym_books.c
            ./etym_books_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 141,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Arab",
        title = "How the camel zakat of the Abu Bakr letter is worked out for a herd, written as a program, placed at 632",
        originalTitle = "Kitab Abi Bakr",
        author = "Abu Bakr, carrying out a letter attributed to the Prophet",
        year = 632,
        summary = "A short program works out the camel zakat of the Abu Bakr letter band by band for herds of up to ninety camels.",
        details = "The letter sets a sheep for each five camels up to 24, a bint makhad (a she-camel in her second year) from 25 camels, a bint labun (third year) from 36, a hiqqah (fourth year) from 46, a jadha'ah (fifth year) from 61, and two bint labun from 76. The sources do not date the letter; 632, the year Abu Bakr became caliph, is the anchor used here, not the year the letter was written, and the schedule is recorded in the hadith collections of Bukhari and Tirmidhi.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as camel_zakat.py.
            2. Run it: python3 camel_zakat.py
        """,
        example = """
            BANDS = [
                (5, 9, "one sheep"),
                (10, 14, "two sheep"),
                (15, 19, "three sheep"),
                (20, 24, "four sheep"),
                (25, 35, "one bint makhad"),
                (36, 45, "one bint labun"),
                (46, 60, "one hiqqah"),
                (61, 75, "one jadha'ah"),
                (76, 90, "two bint labun"),
            ]

            def due(camels):
                if camels < 5:
                    return "nothing due"
                for low, high, animals in BANDS:
                    if low <= camels <= high:
                        return animals
                return "outside this table"

            for camels in (4, 5, 12, 24, 25, 35, 36, 45, 46, 60, 61, 75, 76, 90, 91):
                print(camels, "camels:", due(camels))
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 630 to 640: three dated events of 630 to 634 from China, the steppe and Arabia, sorted and gapped by a short program. */
val db141Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 141,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Dated events",
        title = "Three dated events of 630 to 634 from China, the Turkish steppe and Arabia, put in order with the years between them",
        originalTitle = "Tang, Eastern Turks, Muhammad and Umar",
        author = "The courts and armies named in the events",
        year = 630,
        summary = "Three events of 630 to 634, a Tang victory over the Eastern Turks, the death of Muhammad and the accession of Umar, are sorted by a short program that prints the years between them.",
        details = "The usual dates are 630 for the Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks, 632 for the death of Muhammad and 634 for Umar's accession, and the program sorts them and prints the gap between each pair. None of the three events is a record of this database, and the years are the ones given in the usual histories.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as event_gaps.py.
            2. Run it: python3 event_gaps.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                (634, "Umar becomes the second caliph"),
                (630, "the Tang army defeats the Eastern Turks"),
                (632, "the Prophet Muhammad dies"),
            ]

            events = sorted(EVENTS)
            for year, what in events:
                print(year, what)
            for (first, _), (second, _) in zip(events, events[1:]):
                print("years between", first, "and", second, ":", second - first)
            print("span from the first to the last event:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 620 to 630: the years between the Wude code, Taizong's seizure of power and Bhaskara I's commentary, counted in Python and in C. */
val db142Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 142,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The years between the Wude code of 624, Taizong's seizure of power in 626 and Bhaskara I's commentary of 629, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "The years between the Wude code of 624, Taizong's seizure of power in 626 and Bhaskara I's commentary of 629, counted in Python and C",
        author = "Various",
        year = 624,
        summary = "A Python program and a C program count the years between three dated events of 624 to 629, and a script checks that both print the same figures.",
        details = "The Wude code is dated 624, Taizong took power in 626 and Bhaskara I's commentary is dated 629, so the gaps are 2, 3 and 5 years. The two programs print the same figures, so the check confirms the arithmetic, while the dates come from the usual accounts of each item.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as years.py, years.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### years.py
            WUDE = 624     # the Wude code, as usually dated
            XUANWU = 626   # Taizong's seizure of power at the Xuanwu Gate
            BHASKARA = 629 # Bhaskara I's commentary on the Aryabhatiya
            print("from the Wude code to the Xuanwu Gate:", XUANWU - WUDE)
            print("from the Xuanwu Gate to the commentary:", BHASKARA - XUANWU)
            print("from the Wude code to the commentary:", BHASKARA - WUDE)
            ### years.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int wude = 624, xuanwu = 626, bhaskara = 629;
                printf("from the Wude code to the Xuanwu Gate: %d\n", xuanwu - wude);
                printf("from the Xuanwu Gate to the commentary: %d\n", bhaskara - xuanwu);
                printf("from the Wude code to the commentary: %d\n", bhaskara - wude);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 years.py > python.txt
            cc -o years_c years.c
            ./years_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 620 to 630: Bhaskara I's rational formula for the sine, written out as code and checked against the true sine. */
val db142Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 142,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Sanskrit",
        title = "How Bhaskara I's rational formula gives the sine of an angle, checked against the true sine by a program",
        originalTitle = "jya",
        author = "Bhaskara I",
        year = 629,
        summary = "Bhaskara I's rational formula gives the sine of an angle from a few products and a division, and a short program prints it beside the true sine.",
        details = "Bhaskara I states the rule under Aryabhata's name in his Mahabhaskariya, and some accounts tie it to his commentary of 629 instead, so 629 is the date of the commentary and not a settled date for the rule. The example takes pi as 180 degrees, so each value is an exact fraction that a program can print.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as bhaskara_sine.py.
            2. Run it: python3 bhaskara_sine.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction
            import math

            def bhaskara_sine(degrees):
                # Bhaskara's rule with pi taken as 180 degrees
                product = degrees * (180 - degrees)
                return Fraction(16 * product, 5 * 180 * 180 - 4 * product)

            for degrees in (30, 45, 60, 90):
                approx = bhaskara_sine(degrees)
                exact = math.sin(math.radians(degrees))
                print(f"{degrees} degrees: {approx} = {float(approx):.4f}, sine {exact:.4f}")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 620 to 630: three dated events of Arabia, sorted by a short program that counts the years between them. */
val db142Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 142,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Arabic",
        title = "Three events of 624 to 630 in Arabia, the battle of Badr, the truce of Hudaybiyya and the taking of Mecca, sorted and spaced in code",
        originalTitle = "Three events of 624 to 630 in Arabia, the battle of Badr, the truce of Hudaybiyya and the taking of Mecca, sorted and spaced in code",
        author = "Ibn Ishaq and later biographers",
        year = 624,
        summary = "A short program sorts three events of Arabia from 624 to 630 and prints the years between the first and the last.",
        details = "Early Islamic biographies date the battle of Badr to 624, the truce of Hudaybiyya to 628 and the taking of Mecca to 630, in the Common Era reckoning used here. The program counts the gap from the first event to the last, so the result depends only on those three dates.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as arabia_events.py.
            2. Run it: python3 arabia_events.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                ("taking of Mecca", 630),
                ("battle of Badr", 624),
                ("truce of Hudaybiyya", 628),
            ]
            for name, year in sorted(EVENTS, key=lambda event: event[1]):
                print(year, name)
            first = min(year for _, year in EVENTS)
            last = max(year for _, year in EVENTS)
            print("years from Badr to Mecca:", last - first)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 610 to 620: three dates of the early 610s subtracted in Python and in C. */
val db143Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 143,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Japanese",
        title = "The gaps from Docho's entry in 610 to the Hokke gisho of 615 and the Wuyin calendar of 618, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Hokke gisho",
        author = "Compilers of the Nihon Shoki",
        year = 610,
        summary = "Three dates of the 610s are subtracted by a Python program and by a C program, and a script checks that both print the same gaps.",
        details = "The gaps are 5 years from 610 to 615, 8 years from 610 to 618 and 3 years from 615 to 618, and the two programs print the same lines, so the check confirms the arithmetic. The dates are the usual ones: 610 for the Nihon Shoki entry, 615 for the traditional date of the Hokke gisho, and 618 for the Wuyin calendar, whose rollout some accounts give as 619.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as docho_gaps.py, docho_gaps.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### docho_gaps.py
            PAPER = 610  # the Nihon Shoki entry for the monk Docho, 610
            HOKKE = 615  # the Hokke gisho, traditionally dated 615
            WUYIN = 618  # the Wuyin calendar, adopted 618
            print("gap from 610 to 615:", HOKKE - PAPER)
            print("gap from 610 to 618:", WUYIN - PAPER)
            print("gap from 615 to 618:", WUYIN - HOKKE)
            ### docho_gaps.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int paper = 610, hokke = 615, wuyin = 618;
                printf("gap from 610 to 615: %d\n", hokke - paper);
                printf("gap from 610 to 618: %d\n", wuyin - paper);
                printf("gap from 615 to 618: %d\n", wuyin - hokke);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 docho_gaps.py > python.txt
            cc -o docho_gaps_c docho_gaps.c
            ./docho_gaps_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 610 to 620: how a Tang weight of jin, liang and qian is totalled in qian, worked out by a program. */
val db143Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 143,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "How a Tang weight of jin, liang and qian is turned into qian and back, worked out by a program",
        originalTitle = "jin liang qian",
        author = "Tang officials",
        year = 618,
        summary = "A Tang weight written in jin, liang and qian is turned into qian by a short program, using the ratios of 16 liang to a jin and 10 qian to a liang.",
        details = "The usual accounts do not date this unit rule; 618, the founding year of the Tang, is only the anchor for the record. The program multiplies the weights out and splits the total again with divmod, so a reader can check a sum by hand.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as jin_liang.py.
            2. Run it: python3 jin_liang.py
        """,
        example = """
            JIN_LIANG = 16      # liang in one jin
            LIANG_QIAN = 10     # qian in one liang
            QIAN_PER_JIN = JIN_LIANG * LIANG_QIAN

            def to_qian(jin, liang, qian):
                return jin * QIAN_PER_JIN + liang * LIANG_QIAN + qian

            def split(total):
                jin, rest = divmod(total, QIAN_PER_JIN)
                liang, qian = divmod(rest, LIANG_QIAN)
                return jin, liang, qian

            weights = [(1, 0, 0), (2, 5, 7), (0, 15, 9)]
            for jin, liang, qian in weights:
                print(f"{jin} jin {liang} liang {qian} qian = {to_qian(jin, liang, qian)} qian")
            total = sum(to_qian(*w) for w in weights)
            print("total:", total, "qian")
            jin, liang, qian = split(total)
            print(f"total in jin, liang and qian: {jin} jin {liang} liang {qian} qian")
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 143,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "East Asian",
        title = "Spans of three East Asian rulers, from 593 to 628, counted and sorted in a short program",
        originalTitle = "Suiko tenno, Yangdi and Gaozu",
        author = "Empress Suiko, Yang Di and Li Yuan",
        year = 618,
        summary = "The reigns of Empress Suiko, Sui Yangdi and Tang Gaozu are counted from accession to end, and a short program sorts them by length.",
        details = "Suiko's reign runs from 593 to 628, Yangdi's from 604 to 618 and Gaozu's from 618 to 626, and the lengths are counted in whole years from the years of accession and not from exact days. The three reigns belong to different states, so the program compares only their lengths.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as east_reigns.py.
            2. Run it: python3 east_reigns.py
        """,
        example = """
            REIGNS = [
                ("Empress Suiko of Japan", 593, 628),
                ("Sui Yangdi", 604, 618),
                ("Tang Gaozu", 618, 626),
            ]

            lengths = {name: end - start for name, start, end in REIGNS}
            for name, span in lengths.items():
                print(name, span, "years")
            print("total:", sum(lengths.values()), "years")
            longest = max(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            shortest = min(lengths, key=lengths.get)
            print("longest:", longest, lengths[longest], "years")
            print("shortest:", shortest, lengths[shortest], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 144,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The 609 census written in groups of ten thousand, computed in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "wan (ten thousand)",
        author = "Sui court under Emperor Yang",
        year = 609,
        summary = "The census totals of 609 are split into groups of ten thousand, the Chinese unit wan, by a Python program and by a C program that print the same result.",
        details = "Chinese numbers group by ten thousand rather than by a thousand, so 46,019,956 people is written as 4601 wan 9956, and 8,907,546 households as 890 wan 7546. The two programs print the same two lines, and a script checks that the outputs agree.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as wan_census.py, wan_census.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### wan_census.py
            PEOPLE = 46019956       # the people counted in 609, as the Sui history gives them
            HOUSEHOLDS = 8907546    # the households counted in 609
            print("people:", PEOPLE // 10000, "wan", PEOPLE % 10000)
            print("households:", HOUSEHOLDS // 10000, "wan", HOUSEHOLDS % 10000)
            ### wan_census.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                long people = 46019956, households = 8907546;
                printf("people: %ld wan %04ld\n", people / 10000, people % 10000);
                printf("households: %ld wan %04ld\n", households / 10000, households % 10000);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 wan_census.py > python.txt
            cc -o wan_census_c wan_census.c
            ./wan_census_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 144,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The Sui examination of 605 and its abolition in 1905, a span of 1300 years counted in code",
        originalTitle = "keju",
        author = "Sui court under Emperor Yang",

/** One guide of 600 to 610: how a syllable is placed in the entering tone of the Qieyun, worked out by a short program. */
val db144Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 144,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "How a syllable is placed in the entering tone when its final sound is a stop, p, t or k",
        originalTitle = "ru sheng (entering tone)",
        author = "Compilers of the Qieyun",
        year = 601,
        summary = "A syllable whose final sound is a stop, written here as p, t or k, falls in the entering tone, one of the four tone classes of the Qieyun, and a short program can sort it.",
        details = "The Qieyun of 601 divides its syllables into four tones, and the entering tone is marked by a final stop, so 601 is the year of the dictionary that applied the rule, not the date of the rule itself. The example uses Latin stand-in syllables, not the readings of any real character.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as entering_tone.py.
            2. Run it: python3 entering_tone.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Stand-in syllables, not real readings: a final p, t or k places a syllable in the entering tone.
            SYLLABLES = ["dap", "sin", "kuk", "tang", "mit", "ung"]
            STOPS = ("p", "t", "k")

            entering = [s for s in SYLLABLES if s.endswith(STOPS)]
            others = [s for s in SYLLABLES if not s.endswith(STOPS)]

            print("entering tone:", " ".join(entering))
            print("other tones:", " ".join(others))
            print("counts:", len(entering), len(others))
        """,
    ),

)
