package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 590 to 600: the book counts of four works of the decade, totalled and ranked in Python and in C. */
val db145Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 145,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Mixed",
        title = "The book counts of four works of the 590s, totalled and ranked in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Book counts of four works",
        author = "Authors of the four works",
        year = 594,
        summary = "The book counts of four works of the 590s, ten, four, six and twelve, are totalled and ranked by a Python program and by a C program that print the same result.",
        details = "Gregory of Tours wrote ten books of Histories, Gregory the Great's Dialogues have four, Evagrius's history has six, and the Strategikon has twelve. The two programs print the same six lines, and a script checks that the outputs agree.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as book_counts.py, book_counts.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### book_counts.py
            BOOKS = [("Gregory of Tours, Histories", 10), ("Gregory the Great, Dialogues", 4),
                     ("Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History", 6), ("Strategikon", 12)]
            for title, count in BOOKS:
                print(title, count, "books")
            print("total:", sum(count for _, count in BOOKS), "books")
            longest = max(BOOKS, key=lambda item: item[1])
            print("longest:", longest[0], longest[1], "books")
            ### book_counts.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const char *titles[] = {"Gregory of Tours, Histories", "Gregory the Great, Dialogues",
                                        "Evagrius, Ecclesiastical History", "Strategikon"};
                int books[] = {10, 4, 6, 12};
                int n = 4, total = 0, best = 0;
                for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                    printf("%s %d books\n", titles[i], books[i]);
                    total += books[i];
                    if (books[i] > books[best]) best = i;
                }
                printf("total: %d books\n", total);
                printf("longest: %s %d books\n", titles[best], books[best]);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 book_counts.py > python.txt
            cc -o book_counts_c book_counts.c
            ./book_counts_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 580 to 590: the 500 provisions of the Kaihuang code divided among its twelve sections, in Python and in C. */
val db146Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 146,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The 500 provisions of the Kaihuang code divided among its twelve sections, computed in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Kaihuang lu",
        author = "Compilers of the Kaihuang code",
        year = 583,
        summary = "The Kaihuang code's 500 provisions, spread over twelve sections, come to 41 per section with 8 left over, as a Python program and a C program both print.",
        details = "The totals of twelve sections and 500 provisions are the usual figures for the code, and the division leaves 8 provisions over. The two programs must print the same lines, and the split is only arithmetic, not a record of how the provisions were grouped.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as kaihuang_split.py, kaihuang_split.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### kaihuang_split.py
            SECTIONS = 12       # the twelve sections of the Kaihuang code
            PROVISIONS = 500    # the provisions, as usually given
            print("sections:", SECTIONS, "provisions:", PROVISIONS)
            print("per section:", PROVISIONS // SECTIONS, "left over:", PROVISIONS % SECTIONS)
            ### kaihuang_split.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int sections = 12, provisions = 500;
                printf("sections: %d provisions: %d\n", sections, provisions);
                printf("per section: %d left over: %d\n", provisions / sections, provisions % sections);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 kaihuang_split.py > python.txt
            cc -o kaihuang_split_c kaihuang_split.c
            ./kaihuang_split_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        author = "Justin II, Khosrow I and Maurice",
        year = 572,
        summary = "The war between Byzantium and Persia that began in 572 and ended in 591 lasted 19 years, a count that a Python program and a C program print the same way.",

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 570 to 580: how an Olympiad and the year within it turn into a date BC or AD, worked out in a short program. */
val db147Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 147,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Greek",
        title = "How an Olympiad and its year turn into a date BC or AD, counted from the first Olympiad of 776 BC",
        originalTitle = "Olympiads, four-year blocks counted from 776 BC",
        author = "Greek chronographers in the tradition of Eusebius",
        year = 570,
        summary = "An Olympiad is a block of four years, and a short program turns the Olympiad and the year within it into a date before or after the Christian era.",
        details = "The count starts with the first Olympiad, which begins in 776 BC, and the chronicles of late antiquity used it; the sources do not date its use in the 570s, so 570 is a placed year, and the example converts that year into an Olympiad. The program follows the rule that there is no year zero, so the year before AD 1 is 1 BC.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as olympiad_date.py.
            2. Run it: python3 olympiad_date.py
        """,
        example = """
            # The first Olympiad begins in 776 BC; each Olympiad holds four years.
            def olympiad_to_era(n, k):
                years_after_776_bc = 4 * (n - 1) + (k - 1)
                year = 776 - years_after_776_bc
                return f"{year} BC" if year >= 1 else f"{1 - year} AD"

            for n, k in ((1, 1), (194, 4), (195, 1), (337, 2)):
                print(f"Olympiad {n}, year {k}:", olympiad_to_era(n, k))
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 570 to 580: three dated events of the 570s from Persia, China and Byzantium, put in order by a short program. */
val db147Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 147,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Persia, China and Byzantium",
        title = "Three events of 573 to 578 in Persia, China and Byzantium, ordered in code with their gaps",
        originalTitle = "Three events of 573 to 578 in Persia, China and Byzantium, ordered in code with their gaps",
        author = "Court annalists of Persia, China and Byzantium",
        year = 573,
        summary = "A short program puts three dated events of the 570s in order and prints the gap between each pair of neighbours.",
        details = "The events are the fall of Dara to the Persians in 573, the Northern Zhou's taking of the Northern Qi capital in 577, and the death of Justin II in 578, which brought Tiberius II to the Byzantine throne. The program only sorts the years and subtracts them, so a reader can check the gaps of 4 and 1 years and the span of 5 years against the three entries.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as events_570s.py.
            2. Run it: python3 events_570s.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (578, "Justin II dies and Tiberius II takes the throne"),
                (573, "Dara falls to the Persians"),
                (577, "the Northern Zhou takes the capital of Northern Qi"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            for year, what in events:
                print(year, what)
            gaps = [later[0] - earlier[0] for earlier, later in zip(events, events[1:])]
            print("gaps:", " ".join(str(gap) for gap in gaps))
            print("span:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 560 to 570: the 168 numbered Novels of the Greek text, counted by emperor in Python and in C, placed at 565. */
val db148Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 148,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "The 168 Novels of the Greek text, counted by emperor in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Novellae (Greek text)",
        author = "Justinian, Justin II and Tiberius",
        year = 565,
        summary = "The later laws of the Byzantine emperors, the Novels of the Greek text, number 168, and two programs split them by emperor and print the same result.",
        details = "The Greek text has 168 numbered laws, 159 of them from Justinian's reign and the rest from Justin II and Tiberius. This record is placed: 565, the year Justin II came to the throne, is the anchor, not the date of any law.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as novels.py, novels.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### novels.py
            GREEK_TOTAL = 168   # numbered laws of the Novels in the Greek text
            JUSTINIAN = 159     # laws from the reign of Justinian
            print("laws of Justinian:", JUSTINIAN)
            print("laws of Justin II and Tiberius:", GREEK_TOTAL - JUSTINIAN)
            print("total:", GREEK_TOTAL)
            ### novels.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int total = 168, justinian = 159;
                printf("laws of Justinian: %d\n", justinian);
                printf("laws of Justin II and Tiberius: %d\n", total - justinian);
                printf("total: %d\n", total);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 novels.py > python.txt
            cc -o novels_c novels.c
            ./novels_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 148,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "How a post-consular year counted from the consulship of Basilius in 541 becomes a calendar year, under the two counts in use",
        originalTitle = "post consulatum Basilii",
        author = "Byzantine documentary scribes",
        year = 561,
        summary = "After the last consulship of Basilius in 541, documents counted years from it, and a short program turns a post-consular year into a calendar year under either count.",
        details = "The count after 541 could start with 541 or with 542 as the first year, and papyri of the period use both, so one post-consular year can fall in two calendar years. A papyrus giving post-consular year 21 falls in early 561 on one count and in 562 on the other, and 561 is the year used here.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as post_consular.py.
            2. Run it: python3 post_consular.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Post-consular year 21 under the two counts used in the papyri after 541.
            POST_CONSULAR = 21   # the post-consular year to convert
            FIRST_YEAR_A = 541   # count A: 541 is post-consular year 1
            FIRST_YEAR_B = 542   # count B: 542 is post-consular year 1

            print("count A (541 is year 1):", FIRST_YEAR_A + POST_CONSULAR - 1)
            print("count B (542 is year 1):", FIRST_YEAR_B + POST_CONSULAR - 1)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 560 to 570: four dated events from 561 to 568, from the death of Chlothar I to the Lombard entry into Italy, spaced by a short program. */
val db148Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 148,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Eurasian events",
        title = "Four dated events of 561 to 568, from Chlothar's death to the Lombard entry into Italy, spaced in code",
        originalTitle = "Four dated events of 561 to 568, spaced in code",
        author = "Compilers of the program, from Gregory of Tours and the Byzantine and Irish sources",
        year = 568,
        summary = "Four events of the 560s, from the death of Chlothar I to the Lombard entry into Italy, are set in a short program that prints the gaps between them.",
        details = "Chlothar I of the Franks died in 561, the Fifty Years' Peace between Byzantium and Persia was made in 562, Columba founded the monastery on Iona in 563, and the Lombards entered Italy in 568. The program prints the gaps of 1, 1 and 5 years, the total of 7, and the longest gap, all of which can be checked by subtraction.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as events_560s.py.
            2. Run it: python3 events_560s.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                ("Chlothar I dies", 561),
                ("Fifty Years' Peace", 562),
                ("Columba founds Iona", 563),
                ("Lombards enter Italy", 568),
            ]

            gaps = []
            for (name1, year1), (name2, year2) in zip(EVENTS, EVENTS[1:]):
                gaps.append((name1, name2, year2 - year1))
                print(name1, year1, "to", name2, year2, ":", year2 - year1, "years")
            total = EVENTS[-1][1] - EVENTS[0][1]
            print("total from Chlothar I dies to Lombards enter Italy:", total, "years")
            longest = max(gaps, key=lambda gap: gap[2])
            print("longest gap:", longest[0], "to", longest[1], "(" + str(longest[2]) + " years)")
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 149,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "The years from Jordanes's Getica of 551 to the Pragmatic Sanction of 554, with Taginae between, computed in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Years between three dated entries",
        author = "Jordanes and the Byzantine court",
        year = 551,
        summary = "The years between Jordanes's Getica of 551, the battle of Taginae in 552 and the Pragmatic Sanction of 554 are printed by a Python program and a C program that give the same result.",
        details = "Each gap is a plain subtraction of two dates that the sources give: 1 year from the Getica to Taginae, 2 years from Taginae to the sanction, and 3 years from the Getica to the sanction. The two programs print the same three lines, and a script checks that their outputs agree.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as gap_years.py, gap_years.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### gap_years.py
            GETICA = 551    # Jordanes's Getica, written in 551
            TAGINAE = 552   # the battle of Taginae, in 552
            SANCTION = 554  # the Pragmatic Sanction, in 554
            print("Getica to Taginae:", TAGINAE - GETICA)
            print("Taginae to the Pragmatic Sanction:", SANCTION - TAGINAE)
            print("Getica to the Pragmatic Sanction:", SANCTION - GETICA)
            ### gap_years.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int getica = 551, taginae = 552, sanction = 554;
                printf("Getica to Taginae: %d\n", taginae - getica);
                printf("Taginae to the Pragmatic Sanction: %d\n", sanction - taginae);
                printf("Getica to the Pragmatic Sanction: %d\n", sanction - getica);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 gap_years.py > python.txt
            cc -o gap_years_c gap_years.c
            ./gap_years_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 550 to 560: the founding years of seven dynasties of the Northern and Southern period, sorted and compared in code. */
val db149Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 149,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The founding years of seven Chinese dynasties of the Northern and Southern period, from 386 to 557, sorted and compared in code",
        originalTitle = "Nanbei chao",
        author = "Chinese dynastic chroniclers",
        year = 557,
        summary = "A short program lists the founding years of seven dynasties of the Northern and Southern period, from Northern Wei in 386 to Chen and Northern Zhou in 557, and prints the gaps between them.",
        details = "The founding dates are conventions: the Northern Wei is counted from its revival under Tuoba Gui in 386, although its ruler took the imperial title in 399, and the other dates are the usual ones for each state. Chen and Northern Zhou both begin in 557, so one gap is zero, and the longest gap, 59 years between Liu Song and Southern Qi, is printed on its own line.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as dynasty_years.py.
            2. Run it: python3 dynasty_years.py
        """,
        example = """
            FOUNDED = [
                ("Northern Wei", 386),
                ("Liu Song", 420),
                ("Southern Qi", 479),
                ("Liang", 502),
                ("Northern Qi", 550),
                ("Chen", 557),
                ("Northern Zhou", 557),
            ]
            ordered = sorted(FOUNDED, key=lambda item: (item[1], item[0]))
            gaps = []
            for (name_a, year_a), (name_b, year_b) in zip(ordered, ordered[1:]):
                gaps.append((year_b - year_a, name_a, name_b))
                print(name_a, "to", name_b + ":", year_b - year_a, "years")
            print("dynasties:", len(ordered))
            first, last = ordered[0][1], ordered[-1][1]
            print("span from", first, "to", last, "is", last - first, "years")
            longest = max(gaps)
            print("longest gap:", longest[1], "to", longest[2], "is", longest[0], "years")
            print("sum of gaps:", sum(gap for gap, _, _ in gaps))
        """,
    ),

)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db14Cross.kt
################################################################################
package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1900 to 1910: the same result from two languages, checked by a run script. */
val db14Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Definability",
        title = "Richard's diagonal in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Les principes des mathematiques et le probleme des ensembles (1905)",
        author = "Jules Richard",
        year = 1905,
        summary = "A diagonal rule builds a digit string that differs from every number in a list of definitions, and Python and C each compute it.",
        details = "Richard's 1905 construction uses a list of definitions, each giving the digits of a number, and changes one digit of each. Here five definitions give the digits 45127. The two programs print the same lines, and the run script compares them.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### richard.py
            # Five definitions, each a fraction p/q whose decimal digits define a number.
            definitions = [(1, 3), (1, 7), (1, 4), (1, 9), (2, 3)]

            def digit(p, q, k):
                # The k-th digit after the decimal point of p/q.
                return (p * 10 ** k // q) % 10

            # Diagonal rule: the k-th digit of the new number differs from the k-th digit of the k-th definition.
            diagonal = [(digit(p, q, k) + 1) % 10 for k, (p, q) in enumerate(definitions, start=1)]
            print("diagonal digits: " + "".join(str(d) for d in diagonal))
            differs = all(diagonal[k - 1] != digit(p, q, k) for k, (p, q) in enumerate(definitions, start=1))
            print("differs from every definition:", differs)
            ### richard.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* The k-th digit after the decimal point of p/q, for k >= 1. */
            static int digit(long p, long q, int k) {
                long power = 1;
                for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
                    power *= 10;
                }
                return (int)((p * power / q) % 10);
            }

            int main(void) {
                /* The same five definitions as the Python program. */
                long p[] = {1, 1, 1, 1, 2};
                long q[] = {3, 7, 4, 9, 3};
                int n = 5;
                int diagonal[5];
                int differs = 1;
                for (int k = 1; k <= n; k++) {
                    diagonal[k - 1] = (digit(p[k - 1], q[k - 1], k) + 1) % 10;
                    if (diagonal[k - 1] == digit(p[k - 1], q[k - 1], k)) {
                        differs = 0;
                    }
                }
                printf("diagonal digits: ");
                for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {
                    printf("%d", diagonal[k]);
                }
                printf("\n");
                printf("differs from every definition: %s\n", differs ? "True" : "False");
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 richard.py > python.txt
            cc -o richard_c richard.c
            ./richard_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Radio signals",
        title = "Morse SOS in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "International Radiotelegraph Convention, Berlin (1906)",
        author = "Berlin radiotelegraph conference of 1906",
        year = 1906,
        summary = "The distress signal SOS, three dots, three dashes, three dots, is spelled in Morse by two programs in different languages, and a script checks that they agree.",
        details = "The 1906 Berlin convention adopted this sequence as the ship distress signal, and it took effect in 1908. The programs encode SOS and MARCONI, and the run script compares their output.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### sos.py
            # Morse code for the letters used here; dots and dashes are written as . and -
            MORSE = {"S": "...", "O": "---", "M": "--", "A": ".-", "R": ".-.", "C": "-.-.", "N": "-.", "I": ".."}

            def encode(word):
                return " ".join(MORSE[ch] for ch in word)

            for word in ["SOS", "MARCONI"]:
                print(f"{word}: {encode(word)}")
            ### sos.c
            #include <stdio.h>
            #include <string.h>

            /* Morse code for the letters used here. */
            static const char *morse(char ch) {
                switch (ch) {
                    case 'S': return "...";
                    case 'O': return "---";
                    case 'M': return "--";
                    case 'A': return ".-";
                    case 'R': return ".-.";
                    case 'C': return "-.-.";
                    case 'N': return "-.";
                    case 'I': return "..";
                    default: return "?";
                }
            }

            static void encode(const char *word) {
                for (size_t i = 0; i < strlen(word); i++) {
                    if (i > 0) {
                        printf(" ");
                    }
                    printf("%s", morse(word[i]));
                }
                printf("\n");
            }

            int main(void) {
                printf("SOS: ");
                encode("SOS");
                printf("MARCONI: ");
                encode("MARCONI");
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 sos.py > python.txt
            cc -o sos_c sos.c
            ./sos_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),
)

        instructions = """

        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            def dot(u, v):
                return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(u, v))

            def orthogonalise(vectors):
                basis = []
                for v in vectors:
                    w = [Fraction(x) for x in v]
                    for u in basis:
                        c = dot(w, u) / dot(u, u)
                        w = [wi - c * ui for wi, ui in zip(w, u)]
                    basis.append(w)
                return basis

            vectors = [(1, 1, 0), (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1)]
            basis = orthogonalise(vectors)
            for i, u in enumerate(basis, start=1):
                print(f"u{i} = " + " ".join(str(x) for x in u))
            pairs = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]

            T = 5800.0              # roughly the surface temperature of the Sun, K

            def radiance(lam):
                # Planck's law: spectral radiance per unit wavelength at wavelength lam, in metres.
                return (2 * h * c * c / lam ** 5) / (math.exp(h * c / (lam * k * T)) - 1)

            # Golden-section search for the maximum between 100 nm and 2000 nm.
            lo, hi = 100e-9, 2000e-9
            g = (math.sqrt(5) - 1) / 2
            a = hi - g * (hi - lo)
            b = lo + g * (hi - lo)
            for _ in range(200):

                    lo = a
                else:

                a = hi - g * (hi - lo)

            def is_prime(n):
                if n < 2:
                    return False
                i = 2
                while i * i <= n:
                    if n % i == 0:
                        return False
                    i += 1
                return True

            LIMIT = 5000
            primes = [p for p in range(2, LIMIT) if is_prime(p)]
            print(f"primes below {LIMIT}: {len(primes)}")
            # A Wieferich prime p has p squared dividing 2^(p-1) - 1, which pow() checks with modular arithmetic.
            found = [p for p in primes if pow(2, p - 1, p * p) == 1]

            def complete_mappings(n):
                # A complete mapping of Z_n is a permutation s such that x + s(x), taken mod n, is also a permutation.
                count = 0
                for s in permutations(range(n)):
                    if len({(x + s[x]) % n for x in range(n)}) == n:
                        count += 1
                return count

            for n in (3, 4, 5, 6):
                print(f"Z{n}: {complete_mappings(n)} complete mappings")

        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Numerical methods",
        title = "How a Runge-Kutta step is computed",
        originalTitle = "Beitrag zur naeherungsweisen Integration totaler Differentialgleichungen (1901)",
        author = "Wilhelm Kutta",
        year = 1901,
        summary = "The classical fourth-order step averages four slopes, and for y' = y it multiplies the value by a fixed polynomial in the step size.",
        details = "Kutta's 1901 fourth-order method is shown here in exact fractions. The example takes two steps of size one half for y' = y, shows that one step multiplies the value by 211/128, and compares the result with e.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as rk4.py.
            2. Run it: python3 rk4.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            def rk4_step(y, h):
                # Classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta step for y' = y: four slopes, weighted 1, 2, 2 and 1.
                f = lambda v: v
                k1 = f(y)
                k2 = f(y + h / 2 * k1)
                k3 = f(y + h / 2 * k2)
                k4 = f(y + h * k3)
                return y + h / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)

            h = Fraction(1, 2)
            print("one step factor R(h) =", rk4_step(Fraction(1), h))
            y = Fraction(1)
            for step in range(1, 3):
                y = rk4_step(y, h)
                print(f"after step {step}: y = {y}")
            print("decimal:", float(y))
            e = 2.718281828459045
            print(f"error against e: {e - float(y):.6f}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(

        example = """

            # A step function on [0, 1], given as pieces (start, end, value) that cover the interval.
            pieces = [
                (Fraction(0), Fraction(1, 2), 2),
                (Fraction(1, 2), Fraction(3, 4), 5),
                (Fraction(3, 4), Fraction(1), 2),
            ]

            # Level sets: the measure of each value is the total length of the pieces that take it.
            measure = {}
            for start, end, value in pieces:
                measure[value] = measure.get(value, Fraction(0)) + (end - start)

            total = Fraction(0)
            for value in sorted(measure):
                print(f"level {value}: measure {measure[value]}")
                total += value * measure[value]
            print(f"Lebesgue sum: {total} = {float(total)}")

            # The same number, summed piece by piece.
            pieces_sum = sum(value * (end - start) for start, end, value in pieces)
            print("piece sum agrees:", pieces_sum == total)
        """,

        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as t_test.py.
            2. Run it: python3 t_test.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            sample = [5, 7, 9, 6, 8]
            n = len(sample)
            mean = sum(sample) / n
            s = math.sqrt(sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in sample) / (n - 1))
            se = s / math.sqrt(n)
            critical = 2.7764  # two-sided 5 percent point of Student's t for 4 degrees of freedom, from a table
            print(f"mean {mean}, sample sd {s:.4f}, standard error {se:.4f}")
            for claimed in (5, 6):
                t = (mean - claimed) / se
                verdict = "reject" if abs(t) > critical else "keep"
                print(f"claimed mean {claimed}: t = {t:.4f}, df = {n - 1}, critical {critical}: {verdict}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Numerical methods",
        title = "How Richardson extrapolation removes the leading error",
        originalTitle = "The approximate arithmetical solution by finite differences of physical problems involving differential equations, with an application to the stresses in a masonry dam (1910)",
        author = "Lewis Fry Richardson",
        year = 1910,
        summary = "Two estimates with steps h and h/2 combine to cancel the leading error term, and the step can be repeated to cancel the next one.",
        details = "The example applies the trapezoid rule to the integral of x to the fourth power from 0 to 1, with 1, 2 and 4 intervals, using exact fractions. It extrapolates twice and reaches exactly 1/5. Some sources date Richardson's volume of Philosophical Transactions to 1910 and others to 1911.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as richardson.py.
            2. Run it: python3 richardson.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            def trapezoid(f, n):
                # Trapezoid rule for f on [0, 1] with n equal intervals, in exact fractions.
                h = Fraction(1, n)
                total = (f(Fraction(0)) + f(Fraction(1))) / 2
                for k in range(1, n):
                    total += f(k * h)
                return total * h

            def f(x):
                return x ** 4

            t1 = trapezoid(f, 1)
            t2 = trapezoid(f, 2)
            t4 = trapezoid(f, 4)
            print(f"T(1) = {t1}")
            print(f"T(2) = {t2}")
            print(f"T(4) = {t4}")
            exact = Fraction(1, 5)
            r12 = (4 * t2 - t1) / 3
            r24 = (4 * t4 - t2) / 3
            r = (16 * r24 - r12) / 15
            print(f"first extrapolation: {r12} error {r12 - exact}")
            print(f"second extrapolation: {r24} error {r24 - exact}")
            print(f"combined: {r} exact: {r == exact}")
        """,
    ),
)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 1900 to 1910: larger programs for a pricing formula, a telegraph code, an income table and a tide sum. */
val db14Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Finance",
        title = "Bachelier's option price under a normal model",
        originalTitle = "Theorie de la speculation (1900)",
        author = "Louis Bachelier",
        year = 1900,
        summary = "Bachelier priced an option by assuming that prices move like a random walk with a normal spread, which gives a closed formula for the call price.",
        details = "The example implements the closed formula with the normal density and the normal distribution function, then prints three prices: at the money, one unit out of the money and with a wider spread. The values agree with the standard normal tables.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as bachelier.py.
            2. Run it: python3 bachelier.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            def phi(x):
                # Standard normal density.
                return math.exp(-x * x / 2) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)

            def Phi(x):
                # Standard normal distribution function.
                return 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2)))

            def call_price(spot, strike, sigma_t):
                # Bachelier's formula for a call when the price moves as an arithmetic Brownian motion over the period.
                d = (spot - strike) / sigma_t
                return (spot - strike) * Phi(d) + sigma_t * phi(d)

            cases = [
                ("at the money", 100, 100, 1),
                ("one below the strike", 100, 101, 1),
                ("wider spread", 100, 95, 10),
            ]
            for label, spot, strike, sigma_t in cases:
                print(f"{label}: {call_price(spot, strike, sigma_t):.4f}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Telegraph codes",
        title = "Murray's five-unit code: encode and decode",
        originalTitle = "Printing telegraph with a five-unit code, adapted from Baudot (1901)",
        author = "Donald Murray",
        year = 1901,
        summary = "Each character is sent as five marks, with a shift character for letters, and the program encodes a message and decodes it back.",
        details = "The table uses the five-unit values of the letters and the space in the usual ITA2 chart, which is Murray's code in its standard form. Bit strings are written with the least significant bit on the right, as in those charts. The example encodes HELLO WORLD and decodes it again.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as murray.py.
            2. Run it: python3 murray.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Five-unit values of the letters and the space, as in the usual ITA2 chart.
            # Bit strings are written with the least significant bit on the right.
            LETTERS = {
                "A": 3, "B": 25, "C": 14, "D": 9, "E": 1, "F": 13, "G": 26, "H": 20, "I": 6,
                "J": 11, "K": 15, "L": 18, "M": 28, "N": 12, "O": 24, "P": 22, "Q": 23, "R": 10,
                "S": 5, "T": 16, "U": 7, "V": 30, "W": 19, "X": 29, "Y": 21, "Z": 17, " ": 4,
            }
            LTRS = 31  # letters shift, sent first so that the receiver prints letters

            def to_bits(value):
                return format(value, "05b")

            def encode(text):
                codes = [LTRS] + [LETTERS[ch] for ch in text.upper()]
                return [to_bits(v) for v in codes]

            def decode(bits):
                inverse = {v: k for k, v in LETTERS.items()}
                out = []
                for b in bits:
                    value = int(b, 2)
                    if value != LTRS:
                        out.append(inverse[value])
                return "".join(out)

            message = "HELLO WORLD"
            bits = encode(message)
            print("encoded: " + " ".join(bits))
            print("decoded: " + decode(bits))
            print("round trip: " + str(decode(bits) == message))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Inequality",
        title = "Lorenz curve and the Gini index for five incomes",
        originalTitle = "Methods of measuring the concentration of wealth (1905)",
        author = "Max Otto Lorenz",
        year = 1905,
        summary = "Sorting incomes and adding them up gives the Lorenz curve, and the area between the curve and the diagonal gives the Gini index.",
        details = "The program reads five incomes, prints the cumulative share of income for each rank, and computes the Gini index two ways: from the area under the curve and from all pairs of incomes. Both give 2/5.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as lorenz.py.
            2. Run it: python3 lorenz.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction as F

            incomes = sorted([10, 1, 4, 2, 3])   # five incomes, poorest first
            n = len(incomes)
            total = sum(incomes)
            print("sorted incomes:", incomes, "total:", total)

            # Lorenz points: the poorest i people hold a share of the total income.
            points = [(F(0), F(0))]
            running = 0
            for i, x in enumerate(incomes, start=1):
                running += x
                points.append((F(i, n), F(running, total)))
                print(f"poorest {i} of {n} people hold {F(running, total)} of income")

            # Area under the Lorenz curve by the trapezoid rule; the Gini index is 1 minus twice the area.
            area = sum((points[i][1] + points[i - 1][1]) / 2 * (points[i][0] - points[i - 1][0])
                       for i in range(1, len(points)))
            gini_area = 1 - 2 * area
            print("Gini from the area:", gini_area)

            # The same index from all pairs: mean absolute difference divided by twice the mean.
            mean = F(total, n)
            pair_sum = sum(abs(x - y) for x in incomes for y in incomes)
            gini_pairs = F(pair_sum, 2 * n * n) / mean
            print("Gini from all pairs:", gini_pairs)
            print("the two agree:", gini_area == gini_pairs)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 14,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Harmonic analysis",
        title = "Tide heights by adding harmonic terms",
        originalTitle = "Universal Tide Predictor, built by Lege and Co., London (1906-1908)",
        author = "Edward Roberts",
        year = 1908,
        summary = "Tide heights come from adding cosine terms with fixed speeds, the sum that Roberts's machine evaluated mechanically.",
        details = "This is a Python simulation of the harmonic sum behind the Roberts machine, with two invented constituents, a mean level of 2 metres and speeds of 30 and 60 degrees per hour. It prints heights for hours 0 to 4 and finds the high and low water over one 12-hour cycle.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as tide.py.
            2. Run it: python3 tide.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            MEAN_LEVEL = 2.0   # metres, invented for the example

            def height(hours):
                # Two invented constituents: speeds of 30 and 60 degrees per hour, amplitudes 1.0 and 0.5.
                a = math.radians(30 * hours)
                b = math.radians(60 * hours)
                return MEAN_LEVEL + math.cos(a) + 0.5 * math.cos(b)

            for t in range(5):
                print(f"hour {t}: {height(t):.4f} m")

            # Scan one 12-hour cycle in steps of a quarter hour, then find the high and low water.
            samples = [(height(i / 4), i / 4) for i in range(48)]
            high = max(v for v, _ in samples)
            low = min(v for v, _ in samples)
            high_times = [t for v, t in samples if abs(v - high) < 1e-9]
            low_times = [t for v, t in samples if abs(v - low) < 1e-9]
            print(f"high water {high:.4f} m at hours {high_times}")
            print(f"low water {low:.4f} m at hours {low_times}")
        """,
    ),
)

        details = "The Rule has a prologue and 73 chapters, and the Qimin yaoshu has 92 chapters in ten volumes; the two programs print one line, and a script checks that the outputs agree. The total counts chapters of two different works, so it says nothing about their length or content.",

            ### chapters.c
            #include <stdio.h>

                printf("chapters in the two works: %d\n", rule + qimin);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 540 to 550: four dated events from 536 to 548, the entry into Rome, the lifted siege, the sack of Antioch and the death of Theodora, spaced by a short program. */
val db150Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 150,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "Four dated events of 536 to 548, the entry into Rome, the lifted siege, the sack of Antioch and the death of Theodora, spaced in code",
        originalTitle = "Four dated events of 536 to 548, spaced in code",
        author = "Procopius and the Byzantine chroniclers",
        year = 548,
        summary = "Four events of Justinian's wars and court, from Belisarius's entry into Rome to the death of Theodora, are set in a short program that prints the gaps between them.",
        details = "Belisarius entered Rome in December 536, the Goths lifted their siege of the city in March 538, Khosrow I sacked Antioch in 540, and Theodora died in June 548. The program prints the gaps of 2, 2 and 8 years, their total of 12, and the longest gap, all of which can be checked by subtraction.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as events_540s.py.
            2. Run it: python3 events_540s.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                ("Belisarius enters Rome", 536),
                ("Goths lift the siege of Rome", 538),
                ("Khosrow sacks Antioch", 540),
                ("Theodora dies", 548),
            ]

            gaps = []
            for (name1, year1), (name2, year2) in zip(EVENTS, EVENTS[1:]):
                gaps.append((name1, name2, year2 - year1))
                print(name1, year1, "to", name2, year2, ":", year2 - year1, "years")
            total = EVENTS[-1][1] - EVENTS[0][1]
            print("total from Belisarius enters Rome to Theodora dies:", total, "years")
            longest = max(gaps, key=lambda gap: gap[2])
            print("longest gap:", longest[0], "to", longest[1], "(" + str(longest[2]) + " years)")
        """,
    ),

)

        details = "The Endless Peace between Justinian and Khosrow I was broken when Khosrow invaded Byzantine Syria in 540, and the Fifty Years' Peace of 562 closed the later wars, so the two programs print 8 years of peace and 30 years between the treaties. package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 530 to 540: the Falcidian quarter of Roman law, which kept a fourth of the estate for the heir, worked out by a program. */
val db151Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 151,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Roman",
        title = "How the Falcidian quarter cuts the legacies of a will so the heir keeps a fourth of the estate, worked out by a program",
        originalTitle = "lex Falcidia",
        author = "Compilers of the Digest and the Institutes",
        year = 533,
        summary = "The Falcidian law kept at least a quarter of an estate for the heir, so legacies that claimed more than three quarters were cut back in the same proportion, as a short program shows.",
        details = "The rule comes from the Lex Falcidia of 40 BC, which the Institutes and the Digest of 533 record for later courts, so 533 is the year of the books and not of the law. The program uses whole numbers and one proportion to show the arithmetic of the rule, and it leaves out the exceptions and the way debts and gifts are counted.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as falcidian.py.
            2. Run it: python3 falcidian.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            ESTATE = 800                # net estate after debts, in the example's units
            LEGACIES = [600, 300, 300]  # the legacies of the will, claiming 1200 in all

            limit = Fraction(ESTATE * 3, 4)  # three quarters of the estate: the most that legacies may take
            claimed = sum(LEGACIES)
            print("legacies claimed:", claimed)
            print("three quarters of the estate:", limit)
            if claimed > limit:
                factor = limit / claimed
                cut = [Fraction(value) * factor for value in LEGACIES]
                print("reduction factor:", factor)
                print("legacies after reduction:", " ".join(str(value) for value in cut))
            else:
                cut = LEGACIES
                print("no reduction needed")
            print("heir keeps:", ESTATE - sum(cut))
        """,
    ),

)

val db151Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 151,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "Five events of 531 to 540 in Persia, Constantinople, Africa and Italy, sorted and spaced by a short program",
        originalTitle = "Five events of 531 to 540 in Persia, Constantinople, Africa and Italy, sorted and spaced by a short program",
        author = "Compiled from the standard histories of the period",
        year = 531,
        summary = "Five dated events, from the accession of Khosrow I in Persia to the surrender of Ravenna, are sorted by year and spaced by a short program.",
        details = "The events are the accession of Khosrow I in 531, the Nika riot of 532, Belisarius's victory at Ad Decimum in 533, the dedication of Hagia Sophia in 537 and the surrender of Ravenna in 540. The gaps and the span are simple subtraction, and the list is a short sample of dated events for the decade rather than a full chronology.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as decade_events.py.
            2. Run it: python3 decade_events.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                (537, "Hagia Sophia dedicated in Constantinople"),
                (531, "Khosrow I becomes king of Persia"),
                (540, "Belisarius takes Ravenna"),
                (533, "Ad Decimum, Belisarius's victory in Africa"),
                (532, "Nika riot in Constantinople"),
            ]

            previous = None
            for year, text in sorted(EVENTS):
                if previous is None:
                    print(year, text)
                else:
                    print(year, text, "gap", year - previous)
                previous = year
            span = sorted(EVENTS)[-1][0] - sorted(EVENTS)[0][0]
            print("span from the first to the last:", span, "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 520 to 530: the 532-year Easter cycle of 28 solar years times 19 lunar years, in Python and in C. */
val db152Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 152,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Calendar",
        title = "The 532-year Easter cycle as 28 solar years times 19 lunar years, computed in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "The 532-year Easter cycle as 28 solar years times 19 lunar years, computed in Python and in C",
        author = "Dionysius Exiguus",
        year = 525,
        summary = "The 28-year solar cycle times the 19-year lunar cycle gives the 532-year Easter cycle, and a Python program and a C program print the same count.",
        details = "Twenty-eight solar years and nineteen lunar years return to the same pairing after 532 years, the length of the Easter cycle that sixth-century reckoners worked with. Dionysius's table of 525 begins at AD 532, the first year of this count, so 525 is the year of that table and not the date when the cycle was devised.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as cycle_easter.py, cycle_easter.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### cycle_easter.py
            SOLAR = 28
            LUNAR = 19
            CYCLE = SOLAR * LUNAR
            print("cycle length:", CYCLE)
            print("first year:", 532, "last year:", 532 + CYCLE - 1)
            ### cycle_easter.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int solar = 28;
                int lunar = 19;
                int cycle = solar * lunar;
                printf("cycle length: %d\n", cycle);
                printf("first year: %d last year: %d\n", 532, 532 + cycle - 1);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 cycle_easter.py > python.txt
            cc -o cycle_easter_c cycle_easter.c
            ./cycle_easter_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 152,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "The Antioch earthquake of 526, the death of Justin I in 527 and the battle of Dara in 530, sorted and spaced in code",
        originalTitle = "The Antioch earthquake of 526, the death of Justin I in 527 and the battle of Dara in 530, sorted and spaced in code",
        author = "Sixth-century chroniclers",
        year = 526,
        summary = "A short program puts three events of 526 to 530 from the eastern Roman world in date order and prints the years between them.",
        details = "The earthquake that destroyed Antioch is dated to 526, the emperor Justin I died in 527, and the Byzantine victory at Dara came in 530. The program only subtracts the dates, so the gaps measure the years between the events and say nothing about a link between them.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as dated_events.py.
            2. Run it: python3 dated_events.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (530, "battle of Dara"),
                (526, "Antioch earthquake"),
                (527, "death of Justin I"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            for year, name in events:
                print(year, name)
            for earlier, later in zip(events, events[1:]):
                print("years from", earlier[1], "to", later[1] + ":", later[0] - earlier[0])
            print("years from first to last:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code piece of 510 to 520: the 48 years of Zu Chongzhi's Daming calendar from its presentation in 462 to its approval in 510, in Python and in C. */
val db153Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 153,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "The 48 years from Zu Chongzhi's Daming calendar of 462 to its approval in 510, counted in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Daming li",
        author = "Zu Chongzhi and his son Zu Geng",
        year = 510,
        summary = "A Python program and a C program both print the 48 years from the presentation of the Daming calendar in 462 to its approval in 510, and the 45 years that a 465 start gives.",
        details = "The 462 start follows the Chinese accounts, and 465 is the start that some accounts give, so the programs print both gaps and the six years of Zu Geng's campaign from 504. The two programs print the same lines, and a script checks that their outputs agree.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as daming_gap.py, daming_gap.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### daming_gap.py
            PRESENTED = 462      # the Daming calendar presented to the Liu Song court
            PRESENTED_ALT = 465  # the start that some accounts give
            APPROVED = 510       # the year the Liang court approved it
            CAMPAIGN = 504       # the year Zu Geng began to press for it
            print("from 462 to 510:", APPROVED - PRESENTED, "years")
            print("from 465 to 510:", APPROVED - PRESENTED_ALT, "years")
            print("campaign from 504 to 510:", APPROVED - CAMPAIGN, "years")
            ### daming_gap.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int presented = 462, alt = 465, approved = 510, campaign = 504;
                printf("from 462 to 510: %d years\n", approved - presented);
                printf("from 465 to 510: %d years\n", approved - alt);
                printf("campaign from 504 to 510: %d years\n", approved - campaign);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 daming_gap.py > python.txt
            cc -o daming_gap_c daming_gap.c
            ./daming_gap_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 510 to 520: four dated turns from the 510s in the eastern Roman world and Rome, sorted and spaced by a short program. */
val db153Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 153,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Byzantine",
        title = "Four dated turns of 513 to 519 in the eastern Roman world and Rome, sorted and spaced in code",
        originalTitle = "Four dated turns of 513 to 519 in the eastern Roman world and Rome, sorted and spaced in code",
        author = "Byzantine and papal chroniclers, as summarised in standard histories",
        year = 519,
        summary = "Four dated turns of the 510s, from Vitalian's revolt to the end of the Acacian schism, are set in a short program that prints the gaps between them.",
        details = "Vitalian rose against Emperor Anastasius in 513, Pope Symmachus died in 514, Anastasius died in 518, and the Acacian schism between Rome and Constantinople, which began in 484, ended in 519 when the eastern church accepted the Formula of Hormisdas. The program prints each gap of 1, 4 and 1 years, the total of 6, and the longest gap, all of which can be checked by subtraction.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as turns_510s.py.
            2. Run it: python3 turns_510s.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                ("Vitalian revolt begins", 513),
                ("Pope Symmachus dies", 514),
                ("Anastasius dies", 518),
                ("Acacian schism ends", 519),
            ]

            gaps = []
            for (name1, year1), (name2, year2) in zip(EVENTS, EVENTS[1:]):
                gaps.append((name1, name2, year2 - year1))
                print(name1, year1, "to", name2, year2, ":", year2 - year1, "years")
            total = EVENTS[-1][1] - EVENTS[0][1]
            print("total from Vitalian revolt to Acacian schism end:", total, "years")
            longest = max(gaps, key=lambda gap: gap[2])
            print("longest gap:", longest[0], "to", longest[1], "(" + str(longest[2]) + " years)")
        """,
    ),

)

val db154Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 154,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Greek",
        title = "The arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means of 2 and 8, computed in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Introductio arithmetica",
        author = "Nicomachus of Gerasa, with Boethius",
        year = 500,
        summary = "The three means of 2 and 8 are computed by a Python program and by a C program that print the same three lines.",
        details = "Nicomachus defines the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means of two numbers, and Boethius repeats them in Latin. For 2 and 8 the means are 5, 4 and 3.2, and a script checks that the two programs print the same lines.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as means.py, means.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### means.py
            a, b = 2, 8
            print(f"arithmetic mean: {(a + b) / 2:.1f}")
            print(f"geometric mean: {(a * b) ** 0.5:.1f}")
            print(f"harmonic mean: {2 * a * b / (a + b):.1f}")
            ### means.c
            #include <math.h>
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                double a = 2, b = 8;
                printf("arithmetic mean: %.1f\n", (a + b) / 2);
                printf("geometric mean: %.1f\n", sqrt(a * b));
                printf("harmonic mean: %.1f\n", 2 * a * b / (a + b));
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 means.py > python.txt
            cc -o means_c means.c -lm
            ./means_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 500 to 510: how a ratio is named by its species, as Nicomachus sets them out, worked out by a short program. */
val db154Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 154,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Greek",
        title = "How a ratio is named by its species, multiple, superparticular or superpartient, as Nicomachus names them",
        originalTitle = "Introductio arithmetica",
        author = "Nicomachus of Gerasa, with Boethius",
        year = 500,
        summary = "A ratio of two whole numbers falls into one of Nicomachus's species, and a short program names six ratios in that way.",
        details = "Nicomachus of Gerasa set out the species of ratio in his Introduction to Arithmetic, and Boethius carried the same names into Latin. The rule divides the larger number by the smaller and reads the quotient and the remainder, so 8:3 has quotient 2 and remainder 2 and is a multiple superpartient ratio.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as ratio_species.py.
            2. Run it: python3 ratio_species.py
        """,
        example = """
            def species(a, b):
                # Nicomachus's species for the ratio a:b, with a at least b
                quotient, remainder = divmod(a, b)
                if remainder == 0:
                    return "multiplex"
                if quotient == 1:
                    return "superparticularis" if remainder == 1 else "superpartiens"
                return "multiplex superparticularis" if remainder == 1 else "multiplex superpartiens"

            for a, b in [(3, 2), (4, 3), (5, 3), (6, 3), (7, 2), (8, 3)]:
                print(f"{a}:{b} is {species(a, b)}")
        """,
    ),

)

/** One project of 500 to 510: the spans of four dynasties of the 500s, counted and ranked by a short program. */
val db154Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 154,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Chinese",
        title = "How long four dynasties of the 500s lasted: Liang, Chen, Northern Qi and Northern Zhou, counted in code",
        originalTitle = "Liang shu, Chen shu, Bei Qi shu, Bei Zhou shu",
        author = "Official histories of the four dynasties",
        year = 502,
        summary = "A short program takes the founding and ending years of four dynasties of the 500s and prints how long each one lasted, with the total and the longest.",
        details = "The dates are the usual founding and ending years, taken from the official histories of each dynasty, and the program subtracts the start from the end. The Liang, founded in 502, is the longest of the four, and the record takes its year from that founding.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as dynasty_spans.py.
            2. Run it: python3 dynasty_spans.py
        """,
        example = """
            DYNASTIES = [
                ("Liang", 502, 557),
                ("Chen", 557, 589),
                ("Northern Qi", 550, 577),
                ("Northern Zhou", 557, 581),
            ]

            spans = [(name, end - start) for name, start, end in DYNASTIES]
            for name, start, end in DYNASTIES:
                print(f"{name} {start}-{end}: {end - start} years")
            print("total:", sum(years for _, years in spans), "years")
            longest = max(spans, key=lambda item: item[1])
            print("longest:", longest[0], longest[1], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 499: Aryabhata's rule for the circumference of a circle, computed in Python and in C. */
val db155Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 155,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Circles",
        title = "The circumference rule of Aryabhata in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Aryabhatiya circumference rule",
        author = "Aryabhata",
        year = 499,
        summary = "Aryabhata's rule gives a circle's circumference as 62832 for a diameter of 20000, and two programs, one in Python and one in C, print the same circumferences for five diameters.",
        details = "The rule adds four to one hundred, multiplies by eight and adds sixty-two thousand, which gives an approximate ratio of 3.1416 between circumference and diameter. The two programs use whole-number arithmetic and print the same lines, which the run script compares line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### circle.py
            DIAMETERS = [1, 2, 7, 10, 20000]   # illustrative diameters
            RULE = (100 + 4) * 8 + 62000       # Aryabhata's numerator over 20000
            for d in DIAMETERS:
                tenths = RULE * d // 2           # circumference times 10000
                print(f"diameter {d}: circumference {tenths // 10000}.{tenths % 10000:04d}")
            ### circle.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const long diameters[] = {1, 2, 7, 10, 20000};   /* illustrative diameters */
                const long rule = (100 + 4) * 8 + 62000;          /* Aryabhata's numerator over 20000 */
                for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
                    long d = diameters[i];
                    long scaled = rule * d / 2;                    /* circumference times 10000 */
                    printf("diameter %ld: circumference %ld.%04ld\n", d, scaled / 10000, scaled % 10000);
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 circle.py > python.txt
            cc -o circle_c circle.c
            ./circle_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

val db155Flex: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 155,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Days from Odoacer's death to the end of Kali year 3600",
        originalTitle = "Days between two fixed dates",
        author = "Theoderic the Great and Aryabhata",
        year = 493,
        summary = "Odoacer's death is usually dated to 15 March 493 and the Kali year 3600 ended on 21 March 499, and a short program counts the days between the two dates with a Julian day number.",
        details = "Both dates are given as commonly stated in the Julian calendar, and the example uses a Julian day number, so the count does not depend on the Gregorian rule. The span includes the leap day of 29 February 496.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as odoacer_kali.py.
            2. Run it: python3 odoacer_kali.py
        """,
        example = """
            def julian_day(year, month, day):
                # Julian calendar day number, for dates after the start of the calendar
                a = (14 - month) // 12
                y = year + 4800 - a
                m = month + 12 * a - 3
                return day + (153 * m + 2) // 5 + 365 * y + y // 4 - 32083

            start = julian_day(493, 3, 15)   # death of Odoacer, as commonly given
            end = julian_day(499, 3, 21)     # end of Kali year 3600, as commonly given
            print("days from Odoacer's death to the end of Kali year 3600:", end - start)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind

/** Projects of 490 to 500: a short program that sorts three changes of ruler of the decade and counts the years between them. */
val db155Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 155,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Rulers",
        title = "A timeline of three changes of ruler in the 490s, sorted and counted in code",
        originalTitle = "Timeline of events",
        author = "Chroniclers of Byzantium and Persia",
        year = 491,
        summary = "A short program sorts three changes of ruler in the 490s by year, prints the gap between each pair, and counts the years from the first to the last.",
        details = "The events are the proclamation of Anastasius as Eastern emperor in 491, the deposition of Kavadh of Persia in 496 and his return to the throne in 499, as commonly given. The program sorts the list and prints the gaps, so the output can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (499, "Kavadh of Persia returns to the throne"),
                (491, "Anastasius is proclaimed Eastern emperor"),
                (496, "Kavadh of Persia is deposed"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, what in events:
                gap = "" if previous is None else f" (+{year - previous} years)"
                print(year, what + gap)
                previous = year
            print("years from first to last:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 480 to 490: the years from Zhang Qiujian's Mathematical Classic to Victor of Vita's history, in Python and C. */
val db156Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 156,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Years",
        title = "Years from the Mathematical Classic of Zhang Qiujian to Victor's Vandal history, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Zhang Qiujian suanjing and Historia persecutionis",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 485,
        summary = "A short program counts the years from Zhang Qiujian's Mathematical Classic of 485 to Victor of Vita's history of 488, and a run script checks that the Python and C programs print the same count.",
        details = "Both years are the ones used in this database, 485 for the end of the window given for the Mathematical Classic and 488 for the date used for Victor's history. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, so the check is on the two programs and not on the dates.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### years.py
            ZHANG_QIUJIAN = 485   # end of the usual range for the Mathematical Classic
            VICTOR = 488          # the date of Victor of Vita's history used here
            print("years from the Mathematical Classic to Victor's history:", VICTOR - ZHANG_QIUJIAN)
            ### years.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const int zhang_qiujian = 485;   /* end of the usual range for the Mathematical Classic */
                const int victor = 488;          /* the date of Victor of Vita's history used here */
                printf("years from the Mathematical Classic to Victor's history: %d\n", victor - zhang_qiujian);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 years.py > python.txt
            cc -o years_c years.c
            ./years_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        summary = "A field measured in square bu converts to mu at 240 square bu to the mu, and a short program turns three fields into mu with the square bu left over.",
        details = "The sources do not date this unit rule to the 480s; the rule is older, and 485 is the year of the anchor, the Northern Wei equal-field decree that measured its grants in mu, not the year of the rule. The fields are whole-number rectangles, so the count is exact.",

        """,

/** Guides of 480 to 490: how a household's equal-field grant of land is counted in mu under the rule of 485. */
val db156Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 156,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Land",
        title = "How a household's equal-field grant of land is worked out in mu, by the rule of the Northern Wei",
        originalTitle = "Juntian",
        author = "The Northern Wei court",
        year = 485,
        summary = "Under the equal-field rule of 485, a man aged fifteen or more received 40 mu and a woman received 20 mu, and a short program adds up the grant for one household.",
        details = "The decree is dated to the ninth year of the Taihe era, and a plot went back to the state when its holder died. The example counts a household of four people, with a boy of nine too young for land, and prints the grant for each member and the total.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as equal_field.py.
            2. Run it: python3 equal_field.py
        """,
        example = """
            MEN_MU = 40          # men aged fifteen and up
            WOMEN_MU = 20        # women
            ADULT_AGE = 15

            household = [("man", 40), ("man", 15), ("woman", 30), ("man", 9)]
            total = 0
            for sex, age in household:
                if sex == "man" and age >= ADULT_AGE:
                    mu = MEN_MU
                elif sex == "woman":
                    mu = WOMEN_MU
                else:
                    mu = 0
                total += mu
                print(sex, age, "receives", mu, "mu")
            print("total grant:", total, "mu")
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 156,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Events",
        title = "Three dated events of 483 to 489 from Rome, Persia and Italy, put in order with the years between them",
        originalTitle = "Timeline of three events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 489,
        summary = "A short program puts three events of 483 to 489 from Rome, Persia and Italy in date order and counts the years between them, and the example prints the timeline.",
        details = "The three events are the death of Pope Simplicius in 483, the death of the Persian king Peroz in battle with the Hephthalites in 484, and the battle of Verona in 489, each given by its year. None of them is a record of this database, and the example takes the years as given.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (489, "battle of Verona, Theoderic defeats Odoacer"),
                (483, "death of Pope Simplicius"),
                (484, "death of Peroz I of Persia in battle with the Hephthalites"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, label in events:
                if previous is None:
                    print(year, label, "| first event")
                else:
                    print(year, label, "| years since previous:", year - previous)
                previous = year
            print("span from first to last:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

        author = "No single author",
        year = 472,
        summary = "Four events of 472 to 480 are listed out of order, then sorted by year and printed with the gap in years from the one before.",
        details = "The events are Ricimer's siege of Rome, which ended with the death of Anthemius in 472, Zeno's reign at Constantinople from 474, the death of Gaiseric in 477, and the murder of Julius Nepos in Dalmatia in 480. The program prints each event with its gap from the one before, and then the count and the total span.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as events.py.
            2. Run it: python3 events.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (477, "Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, dies"),
                (472, "Ricimer's siege of Rome ends with the death of Anthemius"),
                (480, "Julius Nepos is murdered in Dalmatia"),
                (474, "Zeno becomes sole emperor at Constantinople"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, text in events:
                if previous is None:
                    print(year, text)
                else:
                    print(year, text, "after", year - previous, "years")
                previous = year
            print("events:", len(events))
            print("span in years:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)
