package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 362 and 363: the day of the year for Julian's school edict and for his death, each in Python and C. */
val db168Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 168,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "The day of the year for Julian's school edict and his death, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Day of the year",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 363,
        summary = "The day of the year for the school edict of 17 June 362 and for the death of Julian on 26 June 363 is worked out in Python and again in C, and a script checks that the two outputs match.",
        details = "Both years are common years, so the example uses a fixed table with 28 days in February and no leap rule. The Python and C programs print the same two lines, and the run script compares them line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### day_count.py
            # Day of the year for two dates of 362 and 363; both are common years, so February has 28 days.
            LENGTHS = [31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]


            def day_of_year(month, day):
                return sum(LENGTHS[:month - 1]) + day


            print("school edict of 17 June 362: day", day_of_year(6, 17))
            print("death of Julian on 26 June 363: day", day_of_year(6, 26))
            ### day_count.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static const int lengths[12] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};

            static int day_of_year(int month, int day) {
                int total = day;
                for (int m = 0; m < month - 1; m++) {
                    total += lengths[m];
                }
                return total;
            }

            int main(void) {
                printf("school edict of 17 June 362: day %d\n", day_of_year(6, 17));
                printf("death of Julian on 26 June 363: day %d\n", day_of_year(6, 26));
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 day_count.py > python.txt
            cc -o day_count_c day_count.c
            ./day_count_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 168,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Timeline",
        title = "Three events of 361 to 366 in the Roman world, sorted and spaced in code",
        originalTitle = "Three dated events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 366,
        summary = "Three dated events of 361 to 366, the death of Constantius II, the revolt of Procopius against Valens and the election of Damasus at Rome, are sorted by year and spaced by a short program.",
        details = "Constantius II died in 361, Procopius revolted against Valens in 365, and Damasus was chosen bishop of Rome in 366. The program prints each event with the gap in years from the one before, and it does only subtraction, so the output can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Three dated events of 361 to 366, sorted by year and spaced by the years between them.
            events = [
                (366, "Damasus chosen bishop of Rome"),
                (361, "death of Constantius II"),
                (365, "revolt of Procopius against Valens"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, label in events:
                if previous is None:
                    print(year, label)
                else:
                    print(year, label, "(+%d)" % (year - previous))
                previous = year
            print("span in years:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)

        details = "The practice is older than the codices of the mid-fourth century, such as Codex Sinaiticus, which use it widely, so 350 is the year of that anchor and not the year the practice began. The record is placed for that reason, and the two programs use ASCII stand-ins for the Greek letters: T theta, E epsilon, O omicron, S sigma, K kappa, Y upsilon, R rho and I iota.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### nomina.py
            # ASCII stand-ins for the Greek letters: T theta, E epsilon, O omicron, S sigma, K kappa, Y upsilon, R rho, I iota
            WORDS = {"theos": "TEOS", "kyrios": "KYRIOS"}
            saved = 0
            for word, letters in WORDS.items():
                print(word, "is written", letters[0] + letters[-1], "from", len(letters), "letters")
                saved += len(letters) - 2
            print("letters saved:", saved)
            ### nomina.c
            #include <stdio.h>
            #include <string.h>

            int main(void) {
                /* the same ASCII stand-ins as nomina.py */
                const char *words[] = {"theos", "kyrios"};
                const char *letters[] = {"TEOS", "KYRIOS"};
                int saved = 0;
                for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
                    size_t n = strlen(letters[i]);
                    printf("%s is written %c%c from %d letters\n", words[i], letters[i][0], letters[i][n - 1], (int)n);
                    saved += (int)n - 2;
                }
                printf("letters saved: %d\n", saved);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 nomina.py > python.txt
            cc -o nomina_c nomina.c
            ./nomina_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 169,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Lent",
        title = "How the forty fasting days of Lent are counted back from Easter",
        originalTitle = "Quadragesima",
        author = "The churches of the fourth century",
        year = 350,
        summary = "Lent has forty fasting days before Easter, and because the six Sundays are not fasting days, Ash Wednesday falls 46 days before Easter Sunday.",
        details = "The rule is the same in every year, and the record uses 350 because that is the rounded date of Cyril's course in Jerusalem, which keeps the year in the decade. The example takes Easter as a fixed day of the year, so the count is the same on every run, and it prints the days, the Sundays and the fasting days.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as lent.py.
            2. Run it: python3 lent.py
        """,
        example = """
            ASH_WEDNESDAY = 54   # day of the year, illustrative
            EASTER = 100         # Easter Sunday as a day of the year, illustrative
            days = EASTER - ASH_WEDNESDAY
            sundays = sum(1 for d in range(days) if (3 + d) % 7 == 0)   # Ash Wednesday is a Wednesday; weekday 0 is Sunday
            print("days from Ash Wednesday to Easter:", days)
            print("Sundays in Lent:", sundays)
            print("fasting days:", days - sundays)
        """,
    ),

)

        title = "The murder of Constans to Constantius's Rome visit, four dated events counted in code",
        originalTitle = "Timeline of 350 to 357",
        author = "No one author",
        year = 350,
        summary = "Four dated events from the murder of Constans in 350 to Constantius's visit to Rome in 357 are sorted by year, and a short program prints the gaps between them.",
        details = "Magnentius's agents killed Constans in 350, the Caesar Gallus was executed in 354, the council of Milan of 355 condemned Athanasius, and Constantius visited Rome in 357. The years are given as commonly stated, and the program prints each event, the gap to the next event and the span of the four.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            EVENTS = [
                (357, "Constantius visits Rome"),
                (350, "Constans is murdered"),
                (355, "council of Milan"),
                (354, "Gallus is executed"),
            ]
            events = sorted(EVENTS)
            for year, name in events:
                print(year, name)
            for (first, _), (second, _) in zip(events, events[1:]):

            print("span", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db16Cross.kt
################################################################################
package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1880 to 1890: the same result from two languages, the Tower of Hanoi and a keyboard adder. */
val db16Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Recursion",
        title = "Tower of Hanoi moves in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "La Tour d'Hanoi",
        author = "Edouard Lucas, writing as N. Claus de Siam",
        year = 1883,
        summary = "The puzzle of moving a tower of disks is solved by the same recursive rule in Python and in C, and both print the same seven moves for three disks.",
        details = "Lucas published the puzzle in 1883 under the pen name N. Claus de Siam, with the tower moved between three pegs. The two programs use the same recursion, and the example prints each move with a count. The seven moves for three disks are the same in both languages.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the two programs in the example as hanoi.py and hanoi.c, one file for each ### line.
            2. Run it: python3 hanoi.py, then cc -o hanoi_c hanoi.c and ./hanoi_c; the two outputs match.
        """,
        example = """
            ### hanoi.py
            def hanoi(n, source, target, spare, moves):
                # Move n disks from source to target, using spare; the largest disk moves once, in the middle.
                if n == 0:
                    return
                hanoi(n - 1, source, spare, target, moves)
                moves.append((n, source, target))
                hanoi(n - 1, spare, target, source, moves)

            moves = []
            hanoi(3, "A", "C", "B", moves)
            for k, (disk, src, dst) in enumerate(moves, start=1):
                print(f"{k}: disk {disk} {src} -> {dst}")
            print(f"moves for 3 disks: {len(moves)}")
            ### hanoi.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static int count = 0;

            /* Move n disks from source to target through spare, printing each move. */
            static void hanoi(int n, char source, char target, char spare) {
                if (n == 0) {
                    return;
                }
                hanoi(n - 1, source, spare, target);
                count++;
                printf("%d: disk %d %c -> %c\n", count, n, source, target);
                hanoi(n - 1, spare, target, source);
            }

            int main(void) {
                hanoi(3, 'A', 'C', 'B');
                printf("moves for 3 disks: %d\n", count);
                return 0;
            }
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Adding machines",
        title = "Keyboard adder with carries in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Key-driven adding machine",
        author = "William Seward Burroughs",
        year = 1888,
        summary = "A column-by-column adder that carries to the left like a keyboard calculator, written in Python and in C, with both programs printing the same register after each entry.",
        details = "Burroughs's key-driven adding machine, patented in August 1888, added each entry column by column and carried to the left. The two programs keep a five-column register, add five entries and print the register with the carry out. The last entry overflows the register and shows the carry.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the two programs in the example as burroughs.py and burroughs.c, one file for each ### line.
            2. Run it: python3 burroughs.py, then cc -o burroughs_c burroughs.c and ./burroughs_c; the two outputs match.
        """,
        example = """
            ### burroughs.py
            def add_into(register, entry):
                # Add the entry column by column from the units, carrying to the next column as a keyboard adder does.
                carry = 0
                for i in range(len(register)):
                    digit = register[i] + entry[i] + carry
                    register[i] = digit % 10
                    carry = digit // 10
                return carry

            register = [0] * 5          # digits, units first
            for amount in (2735, 1468, 9999, 42, 99999):
                digits = [int(d) for d in str(amount).zfill(5)[::-1]]   # units first
                carry_out = add_into(register, digits)
                shown = "".join(str(d) for d in register[::-1])
                print(f"after {amount}: {shown} carry out {carry_out}")
            ### burroughs.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* Add an entry into a five-column register, units first, carrying to the left. */
            static int add_into(int reg[5], const int entry[5]) {
                int carry = 0;
                for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
                    int digit = reg[i] + entry[i] + carry;
                    reg[i] = digit % 10;
                    carry = digit / 10;
                }
                return carry;
            }

            int main(void) {
                int reg[5] = {0, 0, 0, 0, 0};
                int amounts[5] = {2735, 1468, 9999, 42, 99999};
                for (int k = 0; k < 5; k++) {
                    int entry[5];
                    int value = amounts[k];
                    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
                        entry[i] = value % 10;
                        value /= 10;
                    }
                    int carry = add_into(reg, entry);
                    printf("after %d: ", amounts[k]);
                    for (int i = 4; i >= 0; i--) {
                        printf("%d", reg[i]);
                    }
                    printf(" carry out %d\n", carry);
                }
                return 0;
            }
        """,
    ),
)

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Trees",
        title = "Labelled trees counted by Cayley's formula",
        originalTitle = "A Theorem on Trees",
        author = "Arthur Cayley",
        year = 1889,
        summary = "On n labelled vertices there are n to the power n minus 2 trees, and a brute-force count for small n confirms the formula.",
        details = "Cayley's 1889 note gave the count of labelled trees on n vertices as n to the power n minus 2. The example checks every set of n minus 1 edges and keeps those that connect all vertices, for n from 2 to 6. The printed counts are 1, 3, 16, 125 and 1296.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as trees.py.
            2. Run it: python3 trees.py
        """,
        example = """
            from itertools import combinations

            def is_tree(n, edges):
                # n - 1 edges on n vertices form a tree exactly when they never close a cycle.
                parent = list(range(n))
                def find(x):
                    while parent[x] != x:
                        x = parent[x]
                    return x
                for a, b in edges:
                    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
                    if ra == rb:
                        return False
                    parent[ra] = rb
                return True

            for n in range(2, 7):
                all_edges = list(combinations(range(n), 2))
                count = sum(1 for chosen in combinations(all_edges, n - 1) if is_tree(n, chosen))
                print(f"n = {n}: {count} trees")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Colouring",

        year = 1890,
        summary = "A map on a surface of genus g needs at most the number of colours given by Heawood's formula, which is 4 on the sphere and 7 on the torus.",
        details = "Heawood's 1890 paper found a flaw in Kempe's 1879 proof of the four colour theorem and gave a bound for surfaces with g handles. The bound is the integer part of (7 plus the square root of 1 plus 48 g) divided by 2. The example prints the bound for genus 0 to 4, using the integer square root so that no rounding is needed.",
        instructions = """

        """,

            # where H(g) = floor((7 + sqrt(1 + 48 g)) / 2). The integer square root gives the same floor.

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Space-filling curves",
        title = "Peano's space-filling curve on a grid",
        originalTitle = "Sur une courbe, qui remplit toute une aire plane",
        author = "Giuseppe Peano",
        year = 1890,
        summary = "A curve that passes through every cell of a grid, one step to a neighbouring cell at a time, built by repeating a three-by-three pattern.",
        details = "Peano published the first space-filling curve in 1890 in Mathematische Annalen, using a three-by-three pattern of blocks in each level. The example builds the curve for levels 1 to 3 and checks that every step moves to a neighbouring cell. The end cell is the far corner of the grid, as the construction requires.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as peano.py.
            2. Run it: python3 peano.py
        """,
        example = """
            def peano(n):
                # Level n visits every cell of a 3^n by 3^n grid, one neighbouring step at a time.
                if n == 0:
                    return [(0, 0)]
                sub = peano(n - 1)
                size = 3 ** (n - 1)
                blocks = [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (1, 1), (1, 0), (2, 0), (2, 1), (2, 2)]
                turns = ["id", "flip_x", "id", "flip_y", "turn", "flip_y", "id", "flip_x", "id"]
                cells = []
                for (bx, by), turn in zip(blocks, turns):
                    for x, y in sub:
                        if turn == "flip_x":
                            x, y = size - 1 - x, y
                        elif turn == "flip_y":
                            x, y = x, size - 1 - y
                        elif turn == "turn":
                            x, y = size - 1 - x, size - 1 - y
                        cells.append((bx * size + x, by * size + y))
                return cells

            def unit_steps(cells):
                return all(abs(a[0] - b[0]) + abs(a[1] - b[1]) == 1 for a, b in zip(cells, cells[1:]))

            for n in range(1, 4):
                cells = peano(n)
                print(f"level {n}: {len(cells)} cells, {len(cells) - 1} steps, unit steps: {unit_steps(cells)}, ends at {cells[-1]}")
        """,
    ),
)

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Logic diagrams",
        title = "How Venn diagrams check a syllogism",
        originalTitle = "On the Diagrammatic and Mechanical Representation of Propositions and Reasonings",
        author = "John Venn",
        year = 1880,
        summary = "Each premise shades part of a three-circle diagram, and the conclusion holds when every region it would shade is already empty.",
        details = "Venn's 1880 paper gave a diagram of three overlapping circles and a rule for shading the regions that a universal premise rules out. The example runs three syllogisms through that rule, using the eight regions as triples of inside and outside. The program prints how many regions survive the premises and whether the conclusion holds.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as venn.py.
            2. Run it: python3 venn.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Three circles S, M and P. A region is a triple (s, m, p): 1 inside the circle, 0 outside.
            regions = [(s, m, p) for s in (0, 1) for m in (0, 1) for p in (0, 1)]
            POS = {"S": 0, "M": 1, "P": 2}

            def shaded(kind, a, b):
                # Venn shading: "All A are B" empties the part of A outside B; "No A are B" empties the part of A inside B.
                if kind == "A":
                    return {r for r in regions if r[POS[a]] == 1 and r[POS[b]] == 0}
                return {r for r in regions if r[POS[a]] == 1 and r[POS[b]] == 1}

            def test(name, premises, conclusion):
                left = set(regions)
                for kind, a, b in premises:
                    left -= shaded(kind, a, b)
                kind, a, b = conclusion
                # The conclusion holds when every region it would shade is already empty.
                ok = all(r not in shaded(kind, a, b) for r in left)
                print(f"{name}: {len(left)} regions left, {'valid' if ok else 'invalid'}")

            test("Barbara", [("A", "M", "P"), ("A", "S", "M")], ("A", "S", "P"))
            test("Celarent", [("E", "M", "P"), ("A", "S", "M")], ("E", "S", "P"))
            test("AAA-2", [("A", "P", "M"), ("A", "S", "M")], ("A", "S", "P"))
        """,
    ),

            count = 0

        author = "James Joseph Sylvester",

        summary = "Each step takes the unit fraction with the smallest denominator that does not overshoot, so any positive fraction splits into distinct unit fractions.",
        details = "Sylvester's note of 1880 in the American Journal of Mathematics described the greedy method, which Fibonacci had already used in his Liber abaci of 1202. Each step is a ceiling division, and the process always ends; the 1880 date rests on a single secondary bibliography.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as greedy.py.
            2. Run it: python3 greedy.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            def greedy_unit_fractions(x):
                # Each step takes the unit fraction 1/d with the smallest d that does not overshoot x.
                parts = []
                while x > 0:
                    d = -(-x.denominator // x.numerator)   # ceiling of denominator / numerator
                    parts.append(Fraction(1, d))
                    x -= Fraction(1, d)
                return parts

            for x in (Fraction(2, 3), Fraction(5, 6), Fraction(7, 15)):
                parts = greedy_unit_fractions(x)
                print(f"{x} = " + " + ".join(str(p) for p in parts))
        """,
    ),

        instructions = """

        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            # Five invented pairs, not Galton's data: x is one measurement and y is the other.
            x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
            y = [2, 4, 5, 4, 5]
            n = len(x)
            mean_x = Fraction(sum(x), n)
            mean_y = Fraction(sum(y), n)
            dx = [Fraction(a) - mean_x for a in x]
            dy = [Fraction(b) - mean_y for b in y]
            sxy = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(dx, dy))
            sxx = sum(a * a for a in dx)
            syy = sum(b * b for b in dy)
            print("sum of products of deviations:", sxy)
            print("sum of squares for x:", sxx)
            print("sum of squares for y:", syy)
            r2 = sxy * sxy / (sxx * syy)
            print("co-relation squared:", r2)
            print("co-relation:", round(float(r2) ** 0.5, 4))
        """,
    ),

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 1880 to 1890: a feeder with voltage drop, series transformers, an energy meter and a time clock, each a small program. */
val db16Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Distribution",
        title = "A direct-current feeder with voltage drop",
        originalTitle = "Feeder mains of a direct-current station",
        author = "Edison central-station practice",
        year = 1882,
        summary = "A direct-current main fed at 110 volts loses voltage in each section by the current that section carries, and the program finds the voltage at each lamp group.",
        details = "Edison's direct-current stations of the early 1880s fed lamps at about 110 volts over mains that lost voltage along their length. The example works through three sections with loads at their far ends, using exact fractions for the resistances and currents. The program prints the voltage at each tap and the worst drop.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as feeder.py.
            2. Run it: python3 feeder.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            # A direct-current main fed at 110 V, with three sections and lamp groups tapped at their far ends.
            supply = Fraction(110)
            resistance = [Fraction(2, 100), Fraction(3, 100), Fraction(5, 100)]   # ohms in each section
            load = [Fraction(20), Fraction(10), Fraction(5)]                       # amperes drawn at each tap

            voltage = supply
            for k in range(3):
                # The current in section k is the sum of the loads at and beyond its far end.
                current = sum(load[k:])
                voltage -= current * resistance[k]
                print(f"node {k + 1}: {float(voltage):.2f} V")
            print(f"worst drop: {float(supply - voltage):.2f} V")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Transformers",
        title = "A series primary feeding transformer secondaries",
        originalTitle = "Gaulard and Gibbs secondary generator",
        author = "Lucien Gaulard and John Dixon Gibbs",
        year = 1882,
        summary = "Transformers with their primaries wired in series across one high-voltage line each take an equal share of the line voltage and step it down for their own lamp group.",
        details = "Gaulard and Gibbs proposed feeding transformer primaries in series from an alternating line, a design that Stanley's system later used. The dates of their patent and demonstrations are given differently by sources, so the record uses the year of the proposal. The example divides a 2000 volt line among four primaries and computes the secondary voltage.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as series_primary.py.
            2. Run it: python3 series_primary.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            # Transformers whose primary windings are wired in series across one high-voltage line.
            line_volts = 2000
            transformers = 4
            primary_volts = Fraction(line_volts, transformers)   # equal primaries share the line voltage
            turns_ratio = 5                                       # primary turns per secondary turn
            secondary_volts = primary_volts / turns_ratio
            print(f"each primary: {primary_volts} V")
            print(f"each secondary: {secondary_volts} V")
            print("lamp groups fed:", transformers)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Metering",
        title = "Energy from sampled volts and amps",
        originalTitle = "Alternating-current watt-hour meter",
        author = "Oliver Shallenberger",
        year = 1888,
        summary = "An alternating-current meter counts energy by averaging the product of voltage and current over whole cycles, so a current a quarter cycle out of step adds nothing.",
        details = "Shallenberger's alternating-current meter of 1888 was an early commercial meter for this purpose. The example samples one cycle of a sine wave at four points, once with the current in step and once a quarter cycle out. The program prints the average power in each case and the energy for three hours.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as watthour.py.
            2. Run it: python3 watthour.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            # One cycle of a sine wave sampled four times: voltage and current in step, then a quarter cycle apart.
            volts = [0, 100, 0, -100]
            amps_in_step = [0, 2, 0, -2]
            amps_quarter_out = [2, 0, -2, 0]

            def average_power(v, i):
                # The meter averages the product of voltage and current over whole cycles.
                return Fraction(sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v, i)), len(v))

            print("in step:", average_power(volts, amps_in_step), "W")
            print("a quarter cycle out:", average_power(volts, amps_quarter_out), "W")
            hours = 3
            energy = average_power(volts, amps_in_step) * hours / 1000
            print(f"energy in {hours} h: {float(energy):.3f} kWh")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 16,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Time keeping",
        title = "Hours worked from time-clock punches",
        originalTitle = "Time recorder",
        author = "Willard Legrand Bundy",
        year = 1888,
        summary = "A time recorder punched the clock time at each change of activity, and the day's hours are the sum of the intervals between the punches that start work and end it.",
        details = "Bundy's time recorder of 1888 recorded the clock time at each punch, so that the hours of a working day could be added up. The example takes four punches with a lunch break, converts them to minutes, and adds the two working intervals. The program prints the total in hours and minutes and as a decimal.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeclock.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeclock.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Punch times on one day: clock in, lunch out, lunch in, clock out.
            punches = ["08:55", "12:00", "12:30", "17:20"]

            def minutes(clock):
                hours, mins = clock.split(":")
                return int(hours) * 60 + int(mins)

            times = [minutes(p) for p in punches]
            worked = (times[1] - times[0]) + (times[3] - times[2])
            print(f"worked {worked // 60} h {worked % 60} min")
            print(f"decimal hours: {worked / 60:.2f}")
        """,
    ),
)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 346 to 349: the years from the second attempt on Nisibis to the death of Shi Hu, in Python and C. */
val db170Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 170,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Years from the second Persian attempt on Nisibis to the death of Shi Hu, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Years between two dates",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 349,
        summary = "The second Persian attempt on Nisibis came in 346 and the Later Zhao ruler Shi Hu died in 349 by the usual dating, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same three-year span.",
        details = "Shi Hu, ruler of the Later Zhao, is usually said to have died in 349, and the span is computed from the two years alone, so it says nothing about the causes of either event. The run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### span.py
            NISIBIS = 346   # the second Persian attempt on Nisibis, as dated here
            SHI_HU = 349    # the death of Shi Hu of the Later Zhao, as usually dated
            print("years from Nisibis to the death of Shi Hu:", SHI_HU - NISIBIS)
            ### span.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int nisibis = 346;   /* the second Persian attempt on Nisibis, as dated here */
                int shi_hu = 349;    /* the death of Shi Hu of the Later Zhao, as usually dated */
                printf("years from Nisibis to the death of Shi Hu: %d\n", shi_hu - nisibis);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 span.py > python.txt
            cc -o span_c span.c
            ./span_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 340: how analysis and synthesis solve a problem, as Pappus describes them in his Collection of about 340. */
val db170Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 170,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Method",
        title = "How analysis and synthesis solve a problem, as Pappus sets them out",
        originalTitle = "Analysis and synthesis",
        author = "Pappus of Alexandria and the geometers before him",
        year = 340,
        summary = "Pappus describes two ways of solving a problem: analysis works backward from the sought result to what is given, and synthesis runs the same steps forward again.",
        details = "Pappus sets out the two methods in his Collection of about 340, and accounts differ on how much of the method came from earlier geometers such as Euclid. The example uses an illustrative chain of claims, with letters chosen for the purpose rather than Pappus's own propositions.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as analysis.py.
            2. Run it: python3 analysis.py
        """,
        example = """
            NEEDS = {"G": "F", "F": "E", "E": "B"}   # to prove each claim, it is enough to prove the one it names
            GIVEN = {"B", "C"}                       # claims already known
            path = []
            claim = "G"                              # the sought claim
            while claim not in GIVEN:
                path.append(claim)
                claim = NEEDS[claim]
            path.append(claim)
            print("analysis:", " -> ".join(path))
            print("synthesis:", " -> ".join(reversed(path)))
            print("steps of analysis:", len(path) - 1)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 170,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Timelines",
        title = "Three events of 341 to 346, put in order and spaced by a program",
        originalTitle = "Timeline of events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 341,
        summary = "A council of Eastern bishops at Antioch in 341, the accession of Emperor Mu of the Eastern Jin in 344 and the return of Athanasius to Alexandria in 346 are put in order, and a short program prints the gaps.",
        details = "The three events are given by the year usually cited for each, and the program sorts them and prints the gap to the next event. The arithmetic is simple enough to check by hand, and the example counts no reign length.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (346, "Athanasius returns to Alexandria"),
                (341, "council of Eastern bishops at Antioch"),
                (344, "Emperor Mu of the Eastern Jin comes to the throne"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            for (year, label), (next_year, _) in zip(events, events[1:]):
                print(year, label, "gap to next:", next_year - year)
            last_year, last_label = events[-1]
            print("last event:", last_year, last_label)
            print("years from first to last:", last_year - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One cross-code experiment of 330: the Chi-Rho monogram drawn as text in Python and in C, placed at 330 for the city named after Constantine. */
val db171Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 171,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Symbols",
        title = "The Chi-Rho monogram drawn as text in Python and in C",
        originalTitle = "Chi-Rho",
        author = "Christian makers of the Chi-Rho monogram",
        year = 330,
        summary = "The Chi-Rho monogram takes its name from the first two letters of Christos, and a script prints chi and rho side by side as text, with the same output in Python and C.",
        details = "The drawing is a stand-in: each letter is a five-row pattern of hash marks, and the two letters stand side by side rather than overlapped, so the example copies no surviving sign. The year 330 is the placed year, the year Constantinople was dedicated, because the sources do not date a text drawing of the monogram, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### chirho.py
            chi = ["#...#", ".#.#.", "..#..", ".#.#.", "#...#"]
            rho = ["####.", "#...#", "####.", "#....", "#...."]
            for c, r in zip(chi, rho):
                print(c, r)
            ### chirho.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const char *chi[] = {"#...#", ".#.#.", "..#..", ".#.#.", "#...#"};
                const char *rho[] = {"####.", "#...#", "####.", "#....", "#...."};
                for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
                    printf("%s %s\n", chi[i], rho[i]);
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 chirho.py > python.txt
            cc -o chirho_c chirho.c
            ./chirho_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

val db171Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 171,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Measures",
        title = "How a Roman amphora's capacity follows from the cubic foot, with the congius and sextarius",
        originalTitle = "amphora quadrantal",
        author = "Roman measurers of wine and oil",
        year = 332,
        summary = "A Roman amphora was one cubic foot, so a short program turns the foot into litres and divides the amphora into congii and sextarii.",
        details = "The method is much older than this year, and 332 is the placed year, the year of Constantine's campaign against the Goths, not the year of the measure. The Roman foot is taken as 296 millimetres, a round figure, and the program prints the capacities that follow from the cube of that foot, which can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as amphora.py.
            2. Run it: python3 amphora.py
        """,
        example = """
            FOOT_MM = 296                       # the Roman foot, taken as 296 millimetres
            CUBIC_FOOT_MM3 = FOOT_MM ** 3       # one cubic foot, which the amphora was defined to be
            AMPHORA = CUBIC_FOOT_MM3 / 1000000  # cubic millimetres to litres
            print("cubic foot in cubic millimetres:", CUBIC_FOOT_MM3)
            print("amphora: {:.2f} litres".format(AMPHORA))
            print("congius (one eighth of an amphora): {:.2f} litres".format(AMPHORA / 8))
            print("sextarius (one forty-eighth of an amphora): {:.2f} litres".format(AMPHORA / 48))
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 324: the weekday of the battle of Chrysopolis, computed in Python and in C with the same Julian rule. */
val db172Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 172,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Calendars",
        title = "The weekday of the battle of Chrysopolis, computed in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Weekday of 18 September 324",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 324,
        summary = "The battle of Chrysopolis fell on a Friday in the Julian reckoning, and a Python and a C program, each using the same weekday rule, print the same answer.",
        details = "The weekday rule is written for the Julian calendar, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line. The answer depends on the date usually given for the battle, not on the programs.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### weekday.py
            DAYS = ["Saturday", "Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"]
            year, month, day = 324, 9, 18
            k, j = year % 100, year // 100
            h = (day + (13 * (month + 1)) // 5 + k + k // 4 + 5 + 6 * j) % 7
            print("18 September 324 was a", DAYS[h])
            ### weekday.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                static const char *days[] = {"Saturday", "Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday",
                                             "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"};
                int year = 324, month = 9, day = 18;
                int k = year % 100, j = year / 100;
                int h = (day + (13 * (month + 1)) / 5 + k + k / 4 + 5 + 6 * j) % 7;
                printf("18 September 324 was a %s\n", days[h]);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 weekday.py > python.txt
            cc -o weekday_c weekday.c
            ./weekday_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Example of 321: the Sundays of the Julian year of Constantine's Sunday law, counted day by day in code. */
val db172Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 172,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Calendars",
        title = "Sundays in the year of Constantine's Sunday law, counted day by day in code",
        originalTitle = "Julian year 321",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 321,
        summary = "In the Julian reckoning 321, the year of Constantine's Sunday law, a short program counts the days and the Sundays of the year.",
        details = "The year began on a Sunday and had 365 days, so the count comes to 53 Sundays. The example applies a weekday rule for the Julian calendar to every day, so the total can be checked by counting the weeks by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as sundays_321.py.
            2. Run it: python3 sundays_321.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Julian reckoning: a year is a leap year when it divides by four.
            # Zeller's congruence for the Julian calendar: 0 is Saturday, 1 Sunday, ... 6 Friday.
            NAMES = ["Saturday", "Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday"]

            def weekday(year, month, day):
                if month < 3:
                    month += 12
                    year -= 1
                k, j = year % 100, year // 100
                h = (day + (13 * (month + 1)) // 5 + k + k // 4 + 5 + 6 * j) % 7
                return NAMES[h]

            def month_lengths(year):
                leap = year % 4 == 0
                return [31, 29 if leap else 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]

            YEAR = 321
            days = 0
            sundays = 0
            for month, length in enumerate(month_lengths(YEAR), start=1):
                for day in range(1, length + 1):
                    days += 1
                    if weekday(YEAR, month, day) == "Sunday":
                        sundays += 1
            print("year", YEAR, "days:", days)
            print("1 January", YEAR, "was a", weekday(YEAR, 1, 1))
            print("Sundays:", sundays)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

        databaseId = 172,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Week",
        title = "How the seven days of the week take their names from the planets, beginning with Saturn's day",
        originalTitle = "Dies Saturni, dies Solis, dies Lunae",
        author = "Roman and Greek astronomers and astrologers",
        year = 321,
        summary = "The seven days of the week take their names from the planets in a fixed order, and a short program names each day by the planet that rules its first hour.",
        details = "The planets rule the hours in the order Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury and the Moon, and because a day has 24 hours, which leaves three over each time, every new day starts three places further along that order. The method is far older than 321, so the record is placed at 321, the year of Constantine's Sunday law, which names Sunday as the venerable day of the Sun.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as planet_week.py.
            2. Run it: python3 planet_week.py
        """,
        example = """
            HOUR_ORDER = ["Saturn", "Jupiter", "Mars", "Sun", "Venus", "Mercury", "Moon"]
            DAY_NAMES = {"Saturn": "Saturday", "Sun": "Sunday", "Moon": "Monday", "Mars": "Tuesday",
                         "Mercury": "Wednesday", "Jupiter": "Thursday", "Venus": "Friday"}

            # A day has 24 hours, and 24 leaves three over when divided by seven,
            # so each new day starts three places further along the hour order.
            ruler = 0
            for day in range(7):
                planet = HOUR_ORDER[ruler]
                print(DAY_NAMES[planet], "is ruled by", planet)
                ruler = (ruler + 3) % 7
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 313: the days left in the year after the Milan letter was posted, in Python and in C. */
val db173Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 173,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Days left in 313 after the Milan letter was posted, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days to the end of the year",
        author = "Licinius",
        year = 313,
        summary = "After the Milan letter was posted on 13 June 313, 201 days remained in the year, and a script checks that the Python and C programs count the same days.",
        details = "The example counts the days from the posting to the last day of 313 in Python and in C, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line. The year 313 is a common year, so the C program needs only a table of month lengths.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### days.py
            from datetime import date

            posting = date(313, 6, 13)     # the Milan letter posted at Nicomedia, as commonly given
            year_end = date(313, 12, 31)
            print("days from 13 June 313 to 31 December 313:", (year_end - posting).days)
            ### days.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                /* days in each month of 313, a common year */
                int month_days[12] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};
                int before_posting = 0;
                for (int m = 0; m < 5; m++) {   /* January to May */
                    before_posting += month_days[m];
                }
                int posting_day = before_posting + 13;   /* 13 June is day 164 of the year */
                int year_length = 0;
                for (int m = 0; m < 12; m++) {
                    year_length += month_days[m];
                }
                printf("days from 13 June 313 to 31 December 313: %d\n", year_length - posting_day);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 days.py > python.txt
            cc -o days_c days.c
            ./days_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 310 to 320: how the strength of a Roman legion is counted from its cohorts and centuries, using the textbook arrangement. */
val db173Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 173,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Army",
        title = "How the strength of a Roman legion is counted from its cohorts and centuries",
        originalTitle = "Legio",
        author = "Roman military writers",
        year = 310,
        summary = "The textbook Roman legion had ten cohorts of six centuries of eighty men, and a short program adds them up to its full strength.",
        details = "The textbook arrangement is older than the fourth century, and the sources do not date the legion's strength in the 310s, so 310 is only the placed year of this record. The first cohort was in practice double-sized, which the program ignores, so the total is the textbook figure of 4,800 men.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as legion.py.
            2. Run it: python3 legion.py
        """,
        example = """
            COHORTS = 10
            CENTURIES_PER_COHORT = 6
            MEN_PER_CENTURY = 80
            centuries = COHORTS * CENTURIES_PER_COHORT
            men = centuries * MEN_PER_CENTURY
            print("centuries in the legion:", centuries)
            print("men in one cohort:", CENTURIES_PER_COHORT * MEN_PER_CENTURY)
            print("men in the legion:", men)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 310 to 320: four dated events of 311 to 316, sorted and spaced by a short program. */
val db173Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 173,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Timeline",
        title = "Four dated events of 311 to 316 in Rome and China, sorted and spaced by a short program",
        originalTitle = "Timeline of four events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 316,
        summary = "Four events of 311 to 316, the deaths of Galerius and Maximinus Daia, the sack of Luoyang and the fall of Chang'an, are sorted by year and spaced by a short program.",
        details = "Galerius died in 311, Luoyang was sacked in 311, Maximinus Daia died in 313 and Chang'an fell in 316. The program sorts the events with ties in alphabetical order and prints the gap from each event to the next, so the output can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (316, "fall of Chang'an"),
                (311, "sack of Luoyang"),
                (313, "death of Maximinus Daia"),
                (311, "death of Galerius"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, name in events:
                gap = "" if previous is None else f" (gap {year - previous} years)"
                print(year, name + gap)
                previous = year
            print("span in years:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 306 to 308: the days from Constantine's acclamation at York to the Carnuntum conference, counted in Python and in C. */
val db174Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 174,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Days from Constantine's acclamation at York to the Carnuntum conference in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days between two dated events",
        author = "Constantine, Galerius and Licinius",
        year = 306,
        summary = "Constantine's acclamation at York and the Carnuntum conference are counted in days by a Python program and a C program, and a script checks that both print the same count.",
        details = "The dates are as commonly given, 25 July 306 and 11 November 308, and the count is 840 days. The C program uses a civil-date formula written out in the file, so the comparison tests two separate calendar calculations.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### york.py
            from datetime import date

            york = date(306, 7, 25)         # the acclamation at York, as commonly given
            carnuntum = date(308, 11, 11)   # the conference at Carnuntum, as commonly given
            print("days from York to Carnuntum:", (carnuntum - york).days)
            ### york.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* days since 1970 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar, by a civil-date formula */
            static long days_from_civil(long y, unsigned m, unsigned d) {
                y -= m <= 2;
                long era = (y >= 0 ? y : y - 399) / 400;
                unsigned yoe = (unsigned)(y - era * 400);
                unsigned doy = (153 * (m > 2 ? m - 3 : m + 9) + 2) / 5 + d - 1;
                unsigned doe = yoe * 365 + yoe / 4 - yoe / 100 + doy;
                return era * 146097 + (long)doe - 719468;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long york = days_from_civil(306, 7, 25);
                long carnuntum = days_from_civil(308, 11, 11);
                printf("days from York to Carnuntum: %ld\n", carnuntum - york);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 york.py > python.txt
            cc -o york_c york.c
            ./york_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 300 to 310: how Porphyry's Enneads divide fifty-four treatises into six sets of nine, worked out in code. */
val db174Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 174,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Numbering",
        title = "How Porphyry's Enneads divide fifty-four treatises into six sets of nine",
        originalTitle = "Enneads",
        author = "Porphyry of Tyre, editing Plotinus",
        year = 301,
        summary = "Porphyry's edition of Plotinus's treatises divides fifty-four of them into six sets of nine, and a short program shows the split and checks the total.",
        details = "Porphyry published the edition around 301, and the sets are called Enneads, from the Greek word for nine. The arrangement is by subject rather than by date, so the example does not reproduce the subjects, but it numbers the treatises in order and splits the list into sets of nine.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as enneads.py.
            2. Run it: python3 enneads.py
        """,
        example = """
            TREATISES = 54
            PER_ENNEAD = 9
            enneads = TREATISES // PER_ENNEAD
            print("enneads:", enneads)
            for n in range(enneads):
                first = n * PER_ENNEAD + 1
                last = first + PER_ENNEAD - 1
                print("Ennead", n + 1, "treatises", first, "to", last)
            print("treatises checked:", enneads * PER_ENNEAD)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db175Cross.kt

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 293: the days from the naming of the Caesars to the Roman new year of 294, in Python and C. */
val db175Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 175,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Days",
        title = "Days from the naming of the Caesars to the Roman new year of 294, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Day count between two dates",
        author = "Julian calendar reckoners",
        year = 293,
        summary = "Days from the naming of the Caesars on 1 March 293 to the Roman new year of 294 come to 306, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same count.",
        details = "The most common date for the naming of the Caesars is 1 March 293, and the Roman civil year began on 1 January, so the span runs to the Kalends of January 294. The span holds no leap day, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### days.py
            MONTH_DAYS = [31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]

            def julian_leap(year):
                return year % 4 == 0

            def month_length(year, month):
                if month == 2 and julian_leap(year):
                    return 29
                return MONTH_DAYS[month - 1]

            def ordinal(year, month, day):
                # days counted from the start of the Julian calendar to the given date
                total = 0
                for y in range(1, year):
                    total += 366 if julian_leap(y) else 365
                for m in range(1, month):
                    total += month_length(year, m)
                return total + day

            start = ordinal(293, 3, 1)   # the Caesars were named on 1 March 293
            end = ordinal(294, 1, 1)     # the Kalends of January 294
            print("days:", end - start)
            ### days.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static const int month_days[12] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};

            static int julian_leap(int year) {
                return year % 4 == 0;
            }

            static int month_length(int year, int month) {
                if (month == 2 && julian_leap(year)) return 29;
                return month_days[month - 1];
            }

            static long ordinal(int year, int month, int day) {
                long total = 0;
                for (int y = 1; y < year; y++) total += julian_leap(y) ? 366 : 365;
                for (int m = 1; m < month; m++) total += month_length(year, m);
                return total + day;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long start = ordinal(293, 3, 1);   /* the Caesars were named on 1 March 293 */
                long end = ordinal(294, 1, 1);     /* the Kalends of January 294 */
                printf("days: %ld\n", end - start);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 days.py > python.txt
            cc -o days_c days.c
            ./days_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 290 to 300: an Egyptian multiplication by doubling, placed at 293 because the method is far older than the decade. */
val db175Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 175,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Arithmetic",
        title = "How an Egyptian scribe multiplies by doubling, written as code",
        originalTitle = "Doubling method",
        author = "Egyptian scribes",
        year = 293,
        summary = "An Egyptian scribe multiplied two numbers by doubling one of them and keeping the rows whose powers of two add up to the other, and a short program does this for 13 times 21.",
        details = "The method is far older than the period, and the sources do not date it to the 290s, so 293 is the year of the anchor, the naming of the Caesars, not the year the method was devised. The example multiplies 13 by 21 through its doubling table, so the product 273 can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as doubling.py.
            2. Run it: python3 doubling.py
        """,
        example = """
            def egyptian_product(a, b):
                # the doubling table: powers of two up to b, each with the matching multiple of a
                rows = []
                power, multiple = 1, a
                while power <= b:
                    rows.append((power, multiple))
                    power *= 2
                    multiple *= 2
                # add the rows whose powers, taken from the largest down, fit into what is left of b
                chosen = []
                rest = b
                for power, multiple in reversed(rows):
                    if power <= rest:
                        chosen.append(multiple)
                        rest -= power
                return rows, chosen, sum(chosen)

            rows, chosen, total = egyptian_product(13, 21)
            for power, multiple in rows:
                print(power, multiple)
            print("rows added:", sorted(chosen))
            print("product:", total)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

        author = "No single author",
        year = 290,
        summary = "Four dated events of 290 to 298, from China, Rome and Persia, are sorted by year and spaced out by a short program.",
        details = "The events are the death of Emperor Wu of Jin in 290, the naming of the Caesars on 1 March 293, Constantius's reconquest of Britain in 296 and Galerius's victory at Satala in 298. Only the Caesars' date is given to the day, and the program counts the years between the events, so its output can be checked by hand.",

                (290, "death of Emperor Wu of Jin"),
                (296, "Constantius's reconquest of Britain"),
                (293, "Galerius and Constantius named Caesars"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, what in events:
                if previous is None:

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 280: how long the states of Shu and Wu lasted, counted in Python and in C. */
val db176Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 176,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "States",
        title = "How long Shu and Wu lasted as states of the Three Kingdoms, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Years of two states",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 280,
        summary = "Shu lasted from its imperial title in 221 to its fall in 263, and Wu from its imperial title in 229 to its fall in 280, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same counts.",
        details = "Accounts of Wu give 222 as its start as a kingdom and 229 as its start as an empire, and the example uses 229. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, and the counts are 42 years for Shu and 51 years for Wu.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the programs as shu_wu.py and shu_wu.c, and the script as run.sh.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### shu_wu.py
            start_shu, end_shu = 221, 263   # Shu takes the imperial title in 221 and falls in 263
            start_wu, end_wu = 229, 280     # Wu takes the imperial title in 229 and falls in 280
            print("Shu", end_shu - start_shu, "years")
            print("Wu", end_wu - start_wu, "years")
            print("Wu outlasted Shu by", (end_wu - start_wu) - (end_shu - start_shu), "years")
            ### shu_wu.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int start_shu = 221, end_shu = 263;   /* Shu takes the imperial title in 221 and falls in 263 */
                int start_wu = 229, end_wu = 280;     /* Wu takes the imperial title in 229 and falls in 280 */
                printf("Shu %d years\n", end_shu - start_shu);
                printf("Wu %d years\n", end_wu - start_wu);
                printf("Wu outlasted Shu by %d years\n", (end_wu - start_wu) - (end_shu - start_shu));
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 shu_wu.py > python.txt
            cc -o shu_wu_c shu_wu.c
            ./shu_wu_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        year = 280,
        summary = "Four dated events of 280 to 290 are sorted by year, and a short program prints the gap in years between each one and the one before.",
        details = "The events are the Jin conquest of Wu in 280, the death of the Roman emperor Carus in 283, Wani's traditional arrival in Japan in 285, and the death of the Jin emperor Sima Yan in 290. Wani's year is the traditional reckoning, and the other years are the years usually given.",

                (280, "Jin conquest of Wu"),
                (285, "Wani's traditional arrival in Japan"),

            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, name in events:

        """,

    ),

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db177Cross.kt

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 274: the Julian day number and weekday of Aurelian's Sun festival of 25 December, computed in Python and C. */
val db177Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 177,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Calendars",
        title = "The Julian day number and weekday of 25 December 274, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Julian day number",
        author = "Joseph Scaliger, who devised the day count",
        year = 274,
        summary = "The Julian day number of 25 December 274 is 1821495, a Friday, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same day number and weekday.",
        details = "The day number is computed from the Julian calendar rules, which were in use in 274, and the weekday comes from the remainder when the day number is divided by seven, with day 0 a Monday. The two programs print the same lines, and the run script compares their outputs line by line.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### julian.py
            def julian_day_number(year, month, day):
                a = (14 - month) // 12
                y = year + 4800 - a
                m = month + 12 * a - 3
                return day + (153 * m + 2) // 5 + 365 * y + y // 4 - 32083

            jdn = julian_day_number(274, 12, 25)   # 25 December 274 in the Julian calendar
            names = ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"]
            print("julian day number:", jdn)
            print("weekday:", names[jdn % 7])
            ### julian.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int year = 274, month = 12, day = 25;   /* 25 December 274 in the Julian calendar */
                int a = (14 - month) / 12;
                int y = year + 4800 - a;
                int m = month + 12 * a - 3;
                long jdn = day + (153 * m + 2) / 5 + 365L * y + y / 4 - 32083;
                static const char *names[] = {"Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
                                              "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"};
                printf("julian day number: %ld\n", jdn);
                printf("weekday: %s\n", names[jdn % 7]);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 julian.py > python.txt
            cc -o julian_c julian.c
            ./julian_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        originalTitle = "Four dated events",
        author = "Ancient chroniclers of Rome and China",
        year = 270,
        summary = "Four dated events of 270 to 279, from Plotinus's death to the find of the Bamboo Annals, are sorted and spaced by a short program that prints the years between them.",
        details = "Plotinus died in 270, Aurelian's festival of the Sun is dated to 274, Aurelian was killed in 275, and the Bamboo Annals were found in 279, with accounts differing on the find, which some give as 281. The example sorts the four events by year, prints the gap to each earlier event, and reports a span of nine years, using the 279 date.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (279, "the Bamboo Annals are found in a tomb"),
                (270, "Plotinus dies"),
                (275, "Aurelian is killed in Thrace"),
                (274, "Aurelian's Sun festival is set at Rome"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, name in events:
                gap = "" if previous is None else f" (+{year - previous})"
                print(f"{year} {name}{gap}")
                previous = year
            print("span in years:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 262: the line counts of the three versions of Shapur I's inscription, totalled in Python and in C. */
val db178Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 178,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Inscriptions",
        title = "The lines of Shapur I's three versions, totalled and compared in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Res Gestae Divi Saporis",
        author = "Shapur I's court",
        year = 262,
        summary = "The Greek, Middle Persian and Parthian versions of Shapur I's inscription run to 70, 35 and 30 lines, and a Python and a C program total them.",
        details = "The three versions total 135 lines, and the Greek version is about twice the length of the Middle Persian one, so the program prints that ratio. The run script compares the output of the two programs line by line, and 262 is the usual date of the inscription.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### lines.py
            LINES = {"Greek": 70, "Middle Persian": 35, "Parthian": 30}   # line counts of the three versions
            for version, lines in LINES.items():
                print(version, lines, "lines")
            print("total lines:", sum(LINES.values()))
            print("Greek over Middle Persian:", round(LINES["Greek"] / LINES["Middle Persian"], 1))
            ### lines.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                /* line counts of the three versions, as given for each version */
                int greek = 70, middle_persian = 35, parthian = 30;
                printf("Greek %d lines\n", greek);
                printf("Middle Persian %d lines\n", middle_persian);
                printf("Parthian %d lines\n", parthian);
                printf("total lines: %d\n", greek + middle_persian + parthian);
                printf("Greek over Middle Persian: %.1f\n", (double)greek / middle_persian);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 lines.py > python.txt
            cc -o lines_c lines.c
            ./lines_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

/** Examples of 263: Liu Hui's doubling of an inscribed polygon up to 3,072 sides, read as the value of pi. */
val db178Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 178,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Circles",
        title = "Liu Hui's polygon of 3,072 sides, doubled from a hexagon for the value of pi",
        originalTitle = "Gehuan shu",
        author = "Liu Hui",
        year = 263,
        summary = "Liu Hui doubled an inscribed polygon from six sides to 3,072 and read its perimeter as the value of pi, arriving at 3.1416.",
        details = "His commentary, dated to 263, gives 3.14 from the 96-sided polygon and 3.1416 from the 3,072-sided one. The example repeats the doubling with square roots and prints both values to four places, and this record is about pi as a value, not about the commentary as a book.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as pi_polygon.py.
            2. Run it: python3 pi_polygon.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            # A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle of radius 1 has sides equal to the radius.
            sides = 6
            side = 1.0
            for step in range(1, 10):
                # the side of the polygon with twice as many sides: s2 = sqrt(2 - sqrt(4 - s * s))
                side = math.sqrt(2 - math.sqrt(4 - side * side))
                sides *= 2
                if sides in (96, 3072):
                    print(sides, "sides: pi about", f"{sides * side / 2:.4f}")
        """,
    ),

)

/** Guides of 263: Liu Hui's Sea Island method, which finds the height of a far island from two poles and two sightlines. */
val db178Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 178,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Surveying",
        title = "How the height of a far island is found from two poles and two sightlines",
        originalTitle = "Haidao suanjing",
        author = "Liu Hui",
        year = 263,
        summary = "The Sea Island Mathematical Manual finds the height of a far island from two poles and two sightlines, and a short program works the height from the withdrawals.",
        details = "The manual, dated to 263, sets two poles of three zhang, a thousand bu apart, and sights the island from ground level after backing off 123 bu from the front pole and 127 bu from the rear one. Working these data by similar triangles gives a height of 1255 bu, which is 4 li 55 bu, and the example works it out from the two withdrawals. The manual was later issued as a separate book, apart from the commentary.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as sea_island.py.
            2. Run it: python3 sea_island.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Units as the manual uses them: 1 zhang is 10 chi, 1 bu is 6 chi, 1 li is 300 bu.
            POLE_BU = 5          # a pole of 3 zhang, which is 30 chi, is 5 bu
            SPACING_BU = 1000    # the two poles stand 1000 bu apart
            FRONT_BU = 123       # the observer backs off 123 bu from the front pole
            REAR_BU = 127        # and 127 bu from the rear pole

            height = POLE_BU + POLE_BU * SPACING_BU // (REAR_BU - FRONT_BU)
            li, bu = divmod(height, 300)
            print("island height in bu:", height)
            print(f"island height: {li} li {bu} bu")
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)
