package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Examples of 1860 to 1870: short programs for the ciphers, heredity, heat, statistics, matrices and gears of the decade. */
val db18Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Cryptanalysis",
        title = "How Kasiski's test finds the key length of a Vigenere cipher",
        originalTitle = "Die Geheimschriften und die Dechiffrir-Kunst (1863)",
        author = "Friedrich Kasiski",
        year = 1863,
        summary = "Repeated groups of letters in a polyalphabetic ciphertext tend to lie at distances that are multiples of the key length, so the common factors of those distances suggest the key length.",
        details = "Kasiski published the method in 1863, although Babbage had broken similar ciphers earlier without publishing his work, so the priority is disputed. The example uses a 24-letter ciphertext made with a three-letter key, finds every repeated trigram, prints the distances between its occurrences, and counts the factors of those distances.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as kasiski.py.
            2. Run it: python3 kasiski.py
        """,
        example = """
            from collections import Counter

            # A 24-letter Vigenere ciphertext made with a three-letter key.
            cipher = "DLCMERKRBDLCNSEKRBDLCMER"

            # Every trigram that occurs more than once, with the distances between its occurrences.
            positions = {}
            for i in range(len(cipher) - 2):
                positions.setdefault(cipher[i:i + 3], []).append(i)
            repeats = {gram: spots for gram, spots in positions.items() if len(spots) > 1}
            distances = []
            for gram in sorted(repeats):
                spots = repeats[gram]
                for a, b in zip(spots, spots[1:]):
                    distances.append(b - a)
                    print(f"{gram} at {a} and {b}: distance {b - a}")
            print("distances:", distances)

            # Kasiski: the key length is likely to be a factor of most distances, so count the factors of each distance.
            counts = Counter()
            for d in distances:
                for f in range(2, d + 1):
                    if d % f == 0:
                        counts[f] += 1
            for f in sorted(counts):
                print(f"factor {f} appears {counts[f]} times")
            best = max(sorted(counts), key=lambda f: counts[f])
            print(f"suggested key length: {best}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Heredity",
        title = "How Mendel's crosses give the 3 to 1 ratio",
        originalTitle = "Versuche ueber Pflanzen-Hybriden (1866)",
        author = "Gregor Mendel",
        year = 1866,
        summary = "Crossing two plants that differ in one trait gives three dominant offspring to one recessive, and crossing on two traits gives nine, three, three and one.",
        details = "Mendel read his experiments on pea hybrids to the Brno natural history society in 1865, and the paper was printed in 1866. The example lists the four combinations of two heterozygous parents for one trait and the sixteen combinations for two traits, and counts them with exact fractions.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as mendel.py.
            2. Run it: python3 mendel.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction as F
            from itertools import product

            # One trait: each parent is Aa, and each offspring takes one allele from each parent.
            def genotype(x, y):
                if x == y == "A":
                    return "AA"
                if x == y == "a":
                    return "aa"
                return "Aa"

            parent = ["A", "a"]
            counts = {}
            for x, y in product(parent, parent):
                g = genotype(x, y)
                counts[g] = counts.get(g, 0) + 1
            total = sum(counts.values())
            for g in ["AA", "Aa", "aa"]:
                print(f"genotype {g}: {F(counts.get(g, 0), total)}")
            dominant = F(counts["AA"] + counts["Aa"], total)
            print(f"dominant trait: {dominant}")
            print(f"ratio dominant to recessive: {counts['AA'] + counts['Aa']}:{counts['aa']}")

            # Two traits: each parent makes four gamete types, and the sixteen pairings are counted.
            gametes = ["AB", "Ab", "aB", "ab"]
            phenotypes = {}
            for p, q in product(gametes, gametes):
                shape = "dominant" if "A" in p[0] + q[0] else "recessive"
                colour = "dominant" if "B" in p[1] + q[1] else "recessive"
                phenotypes[(shape, colour)] = phenotypes.get((shape, colour), 0) + 1
            for shape in ["dominant", "recessive"]:
                for colour in ["dominant", "recessive"]:
                    print(f"{shape} shape, {colour} colour: {F(phenotypes.get((shape, colour), 0), 16)}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Thermodynamics",
        title = "How Clausius's entropy balances a reversible cycle",
        originalTitle = "Ueber verschiedene fuer die Anwendung bequeme Formen der Hauptgleichungen der mechanischen Waermetheorie (1865)",
        author = "Rudolf Clausius",
        year = 1865,
        summary = "Heat taken in at one temperature and given out at another gives entropy changes that cancel in a reversible cycle, but add up to a gain when heat flows directly between the same reservoirs.",
        details = "Clausius introduced the word entropy in his 1865 paper, for the quantity whose change is heat divided by temperature for reversible exchanges. The example runs a Carnot cycle between temperatures 500 and 250 with exact fractions, then compares it with heat passed directly between the same two reservoirs.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as entropy.py.
            2. Run it: python3 entropy.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction as F

            # Clausius's entropy: a reservoir at temperature T that gives or takes heat Q changes its entropy by Q / T.
            def entropy_change(q, temperature):
                return F(q) / F(temperature)

            T_hot = F(500)
            T_cold = F(250)
            Q_in = F(1000)                  # heat taken from the hot reservoir in one cycle
            Q_out = Q_in * T_cold / T_hot   # Carnot cycle: heat rejected to the cold reservoir
            dS_hot = -entropy_change(Q_in, T_hot)
            dS_cold = entropy_change(Q_out, T_cold)
            print(f"heat rejected: {Q_out}")
            print(f"hot reservoir: {dS_hot}")
            print(f"cold reservoir: {dS_cold}")
            print(f"reversible cycle total: {dS_hot + dS_cold}")

            # Heat passed directly from the hot reservoir to the cold one, with no work done.
            direct = -entropy_change(Q_in, T_hot) + entropy_change(Q_in, T_cold)
            print(f"direct conduction total: {direct}")
            print(f"entropy grows: {direct > 0}")
        """,
    ),

        example = """
            from math import gcd

            # Smith's diagonal form of a two by two integer matrix. The first invariant factor is the gcd of the entries,
            # and the product of the two invariant factors is the absolute value of the determinant.
            A = [[2, 4], [6, 9]]
            print("start: " + str(A))
            (a, b), (c, d) = A
            det = a * d - b * c
            d1 = gcd(gcd(a, b), gcd(c, d))
            d2 = abs(det) // d1
            print(f"first invariant factor: {d1}")
            print(f"second invariant factor: {d2}")
            print(f"first divides second: {d2 % d1 == 0}")

        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Gear design",
        title = "How the Stern-Brocot tree finds a simple gear ratio",
        originalTitle = "Calcul des rouages par approximation, nouvelle methode (1861)",
        author = "Achille Brocot",
        year = 1861,
        summary = "Walking down the Stern-Brocot tree gives the simplest fraction near a target ratio, which a clockmaker can turn into a pair of gear wheels with whole numbers of teeth.",
        details = "Brocot published his gear-train method in the Revue chronometrique in 1861, pages 186 to 194, while a book with the same title is catalogued under 1862, so accounts differ on the date. Stern had described the same tree in 1858, and Brocot arrived at it independently, so the two are credited separately. The example walks the tree toward the golden ratio and stops when the next fraction needs a denominator above ten.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as brocot.py.
            2. Run it: python3 brocot.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction as F

            # Stern-Brocot walk toward a target ratio. Each step makes the mediant of the two bounds,
            # and the walk stops when the mediant needs a denominator above the limit.
            target = 0.6180339887   # about (sqrt 5 - 1) / 2
            limit = 10
            left = (0, 1)           # 0/1
            right = (1, 0)          # 1/0 stands for infinity
            while True:
                n = left[0] + right[0]
                d = left[1] + right[1]
                if d > limit:
                    print(f"next mediant {n}/{d} has denominator {d} above {limit}")
                    break
                m = F(n, d)
                if m < target:
                    left = (n, d)
                    print(f"{m} is below the target, left bound becomes {m}")
                else:
                    right = (n, d)
                    print(f"{m} is above the target, right bound becomes {m}")
            low = F(*left)
            high = F(*right)
            print(f"distance from {low}: {abs(low - target):.4f}")
            print(f"distance from {high}: {abs(high - target):.4f}")
            best = low if abs(low - target) < abs(high - target) else high
            print(f"best with denominator at most {limit}: {best}")
        """,
    ),

)

        details = "Grassmann's Ausdehnungslehre of 1844 was little read, and the second, reworked edition of 1862 set out the exterior product in the form used later.         instructions = """

            2. Run it: python3 grassmann_wedge.py
        """,
        example = """
            from itertools import combinations

            # Exterior product of two vectors in three dimensions: one component for each pair of basis vectors,
            # given by the two by two minors of the matrix whose rows are the vectors.
            def wedge(a, b):
                return {(i, j): a[i] * b[j] - a[j] * b[i] for i, j in combinations(range(3), 2)}

            a = (1, 2, 0)
            b = (0, 1, 3)
            ab = wedge(a, b)
            ba = wedge(b, a)
            print("a wedge b:", [ab[k] for k in sorted(ab)])
            print("b wedge a:", [ba[k] for k in sorted(ba)])
            print("swapping changes the sign:", all(ab[k] == -ba[k] for k in ab))
            print("a wedge a is zero:", all(v == 0 for v in wedge(a, a).values()))
        """,

        originalTitle = "On a New Geometry of Space (1865)",
        author = "Julius Plucker",
        year = 1865,
        summary = "A line in space is described by a direction and a moment, so that the test for two lines meeting becomes a sum of products of whole numbers.",
        details = "Plucker's 1865 paper introduced these line coordinates, which turn questions about lines in space into arithmetic on six numbers. Two lines meet, or are parallel, exactly when the reciprocal product of their coordinates is zero. The example computes the coordinates of four lines through pairs of points with whole-number coordinates, prints them, and tests which pairs meet.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as plucker.py.
            2. Run it: python3 plucker.py
        """,
        example = """
            # A line through points P and Q has Plucker coordinates (d, m): direction d = Q - P and moment m = P x Q.
            def cross(u, v):
                return (u[1] * v[2] - u[2] * v[1], u[2] * v[0] - u[0] * v[2], u[0] * v[1] - u[1] * v[0])

            def dot(u, v):
                return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))

            def plucker(P, Q):
                d = tuple(q - p for p, q in zip(P, Q))
                return d, cross(P, Q)

            def meet(L1, L2):
                # Two lines meet (or are parallel) when the reciprocal product d1.m2 + d2.m1 is zero.
                (d1, m1), (d2, m2) = L1, L2
                return dot(d1, m2) + dot(d2, m1) == 0

            L1 = plucker((1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0))
            L2 = plucker((0, 0, 1), (1, 1, 1))
            L3 = plucker((0, 0, 0), (1, 2, 3))
            L4 = plucker((0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0))
            print("L1 direction", L1[0], "moment", L1[1])
            print("L2 direction", L2[0], "moment", L2[1])
            print("L1 and L2 meet:", meet(L1, L2))
            print("L1 and L3 meet:", meet(L1, L3))
            print("L1 and L4 meet:", meet(L1, L4))
            print("L2 and L3 meet:", meet(L2, L3))
        """,
    ),

)

            variance = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in data) / n

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 1860 to 1870: a sorting demon, a prime count, a factor table and a test on pair-number systems. */
val db18Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Thermodynamics",
        title = "Maxwell's sorting demon in a small simulation",
        originalTitle = "Letter to P. G. Tait, 11 December 1867",
        author = "James Clerk Maxwell",
        year = 1867,
        summary = "A small being opens a door between two chambers only for fast molecules from the left and slow ones from the right, which warms one side without work, as a thought experiment about the second law.",
        details = "Maxwell described the being in a letter to Peter Guthrie Tait dated 11 December 1867, and the idea was printed later in his Theory of Heat in 1871. The example is a deterministic version with ten molecules and fixed speeds, and it checks that the total speed is unchanged while the right chamber ends faster on average.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as demon.py.
            2. Run it: python3 demon.py
        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction as F

            # Ten molecules as speeds in arbitrary units, five in each chamber.
            left = [3, 8, 1, 9, 4]
            right = [7, 2, 6, 5, 10]
            FAST = 6    # the demon passes a molecule from left to right when it is at least this fast
            SLOW = 4    # and from right to left when it is at most this slow

            def average(speeds):
                return F(sum(speeds), len(speeds))

            print(f"start: left {len(left)} molecules, average speed {average(left)}; right {len(right)} molecules, average speed {average(right)}")
            new_left = [v for v in left if v < FAST] + [v for v in right if v <= SLOW]
            new_right = [v for v in right if v > SLOW] + [v for v in left if v >= FAST]
            print(f"after the demon: left {len(new_left)} molecules, average speed {average(new_left)}; right {len(new_right)} molecules, average speed {average(new_right)}")
            print(f"total speed before {sum(left) + sum(right)}, after {sum(new_left) + sum(new_right)}")
            print("right chamber is faster on average: " + str(average(new_right) > average(new_left)))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Number theory",
        title = "Meissel's count of primes below a large number",
        originalTitle = "Meissel's formula for the prime counting function (1870)",
        author = "Ernst Meissel",
        year = 1870,
        summary = "Meissel rewrote Legendre's count so that the main sum needs only the primes up to the cube root of x, which made counts for large x practical by hand.",
        details = "The formula rearranges Legendre's phi-function count, and Meissel's improvement is dated to 1870. Lehmer later called Meissel's large calculation one of the most impressive of the nineteenth century, though slightly inaccurate. The example checks the formula against a sieve for the counts up to 1000, 10000 and 100000.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as meissel.py.
            2. Run it: python3 meissel.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            LIMIT = 100000

            def prime_flags(n):
                flags = [True] * (n + 1)
                flags[0] = flags[1] = False
                for i in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1):
                    if flags[i]:
                        for j in range(i * i, n + 1, i):
                            flags[j] = False
                return flags

            FLAGS = prime_flags(LIMIT)
            PRIMES = [v for v in range(LIMIT + 1) if FLAGS[v]]
            PI = [0] * (LIMIT + 1)            # PI[v] is the number of primes up to v
            for v in range(1, LIMIT + 1):
                PI[v] = PI[v - 1] + (1 if FLAGS[v] else 0)

            def phi(x, a, memo):
                # Legendre's phi: whole numbers up to x with no prime factor among the first a primes.
                if a == 0:
                    return x
                key = (x, a)
                if key not in memo:
                    memo[key] = phi(x, a - 1, memo) - phi(x // PRIMES[a - 1], a - 1, memo)
                return memo[key]

            def cube_root(x):
                r = round(x ** (1 / 3))
                while r ** 3 > x:
                    r -= 1
                while (r + 1) ** 3 <= x:
                    r += 1
                return r

            def meissel_pi(x):
                b = PI[math.isqrt(x)]          # primes up to the square root of x
                c = PI[cube_root(x)]           # primes up to the cube root of x
                total = phi(x, c, {}) + c - 1 + (b + c - 1) * (b - c) // 2
                for i in range(c + 1, b + 1):  # the primes p_i with c < i <= b
                    total -= PI[x // PRIMES[i - 1]]
                return total

            for x in (1000, 10000, 100000):
                value = meissel_pi(x)
                print(f"pi({x}) by Meissel's formula: {value}, sieve count {PI[x]}, agree: {value == PI[x]}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Factor tables",
        title = "Dase's factor table, the smallest factor of each number",
        originalTitle = "Factoren-Tafeln fuer alle Zahlen der siebenten Million (1862)",
        author = "Zacharias Dase and Hermann Rosenberg",
        year = 1862,
        summary = "A table gives the smallest factor of each number in a long range, found by trial division, so a reader sees at once which numbers are prime.",
        details = "Dase died in Hamburg on 11 September 1861, and the seventh-million volume, which covers 6000001 to 7002000, appeared in 1862 with Rosenberg completing the work. The example runs trial division on the first ten numbers of that range and prints the smallest factor of each.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as dase.py.
            2. Run it: python3 dase.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            def smallest_factor(n):
                # Trial division: the smallest divisor from 2 upward, or n itself when n is prime.
                for d in range(2, math.isqrt(n) + 1):
                    if n % d == 0:
                        return d
                return n

            primes = 0
            for n in range(6000001, 6000011):
                f = smallest_factor(n)
                if f == n:
                    primes += 1
                print(f"{n}: smallest factor {f}")
            print(f"primes in the window: {primes}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 18,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Pair numbers",
        title = "Hankel's permanence test on three pair-number systems",
        originalTitle = "Theorie der complexen Zahlensysteme (1867)",
        author = "Hermann Hankel",
        year = 1867,
        summary = "Hankel asked which laws of ordinary arithmetic survive when a new kind of number is built from pairs, and the program tests three such systems for zero divisors.",
        details = "Hankel's 1867 book asked which formal laws of ordinary arithmetic survive when new kinds of number are built from pairs, and he called this the principle of permanence. The example builds three two-dimensional systems in which the new unit squares to minus one, zero or plus one, and counts the pairs of nonzero numbers whose product is zero. Only the systems whose unit squares to zero or to plus one have such pairs.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as pair_systems.py.
            2. Run it: python3 pair_systems.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Pairs (a, b) stand for a + b e, where e squares to s. The product is
            # (a + b e)(c + d e) = (ac + s bd) + (ad + bc) e.
            def mul(x, y, s):
                a, b = x
                c, d = y
                return (a * c + s * b * d, a * d + b * c)

            # Nonzero pairs with coefficients -1, 0 or 1.
            elements = [(a, b) for a in (-1, 0, 1) for b in (-1, 0, 1) if (a, b) != (0, 0)]
            systems = [("complex numbers, e squared -1", -1), ("dual numbers, e squared 0", 0), ("split-complex numbers, e squared 1", 1)]
            for name, s in systems:
                pairs = [(x, y) for x in elements for y in elements if mul(x, y, s) == (0, 0)]
                print(f"{name}: {len(pairs)} zero-divisor pairs")
                if pairs:
                    x, y = pairs[0]
                    print(f"  first pair: {x} times {y} gives {mul(x, y, s)}")
        """,
    ),

)

val db190Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 190,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Years from the Antonine Wall to Huan's accession, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Years between two dated events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 146,
        summary = "The Antonine Wall was begun in 142 and Huan took the Han throne in 146, and the same program counts the four years between them in Python and in C.",
        details = "Both dates are used as commonly stated, and the two programs print the same line, which the run script confirms by comparing their output. The count is plain arithmetic on fixed years, so the output is the same on every run.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### wall_huan.py
            START = 142   # the Antonine Wall is begun
            END = 146     # Huan takes the Han throne
            print("years from the Antonine Wall to Huan's accession:", END - START)
            ### wall_huan.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const int start = 142;   /* the Antonine Wall is begun */
                const int end = 146;     /* Huan takes the Han throne */
                printf("years from the Antonine Wall to Huan's accession: %d\n", end - start);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 wall_huan.py > python.txt
            cc -o wall_huan_c wall_huan.c
            ./wall_huan_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        year = 148,
        summary = "Breath counting runs from one to ten and then starts again, a practice that early Chinese meditation texts teach, and a short program prints the count for chosen breaths.",
        details = "The text traditionally credited to An Shigao, the Anban shouyi jing, teaches counting the breath, and that attribution is traditional rather than proven. The year 148 is the one accounts give for An Shigao's move to Luoyang, and the text itself carries no firm date.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as breath_count.py.
            2. Run it: python3 breath_count.py
        """,
        example = """
            def count_for(breath):
                # The count runs from one to ten and then starts again at one.
                return (breath - 1) % 10 + 1

            for breath in [9, 10, 11, 20, 21, 30]:
                print("breath", breath, "counts", count_for(breath))
        """,

        details = "The Antonine Wall was begun in 142, Shun of Han died in 144, Huan took the Han throne in 146, and An Shigao reached Luoyang in 148, with accounts differing on that last date. The program sorts the four events and prints the gap before each one, which is two years between each pair.",

                (142, "Antonine Wall begun"),
                (146, "Han emperor Huan takes the throne"),
                (144, "Han emperor Shun dies"),
            ]
            events.sort()

            print("span:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0], "years")
        """,

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 138: the days of Hadrian's reign from his accession to his death, in Python and in C. */
val db191Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 191,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Days from Hadrian's accession to his death, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days between two dated events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 138,
        summary = "Hadrian's reign ran from 11 August 117 to his death on 10 July 138, and a script checks that the Python and C programs count the same 7638 days.",
        details = "The accession is given as 11 August 117, although some accounts give 10 August, which would make the count one day longer, and the death of 10 July 138 at Baiae is widely agreed. The span lies between 117 and 138, where the Julian and Gregorian reckonings have the same leap years, so the day count is the same in both; the run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### hadrian.py
            from datetime import date

            accession = date(117, 8, 11)   # Hadrian's accession, as commonly given
            death = date(138, 7, 10)       # Hadrian's death at Baiae, as commonly given
            print("days from accession to death:", (death - accession).days)
            ### hadrian.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* days since 1 January 1970, proleptic Gregorian calendar */
            static long days_from_civil(long y, unsigned m, unsigned d) {
                y -= m <= 2;
                long era = (y >= 0 ? y : y - 399) / 400;
                unsigned yoe = (unsigned)(y - era * 400);
                unsigned doy = (153 * (m > 2 ? m - 3 : m + 9) + 2) / 5 + d - 1;
                unsigned doe = yoe * 365 + yoe / 4 - yoe / 100 + doy;
                return era * 146097 + (long)doe - 719468;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long accession = days_from_civil(117, 8, 11);
                long death = days_from_civil(138, 7, 10);
                printf("days from accession to death: %ld\n", death - accession);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 hadrian.py > python.txt
            cc -o hadrian_c hadrian.c
            ./hadrian_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

/** Examples of 130: a line written without spaces, as early copies were, cut into the names Antinoos and Antinoopolis. */
val db191Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 191,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Writing",
        title = "A line written without spaces, cut into the names Antinoos and Antinoopolis",
        originalTitle = "Scriptio continua",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 130,
        summary = "Greek and Latin copies were written without spaces between words, and a short program cuts a continuous line back into the names Antinoos and Antinoopolis.",
        details = "Antinoopolis was founded in Egypt in 130 and named for Antinous, so the example is dated by its names, while the practice of writing without spaces is older and is not dated here. The word list of the program is a modern aid, and the cut is exact only for the two names listed.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as cut.py.
            2. Run it: python3 cut.py
        """,
        example = """
            # a line written without spaces, as early copies were
            text = "antinoosantinoopolis"
            WORDS = ["antinoos", "antinoopolis"]
            found = []
            pos = 0
            while pos < len(text):
                best = ""
                for word in WORDS:
                    if text.startswith(word, pos) and len(word) > len(best):
                        best = word
                if best == "":
                    best = text[pos]
                found.append(best)
                pos += len(best)
            print(" ".join(found))
            print("words:", len(found))
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 122: the sods in one metre of an illustrative turf rampart, counted in Python and in C. */
val db192Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 192,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Earthworks",
        title = "Turves in one metre of a turf rampart, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Turf rampart",
        author = "Roman soldiers of the frontier",
        year = 122,
        summary = "The first build of Hadrian's Wall used turf in part, and a short Python program and a short C program count the sods in one metre of an illustrative rampart.",
        details = "The sizes are illustrative, a rampart 3 metres wide and 2 metres high with sods 30 by 20 by 10 centimetres, so one metre of rampart holds 1000 sods. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, and the count checks arithmetic, not any figure from the wall.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### turves.py
            WIDTH_CM = 300    # illustrative width of the rampart
            HEIGHT_CM = 200   # illustrative height
            LENGTH_CM = 100   # one metre of rampart
            SOD = 30 * 20 * 10   # illustrative sod, in cubic centimetres
            volume = WIDTH_CM * HEIGHT_CM * LENGTH_CM
            print("sods in one metre:", volume // SOD)
            print("rampart volume in cubic cm:", volume)
            ### turves.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int width = 300, height = 200, length = 100;   /* illustrative rampart, in cm */
                int sod = 30 * 20 * 10;                        /* illustrative sod, in cubic cm */
                int volume = width * height * length;
                printf("sods in one metre: %d\n", volume / sod);
                printf("rampart volume in cubic cm: %d\n", volume);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 turves.py > python.txt
            cc -o turves_c turves.c
            ./turves_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

        databaseId = 192,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Deaths",
        title = "Three deaths of 121 to 130 in China and Egypt, sorted and spaced in code",
        originalTitle = "Three deaths of 121 to 130 in China and Egypt, sorted and spaced in code",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 121,
        summary = "Three deaths of 121 to 130 are sorted by year, and a short program prints the gaps between them and the span of the three.",
        details = "Empress Dowager Deng Sui died in April 121, Emperor An of Han died in 125, and Antinous drowned in the Nile in October 130. The years are the ones the accounts give, and the example prints the sorted list and the gaps, so the span of 9 years can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as deaths.py.
            2. Run it: python3 deaths.py
        """,
        example = """
            deaths = [
                ("Antinous drowned in the Nile", 130),
                ("Empress Dowager Deng Sui died", 121),
                ("Emperor An of Han died", 125),
            ]
            ordered = sorted(deaths, key=lambda item: item[1])
            for name, year in ordered:
                print(year, name)
            for earlier, later in zip(ordered, ordered[1:]):
                print("gap from", earlier[1], "to", later[1], "is", later[1] - earlier[1], "years")
            print("span in years:", ordered[-1][1] - ordered[0][1])
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db193Cross.kt
################################################################################
package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 110 to 120: the days from the death of Trajan to the accession of Hadrian, in Python and C. */
val db193Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 193,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Days from the death of Trajan to the accession of Hadrian, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Julian day numbers",
        author = "Roman chroniclers",
        year = 117,
        summary = "Trajan died on 8 August 117 and Hadrian was acclaimed on 11 August 117, and a Python and a C program count the three days between them with one day-number formula.",
        details = "Both dates are given as commonly stated, and both programs use the same integer formula for the day number in the Julian calendar, so the count of 3 is the same in each. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, and the example tests the arithmetic rather than the succession itself.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### day.py
            def day_number(year, month, day):
                # Julian day number, using the usual integer formula for the Julian calendar
                a = (14 - month) // 12
                y = year + 4800 - a
                m = month + 12 * a - 3
                return day + (153 * m + 2) // 5 + 365 * y + y // 4 - 32083

            trajan = day_number(117, 8, 8)
            hadrian = day_number(117, 8, 11)
            print("day number of the death of Trajan:", trajan)
            print("day number of the accession of Hadrian:", hadrian)
            print("days from Trajan's death to Hadrian's accession:", hadrian - trajan)
            ### day.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static long day_number(long year, long month, long day) {
                long a = (14 - month) / 12;
                long y = year + 4800 - a;
                long m = month + 12 * a - 3;
                return day + (153 * m + 2) / 5 + 365 * y + y / 4 - 32083;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long trajan = day_number(117, 8, 8);
                long hadrian = day_number(117, 8, 11);
                printf("day number of the death of Trajan: %ld\n", trajan);
                printf("day number of the accession of Hadrian: %ld\n", hadrian);
                printf("days from Trajan's death to Hadrian's accession: %ld\n", hadrian - trajan);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 day.py > python.txt
            cc -o day_c day.c
            ./day_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        title = "Armenia, Antioch, Ctesiphon and the Yongning era: four dates of 114 to 120 in order",
        originalTitle = "Dated events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 120,
        summary = "Four dated events of 114 to 120, the annexation of Armenia, an earthquake at Antioch, the capture of Ctesiphon and the start of the Yongning era, are put in order and spaced by a short program.",
        details = "Trajan annexed Armenia in 114, an earthquake struck Antioch in 115, Trajan took Ctesiphon in 116, and the Han Yongning era began in 120, each date as commonly given. The program prints the events in order with the gap in years after each one, so the output is the same on every run.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as events.py.
            2. Run it: python3 events.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (120, "Yongning era begins in Han China"),
                (114, "Trajan annexes Armenia"),
                (116, "Trajan takes Ctesiphon"),
                (115, "earthquake at Antioch"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            for index, (year, label) in enumerate(events):
                gap = "" if index == 0 else f" (+{year - events[index - 1][0]} years)"
                print(year, label + gap)
            print("events:", len(events), "span:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0], "years")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 100: the days from Pliny's Panegyricus to Trajan's death, counted in Python and in C. */
val db194Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 194,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Days",
        title = "Days from Pliny's Panegyricus to Trajan's death, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Panegyricus",
        author = "Pliny the Younger and Trajan",
        year = 100,
        summary = "Pliny's Panegyricus was delivered on 1 September 100 and Trajan died on 8 August 117, and a script checks that the Python and C programs count the same days.",
        details = "Both dates are given as commonly stated and are read here as Julian dates. The first date falls after the leap day of 100, so the Python count and the C count with the Julian leap rule agree for this span, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### pliny_trajan.py
            from datetime import date

            panegyricus = date(100, 9, 1)     # Pliny's Panegyricus, as commonly given
            trajan_death = date(117, 8, 8)    # Trajan's death, as commonly given
            print("days from Pliny's Panegyricus to Trajan's death:", (trajan_death - panegyricus).days)
            ### pliny_trajan.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static int is_leap(int year) {
                return year % 4 == 0;   /* Julian leap rule */
            }

            static long ordinal(int year, int month, int day) {
                static const int month_days[] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};
                long days = 0;
                for (int y = 1; y < year; y++) {
                    days += is_leap(y) ? 366 : 365;
                }
                for (int m = 1; m < month; m++) {
                    days += month_days[m - 1];
                    if (m == 2 && is_leap(year)) {
                        days += 1;
                    }
                }
                return days + day;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long start = ordinal(100, 9, 1);
                long end = ordinal(117, 8, 8);
                printf("days from Pliny's Panegyricus to Trajan's death: %ld\n", end - start);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 pliny_trajan.py > python.txt
            cc -o pliny_trajan_c pliny_trajan.c
            ./pliny_trajan_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db195Cross.kt

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 96 to 98: the days from Domitian's assassination to Nerva's death, counted in Python and in C. */
val db195Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 195,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Time",
        title = "Days from Domitian's murder to Nerva's death, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days between two imperial dates",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 98,
        summary = "The days from Domitian's murder on 18 September 96 to Nerva's death on 27 January 98 are counted in Python and in C, and a run script checks that both print the same count.",
        details = "Most references give the two dates used here, but one passage gives 19 September 96 for Nerva's proclamation and another gives 25 January 98 for Nerva's death, and a different reading changes the count. The span contains no leap day, because the leap day of 96 falls before the murder and 97 and 98 are not leap years, so the count is 496 days. The Python program uses the standard date library and the C program a Julian day count, and both print 496.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### days.py
            from datetime import date

            start = date(1996, 9, 18)   # Domitian's murder, as most references give it
            end = date(1998, 1, 27)     # Nerva's death, as most references give it
            print("days from Domitian's murder to Nerva's death:", (end - start).days)
            ### days.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* days since 1 January of year 1 in the Julian calendar, with a leap year every fourth year */
            static long days_from(int year, int month, int day) {
                static const int before[] = {0, 31, 59, 90, 120, 151, 181, 212, 243, 273, 304, 334};
                long days = 365L * (year - 1) + (year - 1) / 4;
                days += before[month - 1] + day - 1;
                if (month > 2 && year % 4 == 0) {
                    days += 1;
                }
                return days;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long span = days_from(1998, 1, 27) - days_from(1996, 9, 18);
                printf("days from Domitian's murder to Nerva's death: %ld\n", span);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 days.py > python.txt
            cc -o days_c days.c
            ./days_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Dating",
        title = "How an AD year becomes a year counted from the founding of Rome, with 96 as the worked case",
        originalTitle = "Ab urbe condita",

        year = 96,
        summary = "An AD year becomes a Roman year counted from the founding of the city by adding 753, and a short program converts four years of the decade.",
        details = "The method is the Roman count from the founding of the city, in the chronology that Varro used to place the founding in 753 BC, and other Roman writers gave other founding years, so the count depends on the chronology chosen. The year 96 is used as the worked case because it is the year of Domitian's assassination in most references, and the example also prints the founding year itself.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as ab_urbe_condita.py.
            2. Run it: python3 ab_urbe_condita.py
        """,
        example = """
            def auc_year(ad_year):
                # AD 1 is AUC 754, so an AD year is converted by adding 753.
                return ad_year + 753

            for year in [90, 96, 98, 100]:
                print(f"AD {year} is AUC {auc_year(year)}")
            print("753 BC is AUC", 754 - 753)
        """,
    ),

        originalTitle = "Four dated events, sorted",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 98,
        summary = "The death of Ban Gu, the assassination of Domitian, the mission of Gan Ying and the death of Nerva are sorted and spaced by a short program.",
        details = "The program works in whole years, so the gaps it prints do not depend on the calendar. Domitian's assassination is dated 18 September 96 in most references and Nerva's death 27 January 98, and the death of Ban Gu in prison, in 92, comes from the Han history as usually given.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as han_rome_events.py.
            2. Run it: python3 han_rome_events.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (98, "Nerva dies"),
                (92, "Ban Gu dies in prison"),
                (97, "Gan Ying sent toward Daqin"),
                (96, "Domitian is assassinated"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            for index, (year, label) in enumerate(events):
                if index + 1 < len(events):
                    gap = events[index + 1][0] - year
                    print(year, label, "gap to next:", gap)
                else:
                    print(year, label)
            print("span in years:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 81: the days from the death of Titus to the death of Domitian, counted in Python and in C. */
val db196Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 196,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Days",
        title = "Days from the death of Titus to the death of Domitian, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days between two deaths",
        author = "Titus and Domitian",
        year = 81,
        summary = "Titus died on 13 September 81 and Domitian was killed on 18 September 96, and a Python and a C program count the days between the two dates and check that they agree.",
        details = "Accounts differ by a day on the death of Titus, and the count uses 13 September. The span crosses the leap days of 84, 88, 92 and 96, and the count is the same in the Julian and Gregorian reckonings because no century year falls inside it.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### titus_domitian.py
            from datetime import date

            titus = date(81, 9, 13)        # death of Titus, 13 September 81, as usually given
            domitian = date(96, 9, 18)     # death of Domitian, 18 September 96
            print("days from the death of Titus to the death of Domitian:", (domitian - titus).days)
            ### titus_domitian.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* days from a fixed origin for a date in the proleptic Gregorian calendar (Hinnant's method) */
            static long days_from_civil(long y, long m, long d) {
                y -= m <= 2;
                long era = (y >= 0 ? y : y - 399) / 400;
                long yoe = y - era * 400;
                long doy = (153 * (m > 2 ? m - 3 : m + 9) + 2) / 5 + d - 1;
                long doe = yoe * 365 + yoe / 4 - yoe / 100 + doy;
                return era * 146097 + doe - 719468;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long titus = days_from_civil(81, 9, 13);      /* death of Titus, 13 September 81 */
                long domitian = days_from_civil(96, 9, 18);   /* death of Domitian, 18 September 96 */
                printf("days from the death of Titus to the death of Domitian: %ld\n", domitian - titus);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 titus_domitian.py > python.txt
            cc -o titus_c titus_domitian.c
            ./titus_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        """,

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 79: the two dates given for the eruption of Vesuvius, and the days between them, in Python and in C. */
val db197Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 197,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Eruption",
        title = "The two dates given for the eruption of 79, the days between them in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Ante diem nonum Kalendas Septembres",
        author = "Pliny the Younger and the excavators of Pompeii",
        year = 79,
        summary = "Pliny the Younger dates the eruption to 24 August, a charcoal inscription from Pompeii reads XVI K NOV for 17 October, and a script counts the 54 days between the two dates in Python and C.",
        details = "The inscription was found in 2018 in the Casa del Giardino in Regio V, and it gives no year, so its link to 79 rests on the context; accounts differ on whether the eruption fell in August or in the autumn. Both dates fall in 79, which is not a leap year in either calendar, so the day counts agree whichever reckoning is used.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### days.py
            MONTH_DAYS = [31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]   # 79 is not a leap year

            def day_of_year(month, day):
                return sum(MONTH_DAYS[:month - 1]) + day

            traditional = day_of_year(8, 24)   # 24 August, from Pliny the Younger
            graffito = day_of_year(10, 17)     # 17 October, from the Pompeii inscription
            print("days between the two dates:", graffito - traditional)
            ### days.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static const int month_days[12] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};

            static int day_of_year(int month, int day) {
                int total = day;
                for (int m = 0; m < month - 1; m++) {
                    total += month_days[m];
                }
                return total;
            }

            int main(void) {
                int traditional = day_of_year(8, 24);
                int graffito = day_of_year(10, 17);
                printf("days between the two dates: %d\n", graffito - traditional);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 days.py > python.txt
            cc -o days_c days.c
            ./days_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One example of 70 to 80: the eleven years of the decade written in Roman numerals, counted letter by letter in code. */
val db197Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 197,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Numerals",
        title = "The Roman numerals of the years 70 to 80, counted letter by letter",
        originalTitle = "Numeri Romani",
        author = "Roman scribes",
        year = 79,
        summary = "Written in Roman numerals, the eleven years from 70 to 80 take 54 letters in all, and a short program converts each year and counts its letters.",
        details = "The program uses the standard subtractive rule with the letters I, V, X, L, C, D and M, so the year of the eruption, 79, is written LXXIX with five letters. The decade total is fixed, so it can be checked by hand.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as numerals.py.
            2. Run it: python3 numerals.py
        """,
        example = """
            PAIRS = [(1000, "M"), (900, "CM"), (500, "D"), (400, "CD"), (100, "C"), (90, "XC"),
                     (50, "L"), (40, "XL"), (10, "X"), (9, "IX"), (5, "V"), (4, "IV"), (1, "I")]

            def roman(number):
                text = ""
                for value, letters in PAIRS:
                    while number >= value:
                        text += letters
                        number -= value
                return text

            total = 0
            for year in range(70, 81):
                numeral = roman(year)
                total += len(numeral)
                print(year, numeral, len(numeral))
            print("letters in all:", total)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One guide of 70 to 80: how the twenty-four priestly courses of the Temple rotated through the weeks of the year, placed at the year the Temple fell. */
val db197Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 197,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Temple",
        title = "How the twenty-four priestly courses rotate through the weeks of the Temple year",
        originalTitle = "Mishmarot",
        author = "Priests of the Jerusalem Temple",
        year = 70,
        summary = "The twenty-four priestly courses served the Temple in turn, and a short program shows which course serves each week and how often each course returns in a year of fifty-two weeks.",
        details = "First Chronicles lists twenty-four divisions of priests, and the courses served the Temple in turn, each for a week, until the Temple fell in 70. The example takes a year of exactly fifty-two weeks as an illustration, and it shows that the rota returns to the first course after every twenty-four weeks, so four courses serve three times in such a year and twenty serve twice.",
        rare = true,
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as courses.py.
            2. Run it: python3 courses.py
        """,
        example = """
            COURSES = 24
            WEEKS = 52   # illustrative: a year of exactly 52 weeks

            def course_for_week(week):
                return (week - 1) % COURSES + 1

            for week in [1, 24, 25, 52]:
                print("week", week, "course", course_for_week(week))

            served = {}
            for week in range(1, WEEKS + 1):
                course = course_for_week(week)
                served[course] = served.get(course, 0) + 1
            print("courses served three times:", sum(1 for n in served.values() if n == 3))
            print("courses served twice:", sum(1 for n in served.values() if n == 2))
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** One project of 70 to 80: four dated events of the decade, put in order and spaced by a short program. */
val db197Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 197,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Timeline",
        title = "Four dated events from 70 to 79 in order, with the years between them",
        originalTitle = "Timeline of four events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 70,
        summary = "Four dated events of the decade, from the burning of the Temple to the eruption of Vesuvius, are sorted and spaced by a short program that counts the years between them.",
        details = "The census is dated 73 to 74 and the program uses 74, the Natural History is taken as finished in 77 and the eruption as 79, so the gaps count years and not days. The year 70 for the Temple is the start of the timeline, and the program prints the gap from each event to the one before it.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as timeline.py.
            2. Run it: python3 timeline.py
        """,
        example = """
            events = [
                (79, "eruption of Vesuvius"),
                (70, "Temple at Jerusalem burned"),
                (77, "Pliny's Natural History finished"),
                (74, "census of Vespasian and Titus"),
            ]
            events.sort()
            previous = None
            for year, name in events:
                gap = "" if previous is None else f" (+{year - previous})"
                print(year, name + gap)
                previous = year
            print("span in years:", events[-1][0] - events[0][0])
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 69: the days from the death of Galba to the death of Vitellius, in Python and C. */
val db198Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 198,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Emperors",
        title = "Days from Galba's death to Vitellius's death, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days between two deaths",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 69,
        summary = "The days from the death of Galba on 15 January 69 to the death of Vitellius on 20 December 69 are counted in Python and in C, and a script checks that both print the same count.",
        details = "The dates are the commonly given ones in the Roman reckoning, and both fall in 69, which is not a leap year, so the count is the same in the Julian and the Gregorian reckoning. The run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as galba.py, galba.c and run.sh in one folder.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### galba.py
            from datetime import date

            galba = date(69, 1, 15)        # Galba's death, as commonly given
            vitellius = date(69, 12, 20)   # Vitellius's death, as commonly given
            print("days from Galba's death to Vitellius's death:", (vitellius - galba).days)
            ### galba.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static int day_of_year(int year, int month, int day) {
                static const int lengths[] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};
                int leap = (year % 4 == 0);
                int total = day;
                for (int m = 0; m < month - 1; m++) {
                    total += lengths[m];
                    if (m == 1 && leap) total += 1;
                }
                return total;
            }

            int main(void) {
                int galba = day_of_year(69, 1, 15);       /* Galba's death, as commonly given */
                int vitellius = day_of_year(69, 12, 20);  /* Vitellius's death, as commonly given */
                printf("days from Galba's death to Vitellius's death: %d\n", vitellius - galba);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 galba.py > python.txt
            cc -o galba_c galba.c
            ./galba_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 198,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Surveying",
        title = "How a far tower's breadth is found from the width of a sight-rod",
        originalTitle = "Sight-rod method",
        author = "Surveyors of the Greek and Roman world",
        year = 62,
        summary = "A rod of known width, held at a known distance from the eye and seen against a tower of known breadth, gives the distance to the tower, and a short program works one such sum.",
        details = "Hero's book describes the dioptra's use in surveying, but this rod method is a textbook sum of the kind the instrument made possible, not a worked example from that book.         instructions = """
            1. Save the example as sight_rod.py.

        """,
        example = """
            tower_breadth = 60   # feet, illustrative breadth of the tower
            rod_width = 1        # feet, width of the sight-rod
            rod_distance = 4     # feet from the eye to the sight-rod

            print("distance to the tower in feet:", distance)
            print("distance in paces of 5 feet:", distance // 5)
        """,
        rare = true,

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code records of 55: the days from the death of Claudius to the death of Britannicus, in Python and C. */
val db199Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 199,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Days from the death of Claudius to the death of Britannicus, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days between two fixed dates",
        author = "Suetonius and Tacitus, for the two deaths",
        year = 55,
        summary = "The death of Claudius on 13 October 54 and the death of Britannicus in February 55 are a few months apart, and a script prints the days between them in Python and C.",
        details = "Accounts differ on the day of Britannicus's death, which falls between 11 and 12 February 55, so the programs print the days to both dates. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, and the counts 121 and 122 can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### days.py
            from datetime import date

            claudius = date(54, 10, 13)       # the death of Claudius, 13 October 54
            britannicus_a = date(55, 2, 11)   # one account of the death of Britannicus
            britannicus_b = date(55, 2, 12)   # the other account
            print("days to 11 February 55:", (britannicus_a - claudius).days)
            print("days to 12 February 55:", (britannicus_b - claudius).days)
            ### days.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* Julian calendar day count from a fixed origin; years 54 and 55 have the same leap years in both calendars. */
            static int is_leap(int y) { return y % 4 == 0; }

            static long day_number(int y, int m, int d) {
                static const int month_days[] = {31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};
                long n = 365L * (y - 1) + (y - 1) / 4;   /* Julian leap years before year y */
                for (int i = 0; i < m - 1; i++) {
                    n += month_days[i];
                    if (i == 1 && is_leap(y)) n += 1;
                }
                return n + d;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long claudius = day_number(54, 10, 13);
                long britannicus_a = day_number(55, 2, 11);
                long britannicus_b = day_number(55, 2, 12);
                printf("days to 11 February 55: %ld\n", britannicus_a - claudius);
                printf("days to 12 February 55: %ld\n", britannicus_b - claudius);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 days.py > python.txt
            cc -o days_c days.c
            ./days_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 199,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Calendar",
        title = "How Roman inclusive counting names the days of October, with 13 October 54",
        originalTitle = "Ante diem counting",
        author = "Roman pontiffs and clerks of the calendar",
        year = 54,
        summary = "Roman dates were counted back from the Kalends, Nones and Ides with the anchor day counted as one, and a short program names five days of October 54 in that way.",
        details = "In October the Nones fall on the 7th and the Ides on the 15th, so 13 October is written as the third day counted back from the Ides, a.d. III Id. Oct. The example names five days of the month, and 13 October 54 is the day that Claudius died, as the sources give it.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as ante_diem.py.
            2. Run it: python3 ante_diem.py
        """,
        example = """
            ROMAN = {1: "I", 2: "II", 3: "III", 4: "IV", 5: "V", 6: "VI", 7: "VII", 8: "VIII"}

            def name_day(day):
                # October: Kalends 1, Nones 7, Ides 15; the anchor day counts as one
                if day == 1:
                    return "Kal. Oct."
                if day == 7:
                    return "Non. Oct."
                if day == 15:
                    return "Id. Oct."
                if day == 14:
                    return "pridie Id. Oct."
                if day < 7:
                    return "a.d. " + ROMAN[8 - day] + " Non. Oct."
                return "a.d. " + ROMAN[16 - day] + " Id. Oct."

            for day in [1, 7, 13, 14, 15]:
                print(f"{day} October 54: {name_day(day)}")
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db19Cross.kt
################################################################################
package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1850 to 1860: the eight queens count and a digraph cipher, each in Python and C. */
val db19Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 19,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Backtracking",
        title = "Eight queens counted by backtracking, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Solutions of the eight queens problem (1850)",
        author = "Franz Nauck",
        year = 1850,
        summary = "Backtracking places eight queens row by row, and the search finds the 92 placements of the classic puzzle in both Python and C.",
        details = "Max Bezzel posed the problem in 1848, and Nauck published solutions in 1850, reporting the total of 92. Gauss also took up the question in 1850, but his tallies of 72 and 76 fell short of 92, and Nauck's count is the one usually credited.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### queens.py
            def solve(n):
                solutions = []
                queens = []

                def safe(col):
                    row = len(queens)
                    for r, c in enumerate(queens):
                        if c == col or abs(c - col) == row - r:
                            return False
                    return True

                def place():
                    if len(queens) == n:
                        solutions.append(tuple(c + 1 for c in queens))
                        return
                    for col in range(n):
                        if safe(col):
                            queens.append(col)
                            place()
                            queens.pop()

                place()
                return solutions

            found = solve(8)
            print("solutions:", len(found))
            print("first solution:", " ".join(str(c) for c in found[0]))
            ### queens.c
            #include <stdio.h>
            #include <stdlib.h>

            #define N 8

            static int cols[N];
            static long count = 0;
            static int first[N];
            static int have_first = 0;

            static int safe(int row, int col) {
                for (int r = 0; r < row; r++) {
                    int c = cols[r];
                    if (c == col || abs(c - col) == row - r) {
                        return 0;
                    }
                }
                return 1;
            }

            static void place(int row) {
                if (row == N) {
                    if (!have_first) {
                        for (int r = 0; r < N; r++) {
                            first[r] = cols[r] + 1;
                        }
                        have_first = 1;
                    }
                    count++;
                    return;
                }
                for (int col = 0; col < N; col++) {
                    if (safe(row, col)) {
                        cols[row] = col;
                        place(row + 1);
                    }
                }
            }

            int main(void) {
                place(0);
                printf("solutions: %ld\n", count);
                printf("first solution:");
                for (int r = 0; r < N; r++) {
                    printf(" %d", first[r]);
                }
                printf("\n");
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 queens.py > python.txt
            cc -o queens_c queens.c
            ./queens_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 19,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Ciphers",
        title = "Playfair digraph cipher with the MONARCHY key, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Cipher of Wheatstone, popularised by Playfair (1854)",
        author = "Charles Wheatstone, promoted by Lyon Playfair",
        year = 1854,
        summary = "Playfair's digraph cipher encrypts pairs of letters with a 5 by 5 key square, and the example turns HELLO into CFSUPM in Python and C.",
        details = "Wheatstone devised the cipher in 1854, and Lyon Playfair promoted it, which gave it the name. The example uses the MONARCHY key square, inserts an X between doubled letters, and decrypts the result to HELXLO.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### playfair.py
            ALPHABET = "ABCDEFGHIKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"   # J is merged into I

            def key_square(key):
                letters = []
                for ch in (key.upper() + ALPHABET).replace("J", "I"):
                    if ch in ALPHABET and ch not in letters:
                        letters.append(ch)
                return letters

            def digraphs(text):
                clean = [c for c in text.upper().replace("J", "I") if c.isalpha()]
                pairs = []
                i = 0
                while i < len(clean):
                    a = clean[i]
                    b = clean[i + 1] if i + 1 < len(clean) else "X"
                    if a == b:
                        pairs.append((a, "X"))
                        i += 1
                    else:
                        pairs.append((a, b))
                        i += 2
                return pairs

            def transform(square, pairs, step):
                out = []
                for a, b in pairs:
                    ra, ca = divmod(square.index(a), 5)
                    rb, cb = divmod(square.index(b), 5)
                    if ra == rb:
                        out.append(square[ra * 5 + (ca + step) % 5] + square[rb * 5 + (cb + step) % 5])
                    elif ca == cb:
                        out.append(square[((ra + step) % 5) * 5 + ca] + square[((rb + step) % 5) * 5 + cb])
                    else:
                        out.append(square[ra * 5 + cb] + square[rb * 5 + ca])
                return "".join(out)

            square = key_square("MONARCHY")
            cipher = transform(square, digraphs("HELLO"), 1)
            plain = transform(square, [(cipher[i], cipher[i + 1]) for i in range(0, len(cipher), 2)], -1)
            print("encrypted:", cipher)
            print("decrypted:", plain)
            ### playfair.c
            #include <stdio.h>
            #include <string.h>
            #include <ctype.h>

            static const char *ALPHA = "ABCDEFGHIKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

            static int find(const char *square, char ch) {
                for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) {
                    if (square[i] == ch) {
                        return i;
                    }
                }
                return -1;
            }

            static void key_square(const char *key, char *square) {
                int used[26] = {0};
                int n = 0;
                for (int pass = 0; pass < 2; pass++) {
                    const char *src = (pass == 0) ? key : ALPHA;
                    for (size_t i = 0; i < strlen(src); i++) {
                        char ch = (char)toupper((unsigned char)src[i]);
                        if (ch == 'J') {
                            ch = 'I';
                        }
                        if (ch >= 'A' && ch <= 'Z' && !used[ch - 'A']) {
                            used[ch - 'A'] = 1;
                            square[n++] = ch;
                        }
                    }
                }
            }

            static void prepare(const char *text, char *out) {
                char clean[64];
                size_t n = 0;
                for (size_t i = 0; text[i] != '\0'; i++) {
                    if (isalpha((unsigned char)text[i])) {
                        char ch = (char)toupper((unsigned char)text[i]);
                        if (ch == 'J') {
                            ch = 'I';
                        }
                        clean[n++] = ch;
                    }
                }
                size_t k = 0;
                size_t i = 0;
                while (i < n) {
                    char a = clean[i];
                    char b = (i + 1 < n) ? clean[i + 1] : 'X';
                    out[k++] = a;
                    if (a == b) {
                        out[k++] = 'X';
                        i += 1;
                    } else {
                        out[k++] = b;
                        i += 2;
                    }
                }
                out[k] = '\0';
            }

            static void transform(const char *square, const char *text, int step, char *out) {
                size_t len = strlen(text);
                size_t k = 0;
                for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i += 2) {
                    int p = find(square, text[i]);
                    int q = find(square, text[i + 1]);
                    int ra = p / 5, ca = p % 5, rb = q / 5, cb = q % 5;
                    if (ra == rb) {
                        out[k++] = square[ra * 5 + (ca + step + 5) % 5];
                        out[k++] = square[rb * 5 + (cb + step + 5) % 5];
                    } else if (ca == cb) {
                        out[k++] = square[((ra + step + 5) % 5) * 5 + ca];
                        out[k++] = square[((rb + step + 5) % 5) * 5 + cb];
                    } else {
                        out[k++] = square[ra * 5 + cb];
                        out[k++] = square[rb * 5 + ca];
                    }
                }
                out[k] = '\0';
            }

            int main(void) {
                char square[26];
                char prepared[64];
                char cipher[64];
                char plain[64];
                key_square("MONARCHY", square);
                prepare("HELLO", prepared);
                transform(square, prepared, 1, cipher);
                transform(square, cipher, -1, plain);
                printf("encrypted: %s\n", cipher);
                printf("decrypted: %s\n", plain);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 playfair.py > python.txt
            cc -o playfair_c playfair.c
            ./playfair_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),
)
