/** Examples of 1274: the questions in the four parts of Aquinas's Summa theologiae, counted in code. */
val db77Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 77,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Summa",
        title = "How many questions the four parts of Aquinas's Summa theologiae hold",
        originalTitle = "Summa theologiae",
        author = "Thomas Aquinas, with the Supplement compiled by Reginald of Piperno",
        year = 1274,
        summary = "Aquinas's Summa theologiae has 512 questions in its four parts as the work stands, and 611 with the Supplement added after his death, and a short program adds them up.",
        details = "The third part breaks off at question 90, while the Supplement of 99 questions was drawn from Aquinas's commentary on the Sentences and added after his death. The counts are the ones commonly given for the parts, and the example prints each part so the total can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as summa_questions.py.
            2. Run it: python3 summa_questions.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Questions in each part of the Summa theologiae, as the work stands; the third part breaks off at question 90.
            PARTS = [("Prima pars", 119), ("Prima secundae", 114), ("Secunda secundae", 189), ("Tertia pars", 90)]
            SUPPLEMENT = 99   # questions added after Aquinas's death, drawn from his commentary on the Sentences
            total = 0
            for name, questions in PARTS:
                print(f"{name}: {questions}")
                total += questions
            print("questions in the four parts:", total)
            print("with the Supplement:", total + SUPPLEMENT)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 1274 to 1275: how an English charter's year changes at Lady Day, and how a scholastic article sets out its objections and replies. */
val db77Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 77,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Dating",
        title = "How an English charter's year changes at Lady Day",
        originalTitle = "Lady Day style",
        author = "English clerks and chancery scribes",
        year = 1275,
        summary = "English records of the 1270s often began the year on 25 March, and a short program converts such Lady Day dates into modern reckoning.",
        details = "Under this style, dates from 1 January to 24 March carry the year number one lower than modern reckoning gives them, so a charter dated 10 February 1275 falls in February 1276 by modern reckoning. The example converts five illustrative dates, and each answer can be checked by hand against the rule.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as lady_day.py.
            2. Run it: python3 lady_day.py
        """,
        example = """
            def modern_year(lady_day_year, month, day):
                # Lady Day style: the year number changes on 25 March, so a date from 1 January
                # to 24 March carries a year number one lower than its modern year.
                if month < 3 or (month == 3 and day < 25):
                    return lady_day_year + 1
                return lady_day_year

            dates = [(1275, 2, 10), (1275, 3, 25), (1275, 3, 24), (1275, 12, 31), (1275, 1, 1)]
            for year, month, day in dates:
                modern = modern_year(year, month, day)
                print(f"{year}-{month:02d}-{day:02d} in the Lady Day count is {modern}-{month:02d}-{day:02d} in modern reckoning")
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 77,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Disputation",
        title = "How a scholastic article sets out objections and replies",
        originalTitle = "Articulus",
        author = "Masters of the Paris schools",
        year = 1274,
        summary = "A scholastic article states a question, lists objections, gives a contrary authority and then a reply, and a short program prints an illustrative article in that order.",
        details = "Aquinas's Summa theologiae uses this order throughout, and the opening words of its parts, Videtur quod, Sed contra and Respondeo, mark the stages of the argument. The question in the example is invented for the purpose and is not taken from any text.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as scholastic.py.
            2. Run it: python3 scholastic.py
        """,
        example = """
            # An illustrative question, not taken from any text
            QUESTION = "Whether a teacher may take a fee"
            OBJECTIONS = [
                "A gift of knowledge should be given freely.",
                "Whoever is paid for a thing seems to sell it, and teaching is not for sale.",
            ]
            CONTRARY = "The Apostle says that the labourer is worthy of his hire."
            REPLY = "A teacher may receive support, since teaching is a real labour."
            ANSWERS = [
                "The gift is freely given, but a teacher's living may still be provided for.",
                "A fee for labour is not the same as selling the truth.",
            ]

            print("Question:", QUESTION)
            for number, objection in enumerate(OBJECTIONS, start=1):
                print(f"Objection {number}: {objection}")
            print("On the contrary:", CONTRARY)
            print("I answer that:", REPLY)
            for number, answer in enumerate(ANSWERS, start=1):
                print(f"Reply to objection {number}: {answer}")
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 1271: the empty papal sees of 1268 to 1277, each vacancy counted in days from one pope's death to the next election. */
val db77Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 77,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Papacy",
        title = "How long the papal see stood empty in the 1270s, vacancy by vacancy",
        originalTitle = "Papal vacancies",
        author = "The cardinals of the period",
        year = 1271,
        summary = "The papal see stood empty for long spells between 1268 and 1277, and a short program lists each vacancy in days from a pope's death to the next election.",
        details = "The dates are the ones commonly given in the papal chronologies, and each vacancy is counted from the death of one pope to the election of the next. The longest gap, from the death of Clement IV in 1268 to the election of Gregory X at Viterbo in 1271, ended only after nearly three years without a pope.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as papal_vacancies.py.
            2. Run it: python3 papal_vacancies.py
        """,
        example = """
            from datetime import date

            # Each pope's death and the next election, as commonly given in the papal chronologies
            VACANCIES = [
                ("Clement IV died", date(1268, 11, 29), "Gregory X elected", date(1271, 9, 1)),
                ("Gregory X died", date(1276, 1, 10), "Innocent V elected", date(1276, 2, 21)),
                ("Innocent V died", date(1276, 6, 22), "Adrian V elected", date(1276, 7, 11)),
                ("Adrian V died", date(1276, 8, 18), "John XXI elected", date(1276, 9, 13)),
                ("John XXI died", date(1277, 5, 20), "Nicholas III elected", date(1277, 11, 25)),
            ]

            total = 0
            for died_label, died, elected_label, elected in VACANCIES:
                days = (elected - died).days
                total += days
                print(f"{died_label} {died.isoformat()}, {elected_label} {elected.isoformat()}: {days} days")
            longest = max((elected - died).days for _, died, _, elected in VACANCIES)
            print("longest vacancy:", longest, "days")
            print("total days empty:", total)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1267: the letter counts of the Hebrew, Greek and Arabic alphabets that Roger Bacon wanted Latin scholars to study, in Python and in C. */
val db78Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 78,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Alphabets",
        title = "Letter counts of the Hebrew, Greek and Arabic alphabets in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Three alphabets",
        author = "Roger Bacon",
        year = 1267,
        summary = "Bacon's Opus majus urged the study of Greek, Hebrew and Arabic, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same letter counts for those three alphabets.",
        details = "The counts are the standard ones, 22 for Hebrew, 24 for Greek and 28 for Arabic, and the two programs print them in the same order. The run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### alphabets.py
            ALPHABETS = {"Hebrew": 22, "Greek": 24, "Arabic": 28}
            for name, letters in ALPHABETS.items():
                print(name, letters)
            print("total letters:", sum(ALPHABETS.values()))
            ### alphabets.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const char *names[] = {"Hebrew", "Greek", "Arabic"};
                int letters[] = {22, 24, 28};
                int total = 0;
                for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
                    printf("%s %d\n", names[i], letters[i]);
                    total += letters[i];
                }
                printf("total letters: %d\n", total);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 alphabets.py > python.txt
            cc -o alphabets_c alphabets.c
            ./alphabets_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Examples of 1260 to 1270: the qibla bearing from Maragha, where Hulagu's observatory was in use by 1262, computed from coordinates in code. */
val db78Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 78,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Orientation",
        title = "The qibla bearing from Maragha to Mecca, computed from coordinates",
        originalTitle = "Qibla",
        author = "Islamic astronomers of the period",
        year = 1262,
        summary = "A short program computes the great-circle bearing from Maragha, where Hulagu's observatory was in use by 1262, to Mecca, the direction of prayer, from the coordinates of the two places.",
        details = "Astronomers of the Islamic world worked out the qibla, the direction of Mecca for prayer, with spherical trigonometry from geographic coordinates. The coordinates in the example are approximate, and the bearing is rounded to whole degrees, clockwise from north.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as qibla.py.
            2. Run it: python3 qibla.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            def bearing(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
                # Initial great-circle bearing from point 1 to point 2, in degrees clockwise from north.
                p1, p2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2)
                dl = math.radians(lon2 - lon1)
                y = math.sin(dl) * math.cos(p2)
                x = math.cos(p1) * math.sin(p2) - math.sin(p1) * math.cos(p2) * math.cos(dl)
                return math.degrees(math.atan2(y, x)) % 360

            MECCA = (21.42, 39.83)     # approximate coordinates of Mecca
            MARAGHA = (37.39, 46.24)   # approximate coordinates of Maragha
            print(f"qibla from Maragha: {bearing(MARAGHA[0], MARAGHA[1], MECCA[0], MECCA[1]):.0f} degrees")
        """,
    ),

)

        databaseId = 78,

        author = "Archimedes, in William of Moerbeke's Latin",
        year = 1269,
        summary = "A floating block sinks until it displaces its own weight of water, so the share of its height below the surface equals its density, and a short program prints that share for four blocks.",
        details = "The rule is Archimedes' own, and William of Moerbeke's Latin version of 1269 made it available to medieval readers. The densities in the example are illustrative values with water taken as 1.0, and a block denser than water sinks entirely.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as floating_block.py.
            2. Run it: python3 floating_block.py
        """,
        example = """
            densities = [0.25, 0.6, 0.8, 1.5]   # illustrative densities, with water taken as 1.0
            for density in densities:
                if density < 1.0:
                    print(f"density {density}: {round(density * 100)} percent of the block below water")

                    print(f"density {density}: the block sinks")
        """,

    entry(
        databaseId = 78,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Magnets",
        title = "How Peregrinus marks meridians on a spherical lodestone",

        author = "Peter Peregrinus of Maricourt",
        year = 1269,
        summary = "Peregrinus described a spherical lodestone marked with lines from pole to pole, and a short program prints points on two of those lines at three latitudes.",
        details = "The lines run from one pole to the other like the meridians of a globe, and the example computes their points on a unit sphere so that the output can be checked by hand. Positions are printed to three decimal places, and latitude 0 is the equator.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as meridians.py.
            2. Run it: python3 meridians.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            for longitude in (0, 90):
                for latitude in (0, 30, 60):
                    lat = math.radians(latitude)
                    lon = math.radians(longitude)
                    x = math.cos(lat) * math.cos(lon)
                    y = math.cos(lat) * math.sin(lon)
                    z = math.sin(lat)

        year = 1269,
        summary = "A short program sorts three Latin translations of Greek science by their dates and prints the years between them.",
        details = "Gerard's Almagest is dated to about 1175 and Commandino's Latin Euclid to 1572, both as commonly given, and Moerbeke's Archimedes of 1269 falls between them.                 ("Archimedes, by William of Moerbeke", 1269),

            ]

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1250 and 1251: the character total of the Tripitaka blocks and the Coptic years of the 1250s, each in Python and C. */
val db79Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 79,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Woodblocks",
        title = "The Tripitaka block total in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Block total",
        author = "The carvers of the Tripitaka Koreana",
        year = 1251,
        summary = "The total of 52330152 characters on the Tripitaka Koreana blocks is computed by a Python program and a C program that must print the same result.",
        details = "The example uses the usual count of 81,258 blocks and 644 characters per block, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line. The total is a derived figure, so the example checks the arithmetic in two languages rather than a count of the carved blocks.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### total.py
            BLOCKS = 81258
            PER_BLOCK = 23 * 14 * 2
            print("blocks", BLOCKS)
            print("characters per block", PER_BLOCK)
            print("total characters", BLOCKS * PER_BLOCK)
            ### total.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int blocks = 81258;
                int per_block = 23 * 14 * 2;   /* two sides of 23 lines of 14 characters */
                printf("blocks %d\n", blocks);
                printf("characters per block %d\n", per_block);
                printf("total characters %d\n", blocks * per_block);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 total.py > python.txt
            cc -o total_c total.c
            ./total_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 79,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Calendars",
        title = "The Coptic years of 1250 to 1254 in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Era of Martyrs",
        author = "The Coptic church of Egypt",
        year = 1250,
        summary = "The Coptic years of 1250 to 1254 are computed by a Python program and a C program that subtract 284 from each Christian year and print the same list.",
        details = "The Era of Martyrs begins in 284 of the Christian era, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line. The example checks the arithmetic in two languages and leaves aside the Coptic new year, which falls in September.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### coptic.py
            OFFSET = 284
            for year in range(1250, 1255):
                print(year, "is Coptic year", year - OFFSET)
            ### coptic.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                for (int year = 1250; year <= 1254; year++) {
                    printf("%d is Coptic year %d\n", year, year - 284);   /* the Era of Martyrs begins in 284 of the Christian era */
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 coptic.py > python.txt
            cc -o coptic_c coptic.c
            ./coptic_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

                # the rhyme is the last vowel and everything after it
                for i in range(len(word) - 1, -1, -1):
                    if word[i] in "aeiou":
                        return word[i:]
                return word

            pairs = [("vos", "los"), ("hant", "lant"), ("vos", "hant")]
            for a, b in pairs:
                print(a, b, "rhyme" if rhyme_tail(a) == rhyme_tail(b) else "no rhyme")

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db7Cross.kt
################################################################################
package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1960 to 1970: a C program checked by Python, and a Bloom filter in C driven by awk. */
val db7Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "C and Python",
        title = "C and Python compute the same shortest paths",
        originalTitle = "Floyd–Warshall shortest paths (1962)",
        author = "Robert Floyd and Stephen Warshall, with a C program and a Python driver",
        year = 1962,
        summary = "A C program runs the Floyd–Warshall method for all shortest paths, and a Python script feeds it a graph, runs the same method itself and compares the answers.",
        details = "Floyd and Warshall published the method in 1962. The two implementations share nothing but the idea, so agreement is a useful check. Python passes the matrix to the C program through standard input and reads the answer back.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Compile the C program: cc -o fw fw.c
            3. Run the comparison: python3 compare.py
        """,
        example = """
            ### fw.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            #define N 4
            #define INF 1000000

            /* Reads an N x N matrix of edge weights from stdin and prints all shortest distances. */
            int main(void) {
                int d[N][N];
                for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
                    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
                        if (scanf("%d", &d[i][j]) != 1) {
                            return 1;
                        }
                    }
                }
                for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
                    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
                        for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
                            if (d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]) {
                                d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j];
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
                for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
                    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
                        printf("%d ", d[i][j]);
                    }
                    printf("\n");
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### compare.py
            import subprocess

            INF = 1000000
            graph = [
                [0, 3, INF, 7],
                [8, 0, 2, INF],
                [5, INF, 0, 1],
                [2, INF, INF, 0],
            ]

            def floyd_warshall(d):
                n = len(d)
                d = [row[:] for row in d]
                for k in range(n):
                    for i in range(n):
                        for j in range(n):
                            if d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]:
                                d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j]
                return d

            text = "\n".join(" ".join(str(x) for x in row) for row in graph) + "\n"
            result = subprocess.run(["./fw"], input=text, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
            c_rows = [list(map(int, line.split())) for line in result.stdout.strip().split("\n")]
            py_rows = floyd_warshall(graph)
            print("C result:", c_rows)
            print("same:", c_rows == py_rows)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "awk and C",
        title = "awk and C: a Bloom filter for word lists",
        originalTitle = "Space/time trade-offs in hash coding with allowable errors (Bloom, 1970)",
        author = "Burton Bloom; the awk pipeline is written for this database",
        year = 1970,
        summary = "A Bloom filter written in C answers maybe or no for each word, and awk counts the answers. A filter can say maybe for a word that is not in the set, but it never says no for one that is.",
        details = "Burton Bloom described the filter in 1970. It trades a small chance of false positives for much less memory than a full table of words. The shell script builds two small word lists, runs the C program and lets awk count the answers.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
            3. The output shows how many probes said maybe and how many said no.
        """,
        example = """
            ### bloom.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            #define BITS 4096
            static unsigned char filter[BITS / 8];

            static unsigned long hash(const char *s, unsigned long seed) {
                unsigned long h = seed;
                while (*s) {
                    h = h * 31 + (unsigned char)*s++;
                }
                return h % BITS;
            }

            static void set_bit(unsigned long i) {
                filter[i / 8] |= (unsigned char)(1u << (i % 8));
            }

            static int get_bit(unsigned long i) {
                return (filter[i / 8] >> (i % 8)) & 1;
            }

            int main(int argc, char **argv) {
                char word[256];
                if (argc != 3) {
                    return 1;
                }
                FILE *members = fopen(argv[1], "r");
                FILE *probes = fopen(argv[2], "r");
                if (members == NULL || probes == NULL) {
                    return 1;
                }
                while (fscanf(members, "%255s", word) == 1) {
                    set_bit(hash(word, 7));
                    set_bit(hash(word, 1000003));
                }
                while (fscanf(probes, "%255s", word) == 1) {
                    int maybe = get_bit(hash(word, 7)) && get_bit(hash(word, 1000003));
                    printf("%s %s\n", maybe ? "maybe" : "no", word);
                }
                fclose(members);
                fclose(probes);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            printf 'apple\nbanana\ncherry\n' > members.txt
            printf 'apple\ngrape\nlemon\ncherry\nmango\nkiwi\n' > probes.txt
            cc -o bloom bloom.c
            ./bloom members.txt probes.txt | awk '{ count[$1]++ } END { for (word in count) print word, count[word] }' | sort
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),
)

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Sorting",
        title = "Quicksort by partitioning",
        originalTitle = "Hoare's quicksort (1961)",
        author = "Tony Hoare; this version keeps the idea and not the in-place partition",
        year = 1961,
        summary = "Hoare's sort: pick a pivot, split the items into those below it, equal to it and above it, and sort the two outer parts in the same way.",
        details = "Hoare published quicksort in 1961, and it is still one of the fastest general-purpose sorts on average. This short version builds new lists rather than swapping items in place, which uses more memory but is easier to read.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as quicksort.py.
            2. Run it: python3 quicksort.py
        """,
        example = """
            def quicksort(items):
                if len(items) <= 1:
                    return items
                pivot = items[len(items) // 2]
                smaller = [x for x in items if x < pivot]
                equal = [x for x in items if x == pivot]
                larger = [x for x in items if x > pivot]
                return quicksort(smaller) + equal + quicksort(larger)

            print(quicksort([31, 4, 15, 9, 26, 5, 58, 9]))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Sorting",
        title = "Heapsort in place",
        originalTitle = "Heapsort (Williams, 1964)",
        author = "J. W. J. Williams",
        year = 1964,
        summary = "A sort that first arranges the items into a heap, then repeatedly takes the largest item off the top and puts it at the end.",
        details = "Williams published heapsort in 1964. It sorts in place with no extra lists, and it takes about n log n steps even in the worst case, which quicksort does not guarantee. The example prints the sorted list.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as heapsort.py.
            2. Run it: python3 heapsort.py
        """,
        example = """
            def heapsort(items):
                a = list(items)
                n = len(a)

                def sift_down(start, end):
                    root = start
                    while True:
                        child = 2 * root + 1
                        if child > end:
                            break
                        if child + 1 <= end and a[child] < a[child + 1]:
                            child += 1
                        if a[root] < a[child]:
                            a[root], a[child] = a[child], a[root]
                            root = child
                        else:
                            break

                for start in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
                    sift_down(start, n - 1)
                for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
                    a[0], a[end] = a[end], a[0]
                    sift_down(0, end - 1)
                return a

            print(heapsort([31, 4, 15, 9, 26, 5, 58, 9]))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Strings",
        title = "Levenshtein distance",
        originalTitle = "Edit distance (Levenshtein, 1965)",
        author = "Vladimir Levenshtein",
        year = 1965,
        summary = "The fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one word into another, found with a table of prefix distances.",
        details = "Levenshtein described the distance in 1965. The table is filled one row at a time, so only the previous row has to be kept. The example prints three pairs of words and their distances.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as edit_distance.py.
            2. Run it: python3 edit_distance.py
        """,
        example = """
            def levenshtein(a, b):
                # The cheapest way to turn a[:i] into b[:j], one row of the table at a time.
                previous = list(range(len(b) + 1))
                for i, ca in enumerate(a, start=1):
                    current = [i]
                    for j, cb in enumerate(b, start=1):
                        cost = 0 if ca == cb else 1
                        current.append(min(previous[j] + 1, current[j - 1] + 1, previous[j - 1] + cost))
                    previous = current
                return previous[-1]

            for a, b in [("kitten", "sitting"), ("flaw", "lawn"), ("", "abc")]:
                print(repr(a), repr(b), levenshtein(a, b))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Strings",
        title = "Knuth–Morris–Pratt string search",
        originalTitle = "Knuth–Morris–Pratt search (Morris and Pratt, 1970)",
        author = "James Morris, Vaughan Pratt and Donald Knuth",
        year = 1970,
        summary = "A search for a pattern in text that never moves backwards in the text, because a table of the pattern's own prefixes says how far to fall back after a mismatch.",
        details = "Morris and Pratt wrote a technical report on the method in 1970, and the full paper by Knuth, Morris and Pratt appeared in 1977. The example finds every place where 'abra' starts in a text.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as kmp.py.
            2. Run it: python3 kmp.py
        """,
        example = """
            def prefix_table(pattern):
                # For each position, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
                table = [0] * len(pattern)
                k = 0
                for i in range(1, len(pattern)):
                    while k > 0 and pattern[i] != pattern[k]:
                        k = table[k - 1]
                    if pattern[i] == pattern[k]:
                        k += 1
                    table[i] = k
                return table

            def search(text, pattern):
                table = prefix_table(pattern)
                found = []
                k = 0
                for i, ch in enumerate(text):
                    while k > 0 and ch != pattern[k]:
                        k = table[k - 1]
                    if ch == pattern[k]:
                        k += 1
                    if k == len(pattern):
                        found.append(i - len(pattern) + 1)
                        k = table[k - 1]
                return found

            print(search("abracadabra abracadabra", "abra"))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Signals",
        title = "Fast Fourier transform by halving",
        originalTitle = "Cooley–Tukey fast Fourier transform (1965)",
        author = "James Cooley and John Tukey",
        year = 1965,
        summary = "The fast Fourier transform: split the samples into even and odd parts, transform each half, and combine them with twiddle factors, which cuts the work from n squared to n log n.",
        details = "Cooley and Tukey published the method in 1965. The example transforms a short signal, [1, 0, -1, 0], and prints the size of each frequency, rounded to six places.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as fft.py.
            2. Run it: python3 fft.py
        """,
        example = """
            import cmath

            def fft(x):
                n = len(x)
                if n == 1:
                    return list(x)
                even = fft(x[0::2])
                odd = fft(x[1::2])
                result = [0] * n
                for k in range(n // 2):
                    twiddle = cmath.exp(-2j * cmath.pi * k / n) * odd[k]
                    result[k] = even[k] + twiddle
                    result[k + n // 2] = even[k] - twiddle
                return result

            spectrum = fft([1, 0, -1, 0])
            print([round(abs(v), 6) for v in spectrum])
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Data structures",
        title = "Tries for prefix search",
        originalTitle = "Trie memory (Fredkin, 1960)",
        author = "Edward Fredkin",
        year = 1960,
        summary = "A tree of letters in which every word is a path from the root, so all the words that start with a prefix can be found by walking down to it.",
        details = "Fredkin described the trie in 1960, and the name comes from the word retrieval. The example stores five words and lists the words that begin with each prefix.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as trie.py.
            2. Run it: python3 trie.py
        """,
        example = """
            def make_trie(words):
                root = {}
                for word in words:
                    node = root
                    for letter in word:
                        node = node.setdefault(letter, {})
                    node[""] = True        # an empty key marks the end of a word
                return root

            def words_with_prefix(root, prefix):
                node = root
                for letter in prefix:
                    if letter not in node:
                        return []
                    node = node[letter]
                results = []

                def walk(current, path):
                    if "" in current:
                        results.append(prefix + path)
                    for letter in sorted(k for k in current if k != ""):
                        walk(current[letter], path + letter)

                walk(node, "")
                return results

            trie = make_trie(["tea", "ten", "to", "inn", "tec"])
            print(words_with_prefix(trie, "te"))
            print(words_with_prefix(trie, "to"))
            print(words_with_prefix(trie, "x"))
        """,
    ),
)

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Graphics",
        title = "Bresenham's line in one loop",
        originalTitle = "Bresenham's line algorithm (1962, published 1965)",
        author = "Jack Bresenham at IBM",
        year = 1962,
        summary = "A line drawn with whole numbers only: an error term decides when to step sideways, so the loop needs no multiplication or division.",
        details = "Bresenham worked the method out at IBM in 1962 for a plotter driven by an IBM 1401, and he published it in 1965 in the IBM Systems Journal. The example draws a shallow line on a small grid.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as line.py.
            2. Run it: python3 line.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Step along the longer axis; the error term decides when to move the other coordinate.
            def bresenham(x0, y0, x1, y1):
                points = []
                dx, dy = abs(x1 - x0), -abs(y1 - y0)
                sx, sy = (1 if x0 < x1 else -1), (1 if y0 < y1 else -1)
                err = dx + dy
                while True:
                    points.append((x0, y0))
                    if x0 == x1 and y0 == y1:
                        break
                    e2 = 2 * err
                    if e2 >= dy:
                        err += dy
                        x0 += sx
                    if e2 <= dx:
                        err += dx
                        y0 += sy
                return points

            pts = set(bresenham(0, 0, 9, 3))
            for y in range(4):
                print("".join("#" if (x, y) in pts else "." for x in range(10)))
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Cycles",
        title = "Tortoise and hare for cycles",
        originalTitle = "Floyd's cycle-finding method (1967)",
        author = "Robert Floyd",
        year = 1967,
        summary = "Two pointers walk the same sequence, one twice as fast as the other, and they meet inside any loop. A second pass then finds where the loop begins.",
        details = "Robert Floyd's method is usually dated to 1967. The example finds where a sequence of numbers starts to repeat and how long the repeating part is.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as cycle.py.
            2. Run it: python3 cycle.py
        """,
        example = """
            def step(x):
                return (x * x + 1) % 255

            def find_cycle(start):
                # Phase 1: the hare moves twice as fast as the tortoise, until they meet inside the cycle.
                tortoise = step(start)
                hare = step(step(start))
                while tortoise != hare:
                    tortoise = step(tortoise)
                    hare = step(step(hare))
                # Phase 2: start again from the beginning; they meet where the cycle begins.
                mu = 0
                tortoise = start
                while tortoise != hare:
                    tortoise = step(tortoise)
                    hare = step(hare)
                    mu += 1
                # Phase 3: go once around the cycle to measure its length.
                lam = 1
                hare = step(tortoise)
                while tortoise != hare:
                    hare = step(hare)
                    lam += 1
                return mu, lam

            mu, lam = find_cycle(3)
            print(f"the sequence starts repeating after {mu} steps, with a cycle of length {lam}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Matrices",
        title = "Strassen's seven multiplications",
        originalTitle = "Strassen's algorithm for 2 by 2 matrices (1969)",
        author = "Volker Strassen",
        year = 1969,
        summary = "A way to multiply two 2 by 2 matrices with seven multiplications instead of eight, the first step towards faster multiplication of large matrices.",
        details = "Strassen published the method in 1969. Its extra additions cost time on small matrices, but the saving grows when the method is applied recursively to blocks. The example checks the result against the usual formula.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as strassen.py.
            2. Run it: python3 strassen.py
        """,
        example = """
            def strassen(a, b):
                (a11, a12), (a21, a22) = a
                (b11, b12), (b21, b22) = b
                m1 = (a11 + a22) * (b11 + b22)
                m2 = (a21 + a22) * b11
                m3 = a11 * (b12 - b22)
                m4 = a22 * (b21 - b11)
                m5 = (a11 + a12) * b22
                m6 = (a21 - a11) * (b11 + b12)
                m7 = (a12 - a22) * (b21 + b22)
                return ((m1 + m4 - m5 + m7, m3 + m5), (m2 + m4, m1 - m2 + m3 + m6))

            def naive(a, b):
                return tuple(tuple(sum(a[i][k] * b[k][j] for k in range(2)) for j in range(2)) for i in range(2))

            a = ((1, 2), (3, 4))
            b = ((5, 6), (7, 8))
            print(strassen(a, b))
            print(strassen(a, b) == naive(a, b))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.FLEX,
        section = "Sets",
        title = "Union-find with path halving",
        originalTitle = "Equivalence classes with trees (Galler and Fischer, 1964)",
        author = "Bernard Galler and Michael Fischer",
        year = 1964,
        summary = "A way to keep groups of items that have been joined together, where each group is a tree and a find walks up to its root. Path halving keeps the trees shallow.",
        details = "Galler and Fischer described equivalence classes with trees in 1964. The path-halving step, which makes every second node point to its grandparent, was refined later. The example joins a few pairs and prints the groups.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as union_find.py.
            2. Run it: python3 union_find.py
        """,
        example = """
            parent = list(range(8))

            def find(x):
                while parent[x] != x:
                    parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]    # path halving: skip every other step upwards
                    x = parent[x]
                return x

            def union(a, b):
                ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
                if ra != rb:
                    parent[rb] = ra

            for a, b in [(0, 1), (2, 3), (1, 3), (5, 6)]:
                union(a, b)

            groups = {}
            for x in range(8):
                groups.setdefault(find(x), []).append(x)
            print(sorted(groups.values()))
        """,
    ),
)

        details = "Atlas brought demand paging into practice in hardware and software. The example is a toy with three frames of core and a list of addresses. " +

            PAGE_SIZE = 4
            FRAMES = 3
            frames = []          # pages in core, least recently used first

            def access(address):
                page = address // PAGE_SIZE
                offset = address % PAGE_SIZE
                if page in frames:
                    frames.remove(page)
                    frames.append(page)
                    result = "hit"
                else:
                    result = "fault"
                    if len(frames) == FRAMES:
                        evicted = frames.pop(0)
                        result += f", evicts page {evicted}"
                    frames.append(page)
                return f"address {address:2} -> page {page}, offset {offset}: {result}"

            measurements = [1.2, 0.9, 1.1, 1.0, 1.05]
            x = 0.0      # estimate

            r = 0.1      # variance of the measurement noise
            for step, z in enumerate(measurements, start=1):
                k = p / (p + r)          # gain: how much to trust the new measurement
                x = x + k * (z - x)
                p = (1 - k) * p

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 1960 to 1970: small programs in the spirit of the decade, with instructions and code to run. */
val db7Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Conversation",
        title = "ELIZA-style conversation",
        originalTitle = "ELIZA (Weizenbaum, 1966)",
        author = "Joseph Weizenbaum",
        year = 1966,
        summary = "A keyword program in the spirit of ELIZA: each sentence is matched against a few patterns, and the reply turns the captured words around.",
        details = "Weizenbaum wrote ELIZA at MIT and published it in 1966. Its best-known script, DOCTOR, played a psychotherapist by reflecting the user's own words back. This version has four rules and a reflection table, which is enough to show the trick.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as eliza.py.
            2. Run it: python3 eliza.py
            3. Add your own rules to RULES. The first rule that matches is used.
        """,
        example = """
            import re

            # Each rule is a pattern and a reply template. Captured words are reflected (I becomes you) before they are used.
            RULES = [
                (r"i need (.*)", "Why do you need {0}?"),
                (r"i am (.*)", "How long have you been {0}?"),
                (r"my (.*)", "Tell me more about your {0}."),
                (r"(.*)\?", "Why do you ask that?"),
            ]
            REFLECT = {"i": "you", "my": "your", "me": "you", "am": "are"}

            def reflect(text):
                return " ".join(REFLECT.get(word, word) for word in text.split())

            def reply(sentence):
                text = sentence.lower().strip(" .!")
                for pattern, template in RULES:
                    match = re.fullmatch(pattern, text)
                    if match:
                        return template.format(*[reflect(group) for group in match.groups()])
                return "Please go on."

            for line in ["I need a break.", "I am tired.", "My mother worries about me.", "Will it rain?", "Nothing much."]:
                print(">", line)
                print(reply(line))
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Matching",
        title = "Stable matching by Gale and Shapley",
        originalTitle = "College admissions and the stability of marriage (1962)",
        author = "David Gale and Lloyd Shapley",
        year = 1962,
        summary = "The proposal algorithm that pairs men and women so that no man and woman would both prefer each other to their partners.",
        details = "Gale and Shapley published the method in 1962. Men propose in order of preference, and each woman keeps the best proposal so far. The result is always stable, and it favours the proposing side.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as matching.py.
            2. Run it: python3 matching.py
        """,
        example = """
            # Men propose in order of preference; each woman keeps the best proposal so far.
            men = {
                "Adam": ["Eve", "Ruth", "Ada"],
                "Ben": ["Ruth", "Eve", "Ada"],
                "Carl": ["Eve", "Ada", "Ruth"],
            }
            women = {
                "Ada": ["Carl", "Adam", "Ben"],
                "Eve": ["Ben", "Carl", "Adam"],
                "Ruth": ["Adam", "Ben", "Carl"],
            }

            def stable_matching(men, women):
                rank = {w: {m: i for i, m in enumerate(prefs)} for w, prefs in women.items()}
                free = list(men)
                next_choice = {m: 0 for m in men}
                engaged = {}                       # woman -> man
                while free:
                    man = free.pop(0)
                    woman = men[man][next_choice[man]]
                    next_choice[man] += 1
                    if woman not in engaged:
                        engaged[woman] = man
                    elif rank[woman][man] < rank[woman][engaged[woman]]:
                        free.append(engaged[woman])
                        engaged[woman] = man
                    else:
                        free.append(man)
                return {man: woman for woman, man in engaged.items()}

            matching = stable_matching(men, women)
            for man in sorted(matching):
                print(man, "marries", matching[man])
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Editors",
        title = "A TECO-style line editor",
        originalTitle = "TECO, the Text Editor and Corrector (1963)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example, after Dan Murphy's TECO",
        year = 1963,
        summary = "A small editor with one-letter commands and a current line, which appends, jumps, deletes, substitutes and prints the buffer, in the spirit of TECO.",
        details = "TECO worked on a buffer with a pointer to the current line, and each command moved the pointer or changed the text. This version has five commands, enough to show the idea.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as teco.py.
            2. Run it: python3 teco.py
            3. Change the list of commands to edit a different buffer.
        """,
        example = """
            buffer = []
            current = 0

            def run(commands):
                global current
                for command in commands:
                    op, _, rest = command.partition(" ")
                    if op == "a":                       # append a line and make it current
                        buffer.append(rest)
                        current = len(buffer) - 1
                    elif op == "j":                     # jump to line number n, counting from 1
                        current = int(rest) - 1
                    elif op == "d":                     # delete the current line
                        del buffer[current]
                        current = min(current, len(buffer) - 1)
                    elif op == "s":                     # replace the first match in the current line
                        old, new = rest.split(" ", 1)
                        buffer[current] = buffer[current].replace(old, new, 1)
                    elif op == "p":                     # print the buffer and mark the current line
                        for number, line in enumerate(buffer, start=1):
                            mark = "*" if number - 1 == current else " "
                            print(f"{mark} {number} {line}")

            run([
                "a the quick fox",
                "a jumps over",
                "a the lazy dog",
                "j 2",
                "s jumps leaps",
                "p",
                "j 3",
                "d",
                "p",
            ])
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 7,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Concurrency",
        title = "Dining philosophers with ordered forks",
        originalTitle = "The dining philosophers problem (Dijkstra, 1965)",
        author = "Edsger Dijkstra; this version uses threads",
        year = 1965,
        summary = "Five philosophers share five forks around a table. Taking the forks in a fixed order avoids the deadlock in which each holds one fork and waits for the next.",
        details = "Dijkstra posed the problem in 1965. The example runs five threads, and each thread eats three meals. The lower-numbered fork is always taken first, so no circle of waiting can form, and the final count shows that every philosopher ate.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as philosophers.py.
            2. Run it: python3 philosophers.py
            3. Remove the sorting line to see the deadlock risk; the program may then hang.
        """,
        example = """
            import threading

            PHILOSOPHERS = 5
            MEALS = 3
            forks = [threading.Lock() for _ in range(PHILOSOPHERS)]
            meals = [0] * PHILOSOPHERS

            def philosopher(i):
                # Take the lower-numbered fork first: the fixed order prevents the circular wait that causes deadlock.
                first, second = sorted([i, (i + 1) % PHILOSOPHERS])
                for _ in range(MEALS):
                    with forks[first]:
                        with forks[second]:
                            meals[i] += 1

            threads = [threading.Thread(target=philosopher, args=(i,)) for i in range(PHILOSOPHERS)]
            for t in threads:
                t.start()
            for t in threads:
                t.join()
            print("meals:", meals)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),
)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1247: the point of the Tusi couple at quarter turns, in Python and in C. */
val db80Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 80,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Mechanisms",
        title = "The Tusi couple's straight-line motion in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Tusi couple",
        author = "Nasir al-Din al-Tusi",
        year = 1247,
        summary = "The Tusi couple moves a point along a straight diameter, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same positions at quarter turns.",
        details = "The example uses a ring of radius two and a small circle of radius one, so the point's positions at quarter turns are whole numbers, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line. The ratio of the radii is the one the device needs for the point to stay on a diameter.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### tusi.py
            # ring of radius 2, small circle of radius 1 rolling inside it (Tusi couple)
            EXACT = {0: (1, 0), 90: (0, 1), 180: (-1, 0), 270: (0, -1)}   # cos and sin at quarter turns
            for t in [0, 90, 180, 270]:
                cx, cy = EXACT[t]              # centre of the small circle
                px, py = EXACT[(-t) % 360]     # the point turns the other way, at the same rate
                print(f"turn {t} degrees: point at x {cx + px}, y {cy + py}")
            print("on the diameter at every step: yes")
            ### tusi.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                /* cos and sin at quarter turns, for 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees */
                int ex[4] = {1, 0, -1, 0};
                int ey[4] = {0, 1, 0, -1};
                int turns[4] = {0, 90, 180, 270};
                for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
                    int t = turns[i];
                    int cx = ex[i];
                    int cy = ey[i];
                    int k = (((-t) % 360) + 360) % 360 / 90;   /* quarter turn of the point, the other way */
                    int px = ex[k];
                    int py = ey[k];
                    printf("turn %d degrees: point at x %d, y %d\n", t, cx + px, cy + py);
                }
                printf("on the diameter at every step: yes\n");
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 tusi.py > python.txt
            cc -o tusi_c tusi.c
            ./tusi_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 1240 to 1250: the celestial element's rectangle, written as a short program. */
val db80Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 80,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Algebra",
        title = "How the celestial element finds the sides of a rectangle",
        originalTitle = "Tian yuan",
        author = "Li Ye",
        year = 1248,
        summary = "The celestial element stands for the short side of a rectangle, and a short program finds both sides from the area and the difference between them.",
        details = "With the short side x and the long side x plus d, the area x times (x plus d) gives a quadratic, and the example takes its positive root with a whole-number square root. Li Ye's book solves such problems by its own procedures, so the example is a modern check on illustrative areas.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as rectangle.py.
            2. Run it: python3 rectangle.py
        """,
        example = """
            from math import isqrt

            def sides(area, difference):
                # the celestial element x is the short side, and the long side is x + difference
                # x * (x + difference) = area, so root * root = difference * difference + 4 * area
                root = isqrt(difference * difference + 4 * area)
                assert root * root == difference * difference + 4 * area
                short = (root - difference) // 2
                return short, short + difference

            for area, difference in [(35, 2), (60, 4), (12, 1)]:
                short, long = sides(area, difference)
                assert short * long == area
                print("area", area, "difference", difference, "sides", short, long)
        """,
    ),

)

        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Fines",
        title = "A ledger of fines under the Jutland law",
        originalTitle = "Jydske Lov",
        author = "The Jutland assembly",
        year = 1241,
        summary = "The Jutland law set fines for offences, and a short program totals an illustrative ledger of fines by offence.",
        details = "The amounts in the example are invented to show the bookkeeping, and they do not reproduce the fines of the law. The program adds the fines for each offence, sorts the offences by name and prints the grand total.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as fines.py.
            2. Run it: python3 fines.py
        """,
        example = """
            offences = [("wounding", 6), ("theft", 12), ("trespass", 3), ("wounding", 6)]   # illustrative fines
            totals = {}
            for offence, fine in offences:
                totals[offence] = totals.get(offence, 0) + fine
            for offence in sorted(totals):
                print(offence, totals[offence])
            print("total fines", sum(totals.values()))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 80,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Ransoms",
        title = "A ransom of 400,000 bezants paid in instalments",
        originalTitle = "Bezant",

        year = 1250,
        summary = "The chronicles give the ransom of King Louis IX in 1250 as 400,000 bezants, and a short program divides the sum into instalments.",
        details = "Louis was captured after the army's retreat from Mansurah in April 1250, and accounts differ on whether the sum was paid at once or in instalments. The instalments in the example are illustrative, and the program prints the balance still due after each payment.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as ransom.py.
            2. Run it: python3 ransom.py
        """,
        example = """
            ransom = 400000                       # bezants, the sum given in the chronicles
            payments = [150000, 150000, 100000]   # illustrative instalments
            balance = ransom
            for number, paid in enumerate(payments, start=1):
                balance -= paid
                print("instalment", number, "of", paid, "leaves", balance, "bezants due")
            print("total paid", sum(payments))
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1236: the blocks of the Tripitaka Koreana divided by two readings of the carving's length, in Python and C. */
val db81Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 81,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Printing",
        title = "Blocks per year of the Tripitaka carving under two readings, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Palman daejanggyeong carving years",
        author = "The Goryeo carvers",
        year = 1236,
        summary = "The 81,258 blocks of the Tripitaka Koreana give 5417 blocks a year over 15 years or 5078 over 16, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same two figures.",
        details = "The two readings of the carving's length are the ones given in the accounts, and the division is whole-number division in both languages. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, as the other cross records do.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### blocks_year.py
            BLOCKS = 81258
            for years in (15, 16):
                print(years, "years:", BLOCKS // years, "blocks a year")
            ### blocks_year.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const int blocks = 81258;
                const int spans[2] = {15, 16};
                for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
                    printf("%d years: %d blocks a year\n", spans[i], blocks / spans[i]);
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 blocks_year.py > python.txt
            cc -o blocks_year_c blocks_year.c
            ./blocks_year_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 1230 to 1235: a concordance's word places, a pointed arch, a five-part letter and a mason's mark counted by stone. */
val db81Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 81,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Index",
        title = "How a concordance lists the places of each word",
        originalTitle = "Concordance",
        author = "The friars of St Jacques",
        year = 1230,
        summary = "A concordance lists each word of a text in alphabetical order with its places, and a short program builds the same kind of list for a Latin verse.",
        details = "Hugh of Saint-Cher's concordance of about 1230 gave each word with its book and chapter, sorted by letter, so that a reader could find the places where a word is used. The example counts places as word numbers from 1 and prints the list for one verse, so the output can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as concordance.py.
            2. Run it: python3 concordance.py
        """,
        example = """
            text = "In principio erat Verbum et Verbum erat apud Deum et Deus erat Verbum"
            places = {}
            for position, word in enumerate(text.lower().split(), start=1):
                places.setdefault(word, []).append(position)
            for word in sorted(places):
                print(word, " ".join(str(p) for p in places[word]))
            print("distinct words:", len(places))
            print("words in the verse:", len(text.split()))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 81,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Geometry",
        title = "How a pointed arch is struck from two centres",
        originalTitle = "Pointed arch setting-out",
        author = "Gothic masons",
        year = 1230,
        summary = "A pointed arch of two equal arcs is struck from two centres one span apart, and a short program prints the centres and the height of the crown for two spans.",
        details = "Each arc has the span as its radius, so the two arcs meet above the middle at a height equal to the span times the square root of three over two, the height of an equilateral triangle. The example prints the figures for spans of 10 and 6 units, and this form is one of the common pointed arches of the period.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as arch.py.
            2. Run it: python3 arch.py
        """,
        example = """
            import math

            for span in (10, 6):
                left = (0.0, 0.0)
                right = (float(span), 0.0)
                crown_x = span / 2
                crown_y = span * math.sqrt(3) / 2
                print(f"span {span}: centres at {left[0]:.0f} and {right[0]:.0f}")
                print(f"span {span}: crown at {crown_x:.3f} {crown_y:.3f}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 81,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Letters",
        title = "How a medieval letter is set out in five parts",
        originalTitle = "Ars dictaminis",
        author = "Letter-writing masters of Bologna",
        year = 1235,
        summary = "A medieval letter was set out in five parts, greeting, opening, narrative, request and closing, and a short program counts the words in each part of a sample letter.",
        details = "Boncompagno's Rhetorica novissima of 1235 is one of the manuals that teach this five-part form, and later letter-writers copied it. The example gives a short sample letter with one sentence for each part, and it prints the words in each part so the totals can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as letter.py.
            2. Run it: python3 letter.py
        """,
        example = """
            parts = [
                ("salutatio", "greetings to the lord abbot"),
                ("exordium", "since the matter is grave"),
                ("narratio", "the mill of the house was lost in the flood"),
                ("petitio", "we ask that the mill be rebuilt"),
                ("conclusio", "farewell"),
            ]
            total = 0
            for number, (part, text) in enumerate(parts, start=1):
                count = len(text.split())
                total += count
                print(number, part, count)
            print("words in the letter:", total)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 81,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Building",
        title = "How a mason's mark on each stone counts a cutter's work",
        originalTitle = "Mason's marks",
        author = "Masons of the cathedral yards",
        year = 1230,
        summary = "A mason cut a personal mark on each stone he finished, so that the stones of each cutter could be counted, and a short program tallies a sample of marked stones.",
        details = "Marks of this kind are found on the stones of medieval churches, where they are read as signs of who cut each stone. The example uses an illustrative sample of seven stones with the marks a, b and c, and it prints the count for each mark and the total.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as marks.py.
            2. Run it: python3 marks.py
        """,
        example = """
            marks = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "a", "b", "a"]   # illustrative sample of seven stones
            counts = {}
            for mark in marks:
                counts[mark] = counts.get(mark, 0) + 1
            for mark in sorted(counts):
                print("mark", mark, counts[mark])
            print("stones:", len(marks))
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Projects of 1230: a surveyor's sum that turns three strip fields measured in rods into square rods, acres and square yards. */
val db81Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 81,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Measure",
        title = "Acres in three strip fields, from their length and width in rods",
        originalTitle = "Acre and rod",
        author = "English surveyors of the thirteenth century",
        year = 1230,
        summary = "A surveyor measured strip fields in rods, and a short program turns three strips into square rods and acres, since one acre is 160 square rods.",
        details = "The rod or perch is 5.5 yards and the acre is 40 rods by 4 rods, the units that English surveyors used in the thirteenth century and later. The example adds the three strips in square rods, prints the acres and the square yards of one acre, and uses illustrative strip sizes, so the outputs can be checked by hand.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as acres.py.
            2. Run it: python3 acres.py
        """,
        example = """
            ROD_YARDS = 5.5                      # one rod, or perch, is 5.5 yards
            ACRE_RODS = 40 * 4                   # one acre is 40 rods by 4 rods, so 160 square rods
            strips = [("north strip", 40, 4), ("south strip", 20, 3), ("river strip", 30, 5)]   # length and width in rods, illustrative
            total = 0
            for name, length, width in strips:
                square_rods = length * width
                total += square_rods
                print(name, square_rods, "square rods")
            print("total square rods:", total)
            print("square rods in one acre:", ACRE_RODS)
            print("acres:", total // ACRE_RODS, "remainder", total % ACRE_RODS, "square rods")
            print("square yards in one acre:", ACRE_RODS * ROD_YARDS * ROD_YARDS)
        """,
    ),

)

/** Cross-code experiments of 1221 to 1228: days between two deaths and between a death and a canonization, each in Python and C with the same Julian day formula. */
val db82Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 82,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Deaths",
        title = "Days from Dominic's death to Francis's death in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Julian day number",
        author = "Dominican and Franciscan chroniclers",
        year = 1226,
        summary = "Dominic died on 6 August 1221 and Francis on 3 October 1226, and a script checks that the Python and C programs count the same 1884 days with a Julian day formula.",
        details = "Both programs use integer arithmetic with the same formula, so their outputs must match exactly, and the run script compares them line by line. The dates are given as commonly stated in the Julian reckoning.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### days.py
            def jdn(year, month, day):
                a = (14 - month) // 12
                y = year + 4800 - a
                m = month + 12 * a - 3
                return day + (153 * m + 2) // 5 + 365 * y + y // 4 - 32083

            print("days:", jdn(1226, 10, 3) - jdn(1221, 8, 6))
            ### days.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static long jdn(long year, long month, long day) {
                long a = (14 - month) / 12;
                long y = year + 4800 - a;
                long m = month + 12 * a - 3;
                return day + (153 * m + 2) / 5 + 365 * y + y / 4 - 32083;
            }

            int main(void) {
                printf("days: %ld\n", jdn(1226, 10, 3) - jdn(1221, 8, 6));
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 days.py > python.txt
            cc -o days_c days.c
            ./days_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 82,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Deaths",
        title = "Days from Louis VIII's death to Francis's canonization in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Julian day number",

        details = "The two programs share one integer formula for the Julian day number, so their outputs must match, and the run script compares them line by line. Both dates are given as commonly stated.",
        instructions = """

            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """

            print("days:", jdn(1228, 7, 16) - jdn(1226, 11, 8))
            ### count.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static long jdn(long year, long month, long day) {

                long y = year + 4800 - a;
                long m = month + 12 * a - 3;
                return day + (153 * m + 2) / 5 + 365 * y + y / 4 - 32083;
            }

            int main(void) {

/** Examples of 1225 and 1226: a square five above and five below from Fibonacci's book of squares, and the weekday of Francis of Assisi's death in the Julian reckoning. */
val db82Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 82,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Squares",
        title = "Checking a square that stays square five above and five below",
        originalTitle = "Congruum problem",
        author = "Leonardo Fibonacci, with a worked check",
        year = 1225,
        summary = "Fibonacci's Liber quadratorum poses a square that leaves squares when five is added and when five is taken away, and a short program checks the worked answer 41/12 in whole numbers.",
        details = "Scaling by 12 turns the square of 41/12 into 1681 over 144, and adding or taking away five turns it into 2401 and 961 over 144, which are the squares of 49 and 31. The integer check uses an exact square root, so the output does not depend on rounding.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as congruum.py.
            2. Run it: python3 congruum.py
        """,
        example = """
            from math import isqrt

            def square_root(n):
                r = isqrt(n)
                return r if r * r == n else None

            n = 1681              # (41/12) squared, scaled by 144
            step = 5 * 144        # five units, scaled by 144
            up = square_root(n + step)
            down = square_root(n - step)
            print("plus five:", n + step, "is square of", up)
            print("minus five:", n - step, "is square of", down)
            print("both squares:", up is not None and down is not None)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 82,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Calendar",
        title = "The weekday of Francis of Assisi's death, counted from a Julian day number",
        originalTitle = "Julian calendar, 3 October 1226",
        author = "Franciscan chroniclers",
        year = 1226,
        summary = "Francis of Assisi died on 3 October 1226 in the Julian reckoning, and a short program turns that date into a Julian day number and then into a weekday.",
        details = "The usual account places his death on a Saturday, and the program confirms the weekday with a standard formula for the Julian calendar. The day number counts days from a fixed origin, so the same formula works for any date in the Julian reckoning.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as weekday.py.
            2. Run it: python3 weekday.py
        """,
        example = """
            def julian_day_number(year, month, day):
                a = (14 - month) // 12
                y = year + 4800 - a
                m = month + 12 * a - 3
                return day + (153 * m + 2) // 5 + 365 * y + y // 4 - 32083

            WEEKDAYS = ["Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday"]
            jdn = julian_day_number(1226, 10, 3)
            print("julian day number:", jdn)
            print("weekday:", WEEKDAYS[(jdn + 1) % 7])
        """,
    ),

)

val db82Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 82,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Verse",
        title = "How a drottkvaett stanza is counted in syllables",
        originalTitle = "Drottkvaett",
        author = "Skalds of Norway and Iceland",
        year = 1220,
        summary = "A drottkvaett stanza has eight lines of six syllables each, and a short program checks the syllables of each line of an illustrative stanza.",
        details = "Snorri's Hattatal, the list of metres at the end of his Prose Edda, sets out the rules of this court verse, including the count of six syllables in each line. The example uses an illustrative stanza, not a real one, so the count can be checked by hand line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as drottkvaett.py.
            2. Run it: python3 drottkvaett.py
        """,
        example = """
            STANZA = [
                "hal-di-ran-ga-mon-den",
                "sa-ri-to-ven-ka-bal",
                "ra-ma-ni-su-tor-gen",
                "ol-fe-rim-ka-dar-to",
                "ka-lu-me-ban-dro-sir",
                "ti-ver-na-ga-lun-da",
                "mo-ren-ba-tu-ka",
                "ha-sun-di-ka-ro-man",
            ]
            print("lines:", len(STANZA))
            six = 0
            for number, line in enumerate(STANZA, start=1):
                count = len(line.split("-"))
                if count == 6:
                    six += 1
                else:
                    print("line", number, "has", count, "syllables, not six")
            print("lines of six syllables:", six)
        """,
    ),

)

/** Projects of 1220 to 1230: a small program that sorts five Mongol captures of Khwarazmian cities by year and counts them. */
val db82Projects: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 82,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Conquests",
        title = "The Mongol capture of five Khwarazmian cities, sorted and counted by year",
        originalTitle = "Cities taken in 1220 and 1221",
        author = "Mongol commanders under Genghis Khan",
        year = 1221,
        summary = "A short program sorts five cities of the Khwarazmian empire by the year the Mongols took them, then counts the captures in each year.",
        details = "Bukhara and Samarkand fell in 1220, and Urgench, Merv and Nishapur fell in 1221, with the years given as commonly stated, so the output is fixed. The list covers only five cities of the campaign, and the program does not claim that it is complete.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as cities.py.
            2. Run it: python3 cities.py
        """,
        example = """
            CAPTURES = [
                ("Bukhara", 1220),
                ("Samarkand", 1220),
                ("Urgench", 1221),
                ("Merv", 1221),
                ("Nishapur", 1221),
            ]
            by_year = {}
            for city, year in sorted(CAPTURES, key=lambda item: (item[1], item[0])):
                by_year.setdefault(year, []).append(city)
            for year in sorted(by_year):
                print(year, len(by_year[year]), ", ".join(by_year[year]))
            print("cities listed:", len(CAPTURES))
            print("years of capture:", max(year for _, year in CAPTURES) - min(year for _, year in CAPTURES) + 1)
        """,
    ),

)
