package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1215 and 1220: the clauses of Magna Carta in 1215 and 1225, and a kenning builder, each in Python and C. */
val db83Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Law",
        title = "Magna Carta clause counts in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Clauses of Magna Carta",
        author = "King John and his barons",
        year = 1215,
        summary = "The first charter of 1215 had sixty-three clauses and the 1225 version had thirty-seven, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same count of clauses dropped.",
        details = "The example works out the clauses dropped and the share dropped, in Python and in C, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line. The share is printed to one decimal place in both programs.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### clauses.py
            clauses_1215 = 63
            clauses_1225 = 37
            dropped = clauses_1215 - clauses_1225
            print("clauses in 1215:", clauses_1215)
            print("clauses in 1225:", clauses_1225)
            print("clauses dropped:", dropped)
            print("share dropped:", f"{100 * dropped / clauses_1215:.1f} per cent")
            ### clauses.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const int clauses_1215 = 63;
                const int clauses_1225 = 37;
                int dropped = clauses_1215 - clauses_1225;
                printf("clauses in 1215: %d\n", clauses_1215);
                printf("clauses in 1225: %d\n", clauses_1225);
                printf("clauses dropped: %d\n", dropped);
                printf("share dropped: %.1f per cent\n", 100.0 * dropped / clauses_1215);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 clauses.py > python.txt
            cc -o clauses_c clauses.c
            ./clauses_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Poetry",
        title = "A kenning builder in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Kenning",
        author = "Snorri Sturluson",
        year = 1220,
        summary = "A kenning names a thing by two words, such as whale-road for the sea, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same kennings.",
        details = "The two example kennings are the common examples whale-road for the sea and sea-steed for a ship, and the run script compares the outputs line by line. The pattern belongs to the Prose Edda of about 1220.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### kenning.py
            kennings = [("whale", "road", "sea"), ("sea", "steed", "ship")]
            for first, second, meaning in kennings:
                print(first + "-" + second + " names the " + meaning)
            print("kennings listed: " + str(len(kennings)))
            ### kenning.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const char *first[] = {"whale", "sea"};
                const char *second[] = {"road", "steed"};
                const char *meaning[] = {"sea", "ship"};
                int count = 2;
                for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
                    printf("%s-%s names the %s\n", first[i], second[i], meaning[i]);
                }
                printf("kennings listed: %d\n", count);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 kenning.py > python.txt
            cc -o kenning_c kenning.c
            ./kenning_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Examples of 1210 to 1220: the floor of Chomei's ten-foot hut in shaku and metres, and the acres of a field forty by twenty-five rods. */
val db83Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Architecture",
        title = "The ten-foot square hut of the Hojoki in square shaku and metres",
        originalTitle = "Hojo, a square of one jo",
        author = "Kamo no Chomei",
        year = 1212,
        summary = "A hut one jo square has 100 square shaku of floor, and a short program turns its side and floor into metres and counts the mats that fit.",
        details = "The example takes one shaku as 0.3 metre, a round figure, and it uses a mat of six by three shaku as an illustration rather than a fixed standard. The name of the hut, hojo, means a square of one jo, and one jo is ten shaku.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as hut.py.
            2. Run it: python3 hut.py
        """,
        example = """
            SHAKU_IN_METRES = 0.3    # a round figure for the example
            side_shaku = 10          # one jo is ten shaku, so the hut is one jo square
            area_shaku = side_shaku * side_shaku
            print("hut area in square shaku:", area_shaku)
            side_m = side_shaku * SHAKU_IN_METRES
            print("side in metres:", round(side_m, 1))
            print("area in square metres:", round(side_m * side_m, 1))
            mat_area = 6 * 3                 # an illustrative mat of six by three shaku
            print("full mats of 6 by 3 shaku:", area_shaku // mat_area)
            print("square shaku left over:", area_shaku % mat_area)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Land",
        title = "Acres in a field of forty by twenty-five rods",
        originalTitle = "Rod and acre",
        author = "Surveyors of the period",
        year = 1220,
        summary = "A field forty rods long and twenty-five rods wide holds 1000 square rods, which is six and a quarter acres, and a short program makes the sum.",
        details = "One acre is 160 square rods, the standard English measure, and the example works the area out by multiplying the two sides. Fibonacci's Practica geometriae of about 1220 belongs to the same surveying tradition, though the field is only an illustration.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as acres.py.
            2. Run it: python3 acres.py
        """,
        example = """
            length_rods = 40
            width_rods = 25
            ROD_SQUARES_PER_ACRE = 160
            area = length_rods * width_rods
            print("area in square rods:", area)
            print("acres:", area / ROD_SQUARES_PER_ACRE)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Guides of 1210 to 1220: the citation form of the Decretum, a restatement drill, a seasonal arrangement of poems and the morae of a Japanese sentence. */
val db83Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Law",
        title = "How a citation of Gratian's Decretum names its cause, question and canon",
        originalTitle = "Citation form of the Decretum",
        author = "Canon lawyers of the period",
        year = 1215,
        summary = "A citation such as C.11 q.1 c.20 names a place in Gratian's Decretum by cause, question and canon, and a short program spells out each citation in words.",
        details = "The abbreviations are C for causa, q for quaestio, c for canon and D for distinction, and the example expands three citations. The form is the one lawyers used when they cited the Decretum in the glosses of the time, so the guide is dated to the Glossa ordinaria of about 1215.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as decretum.py.
            2. Run it: python3 decretum.py
        """,
        example = """
            ABBREV = {"C": "cause", "q": "question", "c": "canon", "D": "distinction"}
            citations = ["C.11 q.1 c.20", "D.3 c.2", "C.1 q.3 c.9"]
            for cite in citations:
                words = []
                for part in cite.split():
                    letter, number = part.split(".")
                    words.append(ABBREV[letter] + " " + number)
                print(cite, "means", " and ".join(words))
            print("citations expanded:", len(citations))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Rhetoric",
        title = "How one sentence is restated in several words, as the handbook teaches",
        originalTitle = "Restatement of a theme",
        author = "Geoffrey of Vinsauf",
        year = 1210,
        summary = "Geoffrey of Vinsauf's handbook teaches a writer to restate one idea in several words, and a short program lists the variants of one sentence.",
        details = "The example replaces one verb with three synonyms, which gives four variants in all, and it prints each one in turn. The guide follows the handbook's advice to vary a theme, and it is dated to the handbook's date of about 1210.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as restate.py.
            2. Run it: python3 restate.py
        """,
        example = """
            sentence = "the king died"
            synonyms = {"died": ["passed away", "went to God", "was taken"]}
            variants = [sentence] + [sentence.replace("died", word) for word in synonyms["died"]]
            for number, text in enumerate(variants, start=1):
                print(number, text)
            print("variants:", len(variants))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Poetry",
        title = "How a court anthology lists its poems by season",
        originalTitle = "Arrangement by season",

        year = 1216,
        summary = "A court anthology lists the seasons first, and a short program sorts five sample poems by season and then by label.",
        details = "The Shin Kokinshu opens its books with the four seasons, and this guide arranges sample poems in the same order. The labels in the example are invented for illustration, and the guide is dated to the completion of the Shin Kokinshu in 1216.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as seasons.py.
            2. Run it: python3 seasons.py
        """,
        example = """
            SEASONS = ["spring", "summer", "autumn", "winter"]
            poems = [("A", "autumn"), ("B", "spring"), ("C", "winter"), ("D", "spring"), ("E", "summer")]
            ordered = sorted(poems, key=lambda poem: (SEASONS.index(poem[1]), poem[0]))

            print("poems:", len(poems))
        """,

        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as morae.py.
            2. Run it: python3 morae.py
        """,
        example = """
            SYLLABLES = ["yu", "ku", "ka", "wa", "no", "na", "ga", "re", "wa", "ta", "e", "zu", "shi", "te",
                         "shi", "ka", "mo", "mo", "to", "no", "mi", "zu", "ni", "a", "ra", "zu"]
            print("syllables:", len(SYLLABLES))

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Councils",
        title = "Gaps between three general councils of the Latin Church",
        originalTitle = "Gaps between councils",
        author = "The councils of the Latin Church",
        year = 1215,
        summary = "The Third Lateran Council of 1179, the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 and the First Council of Lyon of 1245 were general councils, and a short program measures the gaps between them.",
        details = "The gaps are counted in whole years from one council to the next, using the years of the three councils as commonly given. The span from the first council to the last is printed as well.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as councils.py.
            2. Run it: python3 councils.py
        """,
        example = """
            councils = [("Lateran III", 1179), ("Lateran IV", 1215), ("Lyon I", 1245)]
            for (name_a, year_a), (name_b, year_b) in zip(councils, councils[1:]):
                print(name_a, "to", name_b, year_b - year_a, "years")
            print("span:", councils[-1][1] - councils[0][1], "years")
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 83,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Land",
        title = "Area of a surveyed field of five corners, by triangles",
        originalTitle = "Fan of triangles",
        author = "Land measurers of the period",
        year = 1220,
        summary = "A field with five corners is split into three triangles from one corner, and a short program adds their areas to give the whole field in square rods and acres.",
        details = "The corners are given in rods on a plan, and each triangle's doubled area is a cross product of two sides. Cutting a field into triangles was a standard surveying method of the period, and Fibonacci's Practica geometriae of about 1220 is a handbook of the same craft.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as field.py.
            2. Run it: python3 field.py
        """,
        example = """
            corners = [(0, 0), (30, 0), (50, 20), (30, 40), (0, 30)]   # corners in rods, illustrative
            x0, y0 = corners[0]
            twice_area = 0
            triangles = 0
            for i in range(1, len(corners) - 1):
                x1, y1 = corners[i]
                x2, y2 = corners[i + 1]
                twice_area += (x1 - x0) * (y2 - y0) - (x2 - x0) * (y1 - y0)
                triangles += 1
            print("triangles:", triangles)
            print("area in square rods:", twice_area // 2)
            print("acres:", twice_area / 320)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1206: the strike times of al-Jazari's pegged drum, in Python and in C. */
val db84Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 84,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Automata",
        title = "The strike times of al-Jazari's pegged drum in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Pegged drum",
        author = "Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari",
        year = 1206,
        summary = "Pegs on a turning drum set when each hammer strikes in al-Jazari's 1206 band, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same strike times.",
        details = "The example is illustrative: it sets four pegs at chosen angles on a drum that turns once every four seconds, and both programs print the time of each strike. The run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### pegs.py
            PEG_ANGLES = [30, 120, 210, 300]   # illustrative peg positions, in degrees
            TURN_SECONDS = 4.0                  # one full turn of the drum
            for peg, angle in enumerate(PEG_ANGLES, start=1):
                strike = angle / 360 * TURN_SECONDS
                print(f"peg {peg} strikes at {strike:.3f} s")
            ### pegs.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const int peg_angles[] = {30, 120, 210, 300};   /* illustrative peg positions, in degrees */
                const double turn_seconds = 4.0;                /* one full turn of the drum */
                for (int peg = 0; peg < 4; peg++) {
                    double strike = peg_angles[peg] / 360.0 * turn_seconds;
                    printf("peg %d strikes at %.3f s\n", peg + 1, strike);
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 pegs.py > python.txt
            cc -o pegs_c pegs.c
            ./pegs_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Examples of 1200 to 1210: the days between the sack of Constantinople in 1204 and its recovery in 1261, counted by a Julian day number. */
val db84Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 84,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "Days from the sack of Constantinople to its recovery in 1261",
        originalTitle = "Days between two dates",
        author = "The Fourth Crusade and Michael VIII Palaiologos",
        year = 1204,
        summary = "The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in April 1204 and Michael VIII retook it on 25 July 1261, and a short program counts the days between the two dates.",
        details = "Both dates are given in the Julian calendar, which was in use at the time, and the program converts them with a Julian day number formula so that the count does not depend on the calendar of the computer. Accounts give 12 or 13 April for the breach of the walls, so the count uses 13 April, the date most often given.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as constantinople_days.py.
            2. Run it: python3 constantinople_days.py
        """,
        example = """
            def julian_day_number(year, month, day):
                # January and February count as months 13 and 14 of the year before
                a = (14 - month) // 12
                y = year + 4800 - a
                m = month + 12 * a - 3
                return day + (153 * m + 2) // 5 + 365 * y + y // 4 - 32083

            sack = julian_day_number(1204, 4, 13)
            recovery = julian_day_number(1261, 7, 25)
            print("days from the sack to the recovery:", recovery - sack)
        """,
    ),

)

        title = "Checking that the early sultans of Delhi reigned in turn",
        originalTitle = "Reign list",
        author = "The sultans of Delhi",
        year = 1206,
        summary = "A short program takes four reigns of the early Delhi sultanate, prints each reign's length and the gap between each pair of reigns, so an overlap would show as a negative number.",
        details = "The reign dates are the ones commonly given for these four rulers, and the list is used only to test the program's logic on a short run. A gap of zero means that one reign ended in the year the next began.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as sultans_reigns.py.
            2. Run it: python3 sultans_reigns.py
        """,
        example = """
            reigns = [
                ("Aibak", 1206, 1210),
                ("Aram Shah", 1210, 1211),
                ("Iltutmish", 1211, 1236),
                ("Razia", 1236, 1240),
            ]
            for name, start, end in reigns:
                print(name, "reign length:", end - start)
            for (name_a, _, end), (name_b, start, _) in zip(reigns, reigns[1:]):
                print("gap between", name_a, "and", name_b + ":", start - end)
            print("reigns checked:", len(reigns))
        """,
    ),

)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db85Cross.kt

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1190 and 1191: the days from the drowning of Frederick Barbarossa to the surrender of Acre, counted in Python and in C. */
val db85Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 85,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Time",
        title = "Days from Frederick Barbarossa's death to the surrender of Acre, in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Days between two events",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 1191,
        summary = "Frederick Barbarossa drowned on 10 June 1190 and Acre surrendered on 12 July 1191, and a Python and a C program each count the days between the two dates.",
        details = "The C program counts days with a day-count formula written out by hand, and the run script checks that both programs print 397 days. The dates are given in the reckoning of the time, and the count is the same in the Julian and Gregorian calendars because no century year falls between them.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### acre.py
            from datetime import date

            start = date(1190, 6, 10)   # Frederick Barbarossa's death
            end = date(1191, 7, 12)     # surrender of Acre
            print("days:", (end - start).days)
            ### acre.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            /* Days since the start of the proleptic Gregorian era, by Howard Hinnant's day-count method. */
            static long days_from_civil(long y, unsigned m, unsigned d) {
                y -= m <= 2;
                long era = (y >= 0 ? y : y - 399) / 400;
                unsigned yoe = (unsigned)(y - era * 400);
                unsigned doy = (153 * (m > 2 ? m - 3 : m + 9) + 2) / 5 + d - 1;
                unsigned doe = yoe * 365 + yoe / 4 - yoe / 100 + doy;
                return era * 146097 + (long)doe - 719468;
            }

            int main(void) {
                long start = days_from_civil(1190, 6, 10);   /* Frederick Barbarossa's death */
                long end = days_from_civil(1191, 7, 12);     /* surrender of Acre */
                printf("days: %ld\n", end - start);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 acre.py > python.txt
            cc -o acre_c acre.c
            ./acre_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        details = "The table uses a radius of sixty units, the scale of Ptolemy's tables, with rounded values. Linear interpolation is an approximation: at 75 degrees the program prints 56, while the true value is about 58, so the answer is close but not exact.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as sine_table.py.
            2. Run it: python3 sine_table.py
        """,
        example = """
            SINE = {0: 0, 30: 30, 45: 42, 60: 52, 90: 60}   # radius 60, rounded values

            def sine_between(angle):
                lower = max(a for a in SINE if a <= angle)
                upper = min(b for b in SINE if b >= angle)
                return SINE[lower] + (angle - lower) * (SINE[upper] - SINE[lower]) // (upper - lower)

            for angle in [40, 75]:
                print(f"{angle} degrees: {sine_between(angle)}")
        """,

        year = 1190,
        summary = "A Latin hexameter has six feet, each a dactyl or a spondee, and a short program names the feet of a line given as long and short syllables.",
        details = "A dactyl is a long syllable followed by two short ones, and a spondee is two long syllables. The program reads a line of seventeen syllables, long and short, and names each foot in turn, so it does not handle the other forms the sixth foot can take.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as hexameter.py.
            2. Run it: python3 hexameter.py
        """,
        example = """
            LINE = "LSSLSSLSSLSSLSSLL"   # L long, S short, one letter per syllable
            feet = []
            pos = 0
            while pos < len(LINE):
                if LINE[pos:pos + 3] == "LSS":
                    feet.append("dactyl")
                    pos += 3
                elif LINE[pos:pos + 2] == "LL":
                    feet.append("spondee")
                    pos += 2
                else:
                    feet.append("not a foot")
                    break
            for number, foot in enumerate(feet, start=1):
                print(f"foot {number}: {foot}")
            print(f"feet: {feet.count('dactyl')} dactyls and {feet.count('spondee')} spondee")
        """,
    ),

)

    entry(
        databaseId = 85,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Crusades",
        title = "Deaths of five rulers from 1189 to 1199, in date order",
        originalTitle = "Deaths in date order",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 1199,
        summary = "Five rulers of the late twelfth century died between 1189 and 1199, and a short program sorts their deaths by date and counts the days between them.",
        details = "The dates are the usual ones: Henry II in July 1189, Frederick Barbarossa in June 1190, Saladin in March 1193, Henry VI in September 1197 and Richard I in April 1199. The program uses Python's calendar, and its day counts match the Julian reckoning of the time, because no century year falls between these dates.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as deaths.py.
            2. Run it: python3 deaths.py
        """,
        example = """
            from datetime import date

            deaths = [
                ("Henry II", date(1189, 7, 6)),
                ("Frederick Barbarossa", date(1190, 6, 10)),
                ("Saladin", date(1193, 3, 4)),
                ("Henry VI", date(1197, 9, 28)),
                ("Richard I", date(1199, 4, 6)),
            ]
            deaths.sort(key=lambda item: item[1])
            previous = None
            for name, day in deaths:
                if previous is None:
                    print(day.isoformat(), name)
                else:
                    print(day.isoformat(), name, (day - previous).days, "days later")
                previous = day
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 85,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Coronations",

        originalTitle = "Coronation dates",

        details = "The dates are 19 December 1154, 3 September 1189 and 27 May 1199, as commonly given, and the day counts hold in both the Julian and the Gregorian reckonings because no century year lies between them. The program lists each king with the days that passed before the next coronation.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as coronations.py.
            2. Run it: python3 coronations.py
        """,
        example = """
            from datetime import date

            crownings = [
                ("Henry II", date(1154, 12, 19)),
                ("Richard I", date(1189, 9, 3)),
                ("John", date(1199, 5, 27)),
            ]
            for (first_name, first), (second_name, second) in zip(crownings, crownings[1:]):

        """,
    ),

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db86Cross.kt

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1180: the pulverizer for a linear congruence, written in Python and in C. */
val db86Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 86,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Congruences",
        title = "Solving 13x = 3 modulo 25 by the pulverizer in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Kuttaka",
        author = "Brahmagupta and Bhaskara II",
        year = 1180,
        summary = "The pulverizer, an Indian method for solving congruences, finds x in 13x = 3 modulo 25, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same answer.",
        details = "Brahmagupta described the method in 628, and Bhaskara II taught it again in his treatise of 1150, so the year 1180 stands for its use in the twelfth century. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, and the answer x = 6 can be checked by hand, since 13 times 6 is 78 and 78 leaves 3 when divided by 25.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### pulverize.py
            a, c, m = 13, 3, 25
            old_r, r = a, m
            old_s, s = 1, 0
            while r != 0:
                q = old_r // r
                old_r, r = r, old_r - q * r
                old_s, s = s, old_s - q * s
            g, p = old_r, old_s
            x = (c // g * p) % m
            print("gcd", g)
            print("x", x)
            print("check", a * x % m)
            ### pulverize.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int a = 13, c = 3, m = 25;
                int old_r = a, r = m;
                int old_s = 1, s = 0;
                while (r != 0) {
                    int q = old_r / r;
                    int t = old_r - q * r;
                    old_r = r;
                    r = t;
                    t = old_s - q * s;
                    old_s = s;
                    s = t;
                }
                int g = old_r;
                int p = old_s;
                int x = ((c / g) * p) % m;
                if (x < 0) x += m;
                printf("gcd %d\n", g);
                printf("x %d\n", x);
                printf("check %d\n", (a * x) % m);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 pulverize.py > python.txt
            cc -o pulverize_c pulverize.c
            ./pulverize_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        """,
        example = """
            a = [6, 8, 1, 1]   # units first, for 1186
            b = [5, 4, 3, 2]   # units first, for 2345
            names = ["units", "tens", "hundreds", "thousands"]
            lines = [a[i] + b[i] for i in range(4)]
            carry = 0
            for i in range(4):
                total = lines[i] + carry
                carry = total // 10
                left = total % 10
                print(names[i], total, "left", left, "carry", carry)
                lines[i] = left
            result = sum(d * 10 ** i for i, d in enumerate(lines))

            n = 1185
            root = 0

                digit = 0
                while (root + (digit + 1) * place) ** 3 <= n:
                    digit += 1
                root += digit * place
            print("cube root of", n, "is", root, "remainder", n - root ** 3)
            print("check", root ** 3 + (n - root ** 3))
        """,
    ),

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1170: the perfect consonances of a two-part organum, counted in Python and in C. */
val db87Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 87,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Music",
        title = "Perfect consonances in a two-part organum, counted in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Organum consonances",
        author = "Singers and teachers of Notre-Dame",
        year = 1170,
        summary = "Perfect consonances in two-part organum are the unison, fourth, fifth and octave, and a script checks that the Python and C programs count the same perfect and imperfect points.",
        details = "The intervals in the example are illustrative and are given in semitones, so the unison is zero and the octave twelve. The run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### organum.py
            INTERVALS = [7, 4, 5, 12, 3, 0, 7]   # illustrative intervals between the two voices, in semitones
            PERFECT = {0, 5, 7, 12}              # unison, fourth, fifth and octave
            perfect = [i for i in INTERVALS if i in PERFECT]
            imperfect = [i for i in INTERVALS if i not in PERFECT]
            print("points:", len(INTERVALS))
            print("perfect consonances:", len(perfect))
            print("imperfect consonances:", len(imperfect))
            print("first imperfect point:", INTERVALS.index(imperfect[0]) + 1, "with", imperfect[0], "semitones")
            ### organum.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                int intervals[] = {7, 4, 5, 12, 3, 0, 7};   /* illustrative intervals, in semitones */
                int n = 7;
                int perfect = 0, imperfect = 0, first = 0, first_value = 0;
                for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                    int p = intervals[i] == 0 || intervals[i] == 5 || intervals[i] == 7 || intervals[i] == 12;
                    if (p) {
                        perfect++;
                    } else {
                        imperfect++;
                        if (first == 0) {
                            first = i + 1;
                            first_value = intervals[i];
                        }
                    }
                }
                printf("points: %d\n", n);
                printf("perfect consonances: %d\n", perfect);
                printf("imperfect consonances: %d\n", imperfect);
                printf("first imperfect point: %d with %d semitones\n", first, first_value);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 organum.py > python.txt
            cc -o organum_c organum.c
            ./organum_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

        databaseId = 87,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Roads",
        title = "Counting the days of a pilgrimage road to Santiago, stage by stage",
        originalTitle = "Pilgrimage road",
        author = "Pilgrims on the Way of Saint James",
        year = 1170,
        summary = "A pilgrimage road is planned as a list of stages, and a short program adds up the miles and the days of an illustrative road to Santiago de Compostela.",
        details = "The stage lengths and the daily distance are illustrative and are not taken from a surviving itinerary, so only the arithmetic is meant to be checked. Each stage is rounded up to whole days of travel.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as pilgrim_road.py.
            2. Run it: python3 pilgrim_road.py
        """,
        example = """
            # illustrative stages of a road to Santiago, in miles, not from a surviving itinerary
            STAGES = [("first stage", 120), ("second stage", 90), ("third stage", 150)]
            MILES_PER_DAY = 30   # illustrative daily distance
            total_miles = 0
            total_days = 0
            for name, miles in STAGES:
                days = -(-miles // MILES_PER_DAY)   # whole days of travel, rounded up
                total_miles += miles
                total_days += days
                print(name, miles, "miles", days, "days")
            print("total miles", total_miles)
            print("total days", total_days)
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiment of 1170: the water held by a tide mill's pond in one tide, computed in Python and C with illustrative numbers. */
val db88Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 88,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Water power",
        title = "The water held by a tide mill's pond in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Tide pond",
        author = "Medieval millers",
        year = 1170,
        summary = "A tide mill's pond holds water from one tide, and a script checks that the Python and C programs print the same volume and milling hours.",
        details = "The pond area, the head of water and the rate of release are illustrative numbers, not measurements of the Woodbridge mill, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line. The example multiplies area by head to get the volume and divides by the release rate to get the hours of milling.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the script: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### pond.py
            AREA = 500       # square metres of pond, illustrative
            HEAD = 2         # metres of water held on the ebb, illustrative
            RATE = 100       # cubic metres let out each hour, illustrative
            volume = AREA * HEAD
            print("water held:", volume, "cubic metres")
            print("hours of milling:", volume // RATE)
            print("water in two tides:", 2 * volume, "cubic metres")
            ### pond.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                const int area = 500;   /* square metres of pond, illustrative */
                const int head = 2;     /* metres of water held on the ebb, illustrative */
                const int rate = 100;   /* cubic metres let out each hour, illustrative */
                int volume = area * head;
                printf("water held: %d cubic metres\n", volume);
                printf("hours of milling: %d\n", volume / rate);
                printf("water in two tides: %d cubic metres\n", 2 * volume);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 pond.py > python.txt
            cc -o pond_c pond.c
            ./pond_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Examples of 1160 to 1170: the day number of Becket's death in the Julian reckoning, converted to the Gregorian date. */
val db88Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 88,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Dates",
        title = "The Julian date of Becket's death, counted in the Gregorian calendar",
        originalTitle = "Julian day number",
        author = "The Julian and Gregorian calendars",
        year = 1170,
        summary = "Becket was murdered on 29 December 1170 by the Julian reckoning in use in England, and a short program turns that day into its Gregorian date, 5 January 1171.",
        details = "England followed the Julian calendar in the twelfth century, and the Gregorian calendar then ran seven days ahead of it. The example computes the day number of the Julian date and converts that number back to a Gregorian date, so the seven-day gap appears in the output.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as becket_gregorian.py.
            2. Run it: python3 becket_gregorian.py
        """,
        example = """
            from datetime import date

            def julian_day_number(year, month, day):
                # day number of a date written in the Julian calendar
                a = (14 - month) // 12
                y = year + 4800 - a
                m = month + 12 * a - 3
                return day + (153 * m + 2) // 5 + 365 * y + y // 4 - 32083

            def gregorian_date(day_number):
                # the Gregorian calendar date with this day number
                return date.fromordinal(day_number - 1721425)

            number = julian_day_number(1170, 12, 29)
            same_day = gregorian_date(number)
            print("day number of 29 December 1170 (Julian):", number)
            print("the same day in the Gregorian calendar:", same_day.isoformat())
            print("days added by the calendar change:", (same_day - date(1170, 12, 29)).days)
        """,
    ),

)

        year = 1160,
        summary = "A short program lists which claimants held the papal see in each year from 1160 to 1170 and totals the claimant-years of the schism.",
        details = "The list gives Alexander III, Victor IV, Paschal III and Callixtus III, with each reign shown from its first year to its last, and years are counted whole. Three claimants held the see in 1164 and in 1168, and the program prints a total of 24 claimant-years for the decade.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as popes.py.
            2. Run it: python3 popes.py
        """,
        example = """
            CLAIMANTS = [
                ("Alexander III", 1159, 1181),
                ("Victor IV", 1159, 1164),
                ("Paschal III", 1164, 1168),
                ("Callixtus III", 1168, 1178),
            ]
            total = 0
            three = []
            for year in range(1160, 1171):
                holders = [name for name, start, end in CLAIMANTS if start <= year <= end]
                total += len(holders)
                if len(holders) == 3:

                print(year, len(holders), ", ".join(holders))

            print("years with three claimants:", three)
        """,
    ),

        databaseId = 88,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,

        summary = "A short program measures the reigns of three emperors and counts the years each reign lies inside the decade from 1160 to 1170.",
        details = "Nijo reigned from 1158 to 1165, Rokujo from 1165 to 1168 and Takakura from 1168 to 1180, so the three reigns meet without overlap inside the decade. The program prints each reign's full span and its part inside the decade, and the parts add up to ten years.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as emperors.py.
            2. Run it: python3 emperors.py
        """,
        example = """
            REIGNS = [("Nijo", 1158, 1165), ("Rokujo", 1165, 1168), ("Takakura", 1168, 1180)]
            DECADE_START = 1160
            DECADE_END = 1170
            total = 0
            for name, start, end in REIGNS:
                span = end - start
                inside = min(end, DECADE_END) - max(start, DECADE_START)
                total += inside
                print(name, start, end, "span", span, "inside", inside)
            print("years inside the decade:", total)
        """,

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1150 to 1160: Bhaskara's peacock riddle and the primes of the decade, each in Python and C. */
val db89Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 89,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Puzzles",
        title = "The peacock flock of Bhaskara's riddle in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Peacock riddle",
        author = "Bhaskara II",
        year = 1150,
        summary = "A riddle of Bhaskara's Lilavati asks for a flock whose parts add up to the whole, and a script checks that the Python and C programs both find the flock of 72.",
        details = "The riddle asks for the square root of half the flock, eight ninths of it, and two more birds, which together make the whole flock. The programs test every multiple of 18 up to 200, and the run script compares the two outputs line by line.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder as peacock.py, peacock.c and run.sh.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### peacock.py
            from math import isqrt

            for flock in range(1, 201):
                if flock % 18:
                    continue                  # half the flock and eight ninths must both be whole numbers
                root = isqrt(flock // 2)      # square root of half the flock
                if root * root == flock // 2 and root + 8 * flock // 9 + 2 == flock:
                    print("flock:", flock)
                    print("checked:", root, "+", 8 * flock // 9, "+", 2, "=", flock)
            ### peacock.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int main(void) {
                for (int flock = 1; flock <= 200; flock++) {
                    if (flock % 18 != 0) continue;   /* half the flock and eight ninths must be whole numbers */
                    int half = flock / 2;
                    int root = 0;
                    while ((root + 1) * (root + 1) <= half) root++;   /* whole square root of half the flock */
                    int eight_ninths = 8 * flock / 9;
                    if (root * root == half && root + eight_ninths + 2 == flock) {
                        printf("flock: %d\n", flock);
                        printf("checked: %d + %d + %d = %d\n", root, eight_ninths, 2, flock);
                    }
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 peacock.py > python.txt
            cc -o peacock_c peacock.c
            ./peacock_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 89,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "Numbers",
        title = "The primes of the years 1150 to 1160 in Python and C",
        originalTitle = "Prime test by trial division",
        author = "No single author",
        year = 1155,
        summary = "The years from 1150 to 1160 include two primes, 1151 and 1153, and a script checks that the Python and C programs find the same two by trial division.",
        details = "The programs test each year by dividing it by every number up to its square root, and they print the primes and then their count. The run script compares the two outputs line by line, and the result is the same on every run.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder as primes.py, primes.c and run.sh.
            2. Run it: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### primes.py
            def is_prime(n):
                if n < 2:
                    return False
                d = 2
                while d * d <= n:
                    if n % d == 0:
                        return False
                    d += 1
                return True

            primes = [n for n in range(1150, 1161) if is_prime(n)]
            for p in primes:
                print(p)
            print("count:", len(primes))
            ### primes.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            int is_prime(int n) {
                if (n < 2) return 0;
                for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
                    if (n % d == 0) return 0;
                }
                return 1;
            }

            int main(void) {
                int count = 0;
                for (int n = 1150; n <= 1160; n++) {
                    if (is_prime(n)) {
                        printf("%d\n", n);
                        count++;
                    }
                }
                printf("count: %d\n", count);
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            python3 primes.py > python.txt
            cc -o primes_c primes.c
            ./primes_c > c.txt
            cat python.txt
            diff python.txt c.txt && echo "same result"
        """,
    ),

)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind

/** Guides of 1150 to 1160: the rule of three, the rules of signs, pulley blocks in a water clock, the climates of a world map and Bhaskara's lotus problem. */
val db89Guides: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 89,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Roots",
        title = "How the Indian digit method finds the whole square root of a number",
        originalTitle = "Square root by digit pairs",
        author = "Aryabhata and Indian arithmetic of the 1150s",
        year = 1150,
        summary = "The Indian digit method takes a square root two digits at a time, and a short program applies it to three numbers and checks each against an exact integer root.",
        details = "Aryabhata gave the rule in 499, and it was still taught in Indian arithmetic in the 1150s. The example groups the digits in pairs, finds each root digit by trying the largest digit that fits, and reports the whole root and the remainder for each number.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as digit_root.py.
            2. Run it: python3 digit_root.py
        """,
        example = """
            from math import isqrt

            def digit_root(n):
                # digit pairs from the right; each step takes the largest digit that keeps the square inside the remainder
                pairs = []
                while n > 0:
                    pairs.append(n % 100)
                    n //= 100
                pairs.reverse()
                root, rest = 0, 0
                for pair in pairs:
                    rest = rest * 100 + pair
                    d = 0
                    while (20 * root + (d + 1)) * (d + 1) <= rest:
                        d += 1
                    rest -= (20 * root + d) * d
                    root = root * 10 + d
                return root, rest

            for number in (1154, 2025, 1150):
                root, remainder = digit_root(number)
                print(number, "root", root, "remainder", remainder, "matches isqrt:", root == isqrt(number) and remainder == number - root * root)
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 89,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Signs",
        title = "How the rules of signs give the product of two negative numbers",
        originalTitle = "Rules of signs",
        author = "Brahmagupta and Bhaskara II",
        year = 1150,
        summary = "The rules of signs say that a negative times a negative is positive, and a short program applies them to four products and checks each against Python's own multiplication.",
        details = "Brahmagupta stated the rules for adding and multiplying positive and negative quantities in 628, and Bhaskara II's Bijaganita of 1150 repeats them for algebra. The example applies the rules to four products and prints whether each result agrees with ordinary multiplication, so the sign rule is tested rather than assumed.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as signs.py.
            2. Run it: python3 signs.py
        """,
        example = """
            def sign_product(p, q):
                # rule of signs: like signs give a positive product, unlike signs a negative one
                magnitude = abs(p) * abs(q)
                negative = (p < 0) != (q < 0)
                return -magnitude if negative else magnitude

            for p, q in [(-3, -4), (-3, 4), (3, -4), (3, 4)]:
                value = sign_product(p, q)
                print(f"({p}) x ({q}) = {value}, matches: {value == p * q}")
        """,
    ),

    entry(

        details = "The problem is one of the riddles in Bhaskara II's Lilavati, and its answer is a depth of three and three quarter cubits. The example uses exact fractions and checks that the depth fits the right triangle, so the result does not depend on rounding.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as lotus.py.

        """,
        example = """
            from fractions import Fraction

            distance = Fraction(2)          # cubits the flower is pushed sideways
            stalk_above = Fraction(1, 2)    # cubits of stalk above the water
            depth = (distance ** 2 - stalk_above ** 2) / (2 * stalk_above)
            print("depth in cubits:", depth, "=", float(depth))

            print("the right triangle fits:", check)

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Cross-code experiments of 1970 to 1980: a C encoder checked by Python, and a C factoring program reported by a shell pipeline. */
val db8Cross: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "C and Python",
        title = "C and Python: an LZ78 round trip",
        originalTitle = "LZ78 encoding in C, decoding in Python (Ziv and Lempel, 1978)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1978,
        summary = "A C program encodes text with LZ78, and a Python script decodes the tokens it prints and checks that the original text comes back.",
        details = "The encoder keeps its dictionary as a trie, a table of child nodes for each character, and prints one token per phrase. The decoder rebuilds the phrases from the tokens. The two programs share only the format of the tokens.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Compile the encoder: cc -o lz78 lz78.c
            3. Run the round trip: python3 roundtrip.py
        """,
        example = """
            ### lz78.c
            #include <stdio.h>
            #include <string.h>

            #define MAX_NODES 256

            /* LZ78 encoder: one "index character" line per phrase, with a trie of the phrases. */
            static int child[MAX_NODES][256];

            int main(void) {
                int next_index = 1;   /* index 0 is the empty phrase */
                int node = 0;
                int c;
                memset(child, 0, sizeof(child));
                while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) {
                    if (child[node][c] != 0) {
                        node = child[node][c];
                    } else {
                        printf("%d %c\n", node, c);
                        child[node][c] = next_index++;
                        node = 0;
                    }
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### roundtrip.py
            import subprocess

            text = "abababababab"
            result = subprocess.run(["./lz78"], input=text, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
            tokens = []
            for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
                index, ch = line.split()
                tokens.append((int(index), ch))

            entries = [""]
            pieces = []
            for index, ch in tokens:
                phrase = entries[index] + ch
                entries.append(phrase)
                pieces.append(phrase)

            print("tokens:", tokens)
            print("round trip ok:", "".join(pieces) == text)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.CROSS,
        section = "C and awk",
        title = "A factoring pipeline: C and awk",
        originalTitle = "Pollard's rho in C, reported by awk (1975)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example, after Pollard's method",
        year = 1975,
        summary = "A C program factors numbers with Pollard's rho method, and awk turns its output into a report, all in one shell pipeline.",
        details = "The factoring runs in C with 64-bit arithmetic, and each line of its output is a number with its two factors, smallest first. awk only formats the report, so the work is split between two tools that each do what they are good at.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the files below in one folder.
            2. Run the pipeline: sh run.sh
        """,
        example = """
            ### factor.c
            #include <stdio.h>

            static unsigned long long gcd(unsigned long long a, unsigned long long b) {
                while (b) {
                    unsigned long long t = a % b;
                    a = b;
                    b = t;
                }
                return a;
            }

            static unsigned long long rho(unsigned long long n) {
                unsigned long long c;
                for (c = 1; ; c++) {
                    unsigned long long x = 2, y = 2, d = 1;
                    while (d == 1) {
                        x = (x * x + c) % n;
                        y = (y * y + c) % n;
                        y = (y * y + c) % n;
                        d = gcd(x > y ? x - y : y - x, n);
                    }
                    if (d != n) {
                        return d;
                    }
                }
            }

            int main(void) {
                unsigned long long n;
                while (scanf("%llu", &n) == 1) {
                    unsigned long long f = rho(n);
                    unsigned long long g = n / f;
                    if (f > g) {
                        unsigned long long t = f;
                        f = g;
                        g = t;
                    }
                    printf("%llu %llu %llu\n", n, f, g);
                }
                return 0;
            }
            ### run.sh
            printf '8051\n10403\n1000001\n' > numbers.txt
            cc -O2 -o factor factor.c
            ./factor < numbers.txt | awk '{ printf "%s = %s x %s\n", $1, $2, $3 }'
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),
)

# FILE: RetroDatabases/app/src/main/java/com/example/retrodatabases/data/seed/Db8Examples.kt

package com.example.retrodatabases.data.seed

import com.example.retrodatabases.data.Kind
import com.example.retrodatabases.data.RecordEntity

/** Examples of 1970 to 1980: classic algorithms of the decade, each with a short program that prints a checkable result. */
val db8Examples: List<RecordEntity> = listOf(

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Strings",
        title = "Boyer–Moore string search",
        originalTitle = "A fast string searching algorithm (Boyer and Moore, 1977)",
        author = "Robert Boyer and J Strother Moore",
        year = 1977,
        summary = "A string search that compares from the end of the pattern and skips ahead with a bad-character table, so many characters of the text are never looked at.",
        details = "Boyer and Moore published the method in 1977. The example uses the bad-character rule only, and prints the positions where the pattern occurs, including overlapping matches.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as boyer_moore.py.
            2. Run it: python3 boyer_moore.py
        """,
        example = """
            def boyer_moore(text, pattern):
                # Bad-character table: the last position of each letter in the pattern.
                last = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(pattern)}
                found = []
                shift = 0
                while shift <= len(text) - len(pattern):
                    j = len(pattern) - 1
                    while j >= 0 and pattern[j] == text[shift + j]:
                        j -= 1
                    if j < 0:
                        found.append(shift)
                        shift += 1
                    else:
                        shift += max(1, j - last.get(text[shift + j], -1))
                return found

            print(boyer_moore("here is a simple example", "example"))
            print(boyer_moore("abababa", "aba"))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Strings",
        title = "Aho–Corasick multiple search",
        originalTitle = "Efficient string matching: an aid to bibliographic search (1975)",
        author = "Alfred Aho and Margaret Corasick",
        year = 1975,
        summary = "A search for many patterns at once: a trie of the patterns with failure links, so the text is read in one pass whatever the number of patterns.",
        details = "Aho and Corasick published the method in 1975, for searching a bibliography for a set of keywords. The example finds four patterns in one word and prints where each one starts.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as aho_corasick.py.
            2. Run it: python3 aho_corasick.py
        """,
        example = """
            from collections import deque

            def build(patterns):
                goto = [{}]
                out = [set()]
                for p in patterns:
                    node = 0
                    for ch in p:
                        if ch not in goto[node]:
                            goto.append({})
                            out.append(set())
                            goto[node][ch] = len(goto) - 1
                        node = goto[node][ch]
                    out[node].add(p)
                fail = [0] * len(goto)
                queue = deque()
                for child in goto[0].values():
                    queue.append(child)
                while queue:
                    node = queue.popleft()
                    for ch, child in goto[node].items():
                        queue.append(child)
                        f = fail[node]
                        while f and ch not in goto[f]:
                            f = fail[f]
                        fail[child] = goto[f].get(ch, 0)
                        out[child] |= out[fail[child]]
                return goto, fail, out

            def search(text, patterns):
                goto, fail, out = build(patterns)
                matches = []
                node = 0
                for i, ch in enumerate(text):
                    while node and ch not in goto[node]:
                        node = fail[node]
                    node = goto[node].get(ch, 0)
                    for p in out[node]:
                        matches.append((i - len(p) + 1, p))
                return sorted(matches)

            print(search("ushers", ["he", "she", "his", "hers"]))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Number theory",
        title = "Pollard's rho factoring",
        originalTitle = "A Monte Carlo method for factorization (Pollard, 1975)",
        author = "John Pollard",
        year = 1975,
        summary = "A factoring method that runs a pseudo-random sequence modulo the number, and uses a greatest common divisor to catch a factor when two runners meet.",
        details = "Pollard published the method in 1975. It finds small factors quickly and needs no table of primes. The example factors two numbers, each the product of two primes.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as pollard.py.
            2. Run it: python3 pollard.py
        """,
        example = """
            from math import gcd

            def pollard_rho(n):
                # Two runners step through x -> x*x + c modulo n; their difference shares a factor with n when they meet.
                if n % 2 == 0:
                    return 2
                c = 1
                while True:
                    x = y = 2
                    d = 1
                    while d == 1:
                        x = (x * x + c) % n
                        y = (y * y + c) % n
                        y = (y * y + c) % n
                        d = gcd(abs(x - y), n)
                    if d != n:
                        return d
                    c += 1

            for n in [8051, 10403]:
                f = pollard_rho(n)
                print(n, "=", min(f, n // f), "*", max(f, n // f))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Number theory",
        title = "Miller–Rabin primality test",
        originalTitle = "Miller–Rabin test (Miller, 1976; Rabin, 1980)",
        author = "Gary Miller and Michael Rabin",
        year = 1976,
        summary = "A test that checks whether a number behaves like a prime under powers of several bases; with the fixed bases used here it is reliable for every number in a large range.",
        details = "Miller described the test in 1976, and Rabin's randomised version followed in 1980. The example uses six fixed bases, which are enough for every number up to about 3.47 times ten to the twelfth.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as miller_rabin.py.
            2. Run it: python3 miller_rabin.py
        """,
        example = """
            def is_prime(n):
                if n < 2:
                    return False
                for p in [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13]:
                    if n % p == 0:
                        return n == p
                d, s = n - 1, 0
                while d % 2 == 0:
                    d //= 2
                    s += 1
                for a in [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13]:
                    x = pow(a, d, n)
                    if x in (1, n - 1):
                        continue
                    for _ in range(s - 1):
                        x = x * x % n
                        if x == n - 1:
                            break
                    else:
                        return False
                return True

            print([n for n in range(2, 50) if is_prime(n)])
            print(is_prime(1000003), is_prime(1000001))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Graphs",
        title = "Tarjan's strongly connected components",
        originalTitle = "Depth-first search and linear graph algorithms (Tarjan, 1972)",
        author = "Robert Tarjan",
        year = 1972,
        summary = "Finds the strongly connected components of a directed graph in one depth-first search, using a stack and low-link numbers.",
        details = "Tarjan published the algorithm in 1972. A component is complete when a node's low-link number equals its own index, and the nodes above it on the stack form the component. The example finds three components in a small graph.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as tarjan.py.
            2. Run it: python3 tarjan.py
        """,
        example = """
            def tarjan(graph):
                index, low = {}, {}
                stack, on_stack = [], set()
                result = []
                counter = [0]

                def visit(v):
                    index[v] = low[v] = counter[0]
                    counter[0] += 1
                    stack.append(v)
                    on_stack.add(v)
                    for w in graph.get(v, []):
                        if w not in index:
                            visit(w)
                            low[v] = min(low[v], low[w])
                        elif w in on_stack:
                            low[v] = min(low[v], index[w])
                    if low[v] == index[v]:
                        component = []
                        while True:
                            w = stack.pop()
                            on_stack.discard(w)
                            component.append(w)
                            if w == v:
                                break
                        result.append(sorted(component))

                for v in sorted(graph):
                    if v not in index:
                        visit(v)
                return sorted(result)

            graph = {1: [2], 2: [3], 3: [1, 4], 4: [5], 5: [6], 6: [4], 7: [6]}
            print(tarjan(graph))
        """,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.EXAMPLE,
        section = "Compression",
        title = "LZ78 compression",
        originalTitle = "Compression of individual sequences via variable-rate coding (Ziv and Lempel, 1978)",
        author = "Jacob Ziv and Abraham Lempel",
        year = 1978,
        summary = "A compression method that builds a dictionary of phrases as it reads, and writes each new phrase as the index of a known phrase plus one character.",
        details = "Ziv and Lempel published the method in 1978. The decoder rebuilds the same dictionary from the tokens alone, so no table is sent with the data. The example encodes a repeated text and decodes it back.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as lz78.py.
            2. Run it: python3 lz78.py
        """,
        example = """
            def lz78_encode(text):
                dictionary = {"": 0}
                output = []
                current = ""
                for ch in text:
                    if current + ch in dictionary:
                        current += ch
                    else:
                        output.append((dictionary[current], ch))
                        dictionary[current + ch] = len(dictionary)
                        current = ""
                if current:
                    output.append((dictionary[current], ""))
                return output

            def lz78_decode(tokens):
                entries = [""]
                pieces = []
                for index, ch in tokens:
                    phrase = entries[index] + ch
                    entries.append(phrase)
                    pieces.append(phrase)
                return "".join(pieces)

            tokens = lz78_encode("abababababab")
            print(tokens)
            print(lz78_decode(tokens) == "abababababab")
        """,
    ),
)

            # Four bands of four rows each, from dark grey to white.
            WIDTH, HEIGHT = 32, 16
            image = [[[0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0][y // 4] for _ in range(WIDTH)] for y in range(HEIGHT)]
            for y in range(HEIGHT):
                for x in range(WIDTH):
                    old = image[y][x]
                    new = 1.0 if old >= 0.5 else 0.0
                    error = old - new
                    image[y][x] = new
                    if x + 1 < WIDTH:
                        image[y][x + 1] += error * 7 / 16
                    if y + 1 < HEIGHT:
                        if x > 0:

            for row in image:

            import random

            random.seed(1975)
            trials = 100000
            stay_wins = switch_wins = 0
            for _ in range(trials):
                car = random.randrange(3)
                pick = random.randrange(3)
                # The host opens a door that is neither the pick nor the car.
                opened = next(d for d in range(3) if d != pick and d != car)
                switched = next(d for d in range(3) if d != pick and d != opened)
                stay_wins += pick == car
                switch_wins += switched == car
            print(f"stay: {stay_wins / trials:.3f}")

        """,

            def local(p):
                clock[p] += 1
                print(f"{p} local event: clock {clock[p]}")

            def send(p):
                clock[p] += 1
                print(f"{p} sends with clock {clock[p]}")
                return clock[p]

            def receive(p, stamp):
                clock[p] = max(clock[p], stamp) + 1

        year = 1974,
        summary = "A join matches the rows of two tables on a shared column. The simplest method checks every pair of rows, and System R's optimiser chose cheaper methods when it could.",
        details = "The example joins two small tables by checking each employee against each department. The result has one row for each matching pair, with the columns of both tables.",
        instructions = """

            2. Run it: python3 join.py
        """,
        example = """
            employees = [
                {"name": "Ann", "dept": 10},
                {"name": "Bob", "dept": 20},
                {"name": "Cy", "dept": 10},
            ]
            departments = [
                {"dept": 10, "title": "Research"},
                {"dept": 20, "title": "Sales"},
            ]

            def nested_loop_join(left, right, key):
                # For every row on the left, scan the right table for rows with the same key.
                result = []
                for l in left:
                    for r in right:
                        if l[key] == r[key]:
                            result.append({**l, **r})
                return result

            for row in nested_loop_join(employees, departments, "dept"):
                print(row["name"], "works in", row["title"])
        """,

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.GUIDE,
        section = "Object-oriented",
        title = "How a message finds its method",
        originalTitle = "Message lookup through the superclass chain (Smalltalk, 1972)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example",
        year = 1972,
        summary = "A message is looked up in the receiver's class, then in its superclass, and so on up the chain, which is how inherited methods are found.",
        details = "Each class keeps a table of its own methods and a pointer to its superclass. The example builds three classes and sends them messages, and it reports which class answered each one.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as lookup.py.
            2. Run it: python3 lookup.py
        """,
        example = """
            class Cls:
                def __init__(self, name, superclass=None):
                    self.name = name
                    self.superclass = superclass
                    self.methods = {}

                def lookup(self, selector):
                    cls = self
                    while cls is not None:
                        if selector in cls.methods:
                            return cls.methods[selector], cls.name
                        cls = cls.superclass
                    return None, None

            def send(receiver_class, selector, *args):
                method, found_in = receiver_class.lookup(selector)
                if method is None:
                    return f"{selector} is not understood by {receiver_class.name}"
                return f"{selector} is answered by {found_in}: {method(*args)}"

            Object = Cls("Object")
            Number = Cls("Number", Object)
            Integer = Cls("Integer", Number)

            Object.methods["describe"] = lambda x: "something"
            Number.methods["double"] = lambda x: x * 2
            Integer.methods["isEven"] = lambda x: x % 2 == 0

            print(send(Integer, "describe", 4))
            print(send(Integer, "double", 4))
            print(send(Integer, "isEven", 4))
            print(send(Number, "isEven", 4))
        """,
    ),
)

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Games",
        title = "Mastermind scoring",
        originalTitle = "Mastermind, the code-breaking game (1970)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example; the game was devised in 1970 by Mordecai Meirowitz",
        year = 1970,
        summary = "The scoring rule of Mastermind: a black peg means a right colour in the right place, a white peg a right colour in the wrong place, and the guesser reads only these pegs.",
        details = "Each colour in the code and in the guess is counted once, so repeated colours score correctly. The example plays three guesses against a fixed secret and prints the feedback for each.",
        instructions = """
            1. Save the example as mastermind.py.
            2. Run it: python3 mastermind.py
            3. Change the secret or the guesses to see other feedback.
        """,
        example = """
            COLOURS = "RGBY"   # red, green, blue, yellow

            def feedback(secret, guess):
                black = sum(s == g for s, g in zip(secret, guess))
                # White pegs: right colours in wrong places, counted once for each colour.
                common = sum(min(secret.count(c), guess.count(c)) for c in COLOURS)
                return black, common - black

            secret = "RGBY"
            for guess in ["RRGG", "RGBY", "BBYY"]:
                black, white = feedback(secret, guess)
                print(guess, "black", black, "white", white)
        """,
        rare = true,
    ),

    entry(
        databaseId = 8,
        kind = Kind.PROJECT,
        section = "Games",
        title = "A text adventure in the Zork style",
        originalTitle = "Zork, the text adventure (1977)",
        author = "Written as a teaching example, in the spirit of Zork",
        year = 1977,
        summary = "A small text adventure engine with rooms, exits and items, driven by a list of typed commands, in the spirit of Zork.",
        details = "Zork grew out of Dungeon, a game that MIT students wrote on a PDP-10 in the late 1970s. This engine keeps the same shape: a room describes itself and the things in it, and commands move the player or change the inventory.",
        instructions = """
